Sports.title: How to fix Liverpool's leaky midfield: Snap up a new No 6, the unpalatable Florian Wirtz option, change the roles of Milos Kerkez and Jeremie Frimpong or bring in the academy kid who lit up pre-season
Sports.content:
Liverpool may be on the verge of splashing over £100m on their Mo Salah replacement with the French wonder winger Bradley Barcola on his way through the door, but he won't solve their midfield muddle.

The lack of a No 6, a screen, a player to snuff out danger and do the dirty work was glaringly obvious at Newcastle last week. It is a problem for new boss Andoni Iraola as he tries to get his feet under the table at Anfield.

During game one of the new regime, that Liverpool weakness, that openness in the centre of the park, was laid bare - a continuation of the problem that plagued Arne Slot and ultimately led to him losing his job.

For Newcastle’s first goal, Ryan Gravenberch tried a pass at the edge of the penalty area he was attacking. The Dutchman lost possession and, seconds later, the home team were on the charge. With one pass, they bypassed the midfield and were clean through on Liverpool’s two central defenders, with the full backs busting a gut to recover. Gravenberch and midfield partner Dominik Szoboszlai? Nowhere to be seen.

Later in the game, Gravenberch again lost possession at the edge of the box. This time, there were bodies for Yoane Wissa to get through – which he did too easily – but again, within seconds, Liverpool went from a promising attack to being vulnerable and exposed. Gravenberch, Szoboszlai and fellow midfielder Florian Wirtz? Jogging back.

The response to the game has been loud cries of ‘sign a defensive midfielder’ from fans and pundits including Daniel Sturridge and Jamie Carragher on Sky Sports. It formed the basis of Daily Mail Sport’s match analysis and was the talking point in Iraola’s post-match press briefing.

But is it as simple as that? And what are the other options to fix this midfield mess?

Yoane Wissa makes his way through the wide open spaces in the Liverpool midfield at St James' Park as Ryan Gravenberch gives chase

Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola shows his displeasure during the 2-2 draw

SIGN A NEW No 6

This is not an overreaction based on one game of football. They have needed a No 6 since Fabinho left in 2023.

That summer, they had tried to sign Romeo Lavia, then of Southampton, and Moises Caicedo, then of Brighton. Both moved to Chelsea.

They ended up signing a stop-gap option in Wataru Endo, who arrived from Stuttgart on Deadline Day. The Japan international is the only specialist No 6 at the club but very rarely plays there and is often used as back-up in defence. He is also 33 and not a long-term solution.

Jurgen Klopp cobbled something together with Alexis Mac Allister, Curtis Jones and Trent Alexander-Arnold also playing in the holding role in a season where they made a fair title charge until it fizzled out in mid-March. The next summer, a deal for Real Sociedad and Spain No 6 Martin Zubimendi was advanced and Slot had spoken to the player. He decided to stay put and ultimately ended up at Arsenal a year later.

Slot found a revelation in pre-season as he converted the lesser-seen Gravenberch into a holding midfielder. He and Mac Allister formed a formidable duo on and off the ball as Liverpool romped to the Premier League title.

But it all fell apart from there as neither could sustain that level going into last season. Mac Allister, privately, was taken aback by some of the criticism he received but he seemed to struggle physically for the entire campaign. Jones’s exit this summer further compounds the lack of numbers in the position.

So, will they sign a defensive midfielder this summer? The messaging all window has been clear: wide attack is the priority – not a new No 6.

Lamine Camara at Monaco is a name that has circled in the last 24 hours – with Chelsea also said to be linked – but the word from Liverpool sources remains the same: The Reds are not in the market for midfielders. And that will only change if another midfielder leaves.

Liverpool have been trying to solve their No6 problem for ages and thought they had when they lined up Martin Zubimendi. He opted to stay at Real Sociedad, however, before joining Arsenal

Chelsea's Romeo Lavia is another midfielder Liverpool tried, and failed, to sign

DROP MEGA-MONEY WIRTZ

Given the £116m fee paid for Wirtz last year, this one will not go down well. It cannot be a long-term solution either.

But pushing Szoboszlai higher and having a more solid base achieves two things: it allows the Hungary star to have more of an attacking input and should, in theory, mean a double-pivot to shield the defence.

Iraola wants Wirtz and Alexander Isak to work in tandem up top and he will certainly not write them off after one sub-par game in the hostile environment of Newcastle. There are huge hopes for Wirtz this coming year.

One unpalatable option for Liverpool is to drop their big-money signing Florian Wirtz

TRUST THE IRAOLA PROCESS

It’s not like football fans to overreact, is it?

After five games last season, Liverpool looked likely to storm the league but their form fell off a cliff. Iraola was brought to the club because of his proven track record to improve players. Look at the likes of Antoine Semenyo, Milos Kerkez, Dean Huijsen, Ilya Zabarnyi as examples of those he took from unproven to big-money sales.

Tyler Adams, Eli Junior Kroupi and Rayan may also bag big sums for Bournemouth in the not-too-distant future, though the Cherries are keen to back Marco Rose as much as possible this season and are unlikely to sanction a sale for one of their big attackers.

Iraola insists it is not a personnel problem that plagued his midfield last weekend – and there is no guarantee a new signing would aid that. With time, the Basque will hope to solidify the issue.

Iraola wants his players to be front-footed and believes, over the course of a season, the positives outweigh the negatives.

CHANGE FORMATION COMPLETELY

Here’s a rogue one that has been suggested this week: Iraola should change to a different system altogether.

Jeremie Frimpong and Kerkez have struggled as full backs but what if they were wing backs with less defensive responsibilities? Wirtz’s best form came in a 3-4-2-1 formation under Xabi Alonso at Bayer Leverkusen.

This one is more of a fan hope than a realistic possibility, though. Otherwise their summer-long pursuit of wide forwards would be redundant – and the club also identified Iraola because he played a system similar to that which the squad is accustomed.

Another option is to convert full backs Milos Kerkez (above) and Jeremie Frimpong into wing backs - and bolster the middle of midfield with a 3-4-2-1 formation

GIVE THE KIDS A GO

Trusting youth players is in Iraola's identity. At his boyhood team Athletic Club, there is a long-standing policy to only have Basque players in the squad. They cannot go out and spend mega-money on a transfer target, but instead have to work with what they already have at their disposal.

Keeping this in mind, 19-year-old midfielder Trey Nyoni will be given chances to impress. The young Englishman played just 21 minutes in the Premier League last term but was a star of pre-season and deserves more chances in the coming weeks.

The 19-year-old midfielder Trey Nyoni impressed during pre-season for Liverpool

He is small in stature but plays with a maturity beyond his years. Daily Mail Sport has been present for many of his youth-team appearances where he showed he is an elegant midfielder who always demands possession and can dictate play from deep.

Nyoni can certainly push for minutes this term.

Another back-up option is academy graduate James McConnell. He spent the first half of last season at Ajax and the second half on the treatment table. But he is fit now and has been asked to stick around. He had agreed a loan move to Preston North End but that has been put on the back-burner for now at least.

Sports.title: 'Welsh rugby has two choices - cut one of its clubs or face cataclysmic collapse. We must be brave and do the right thing': Wales rugby chief ABI TIERNEY hits back at 'toxic' abuse and insists one region must go to save the national sport
Sports.content:
'Welsh rugby has two choices - cut one of its clubs or face cataclysmic collapse. We must be brave and do the right thing': Wales rugby chief ABI TIERNEY hits back at 'toxic' abuse and insists one region must go to save the national sport

Unlock more of the best of our rugby coverage with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

Welsh Rugby Union chief executive Abi Tierney has slammed the ‘toxic tactics’ of her critics, insisting it will be ‘cataclysmic’ for Wales if the country doesn’t follow through on the plan to cut one of its four men’s domestic teams.

In July, the WRU reiterated its proposal to move to three sides from 2028, with the Newport-based Dragons and capital side Cardiff – who are owned by the governing body – to be handed licenses to continue. That left the Ospreys and Scarlets to compete for the one remaining spot in west Wales.

The WRU’s move has come in response to more than three years of poor rugby performance and significant monetary challenges. But the proposal has been met with strong criticism.

Hayley Parsons, the founder of GoCompare and a former Cardiff board member, has led calls for Tierney and the entire WRU executive board to resign with dual code Welsh rugby legend Jonathan Davies and others backing her up.

Breaking her silence in her first interview in months, Tierney has hit back at the self-appointed ‘coalition of the willing’ and doubled down on the WRU’s aims.

‘It's really hard,' she tells Daily Mail Sport. 'But I'm not doing this to be popular. I'm doing it because based on all the evidence and analysis, I genuinely believe this is the best thing for Welsh rugby.

WRU Chief Executive Abi Tierney has hit back at her critics' 'toxic tactics'

In 2019, Wales were Six Nations Grand Slam champions, World Cup semi-finalists and briefly, World Rugby’s No1-ranked side

'I love Welsh rugby and I want to see it survive. I'm really worried several previous regimes have had reports done which have all said we need to do this, but when it’s got nasty, people have backed away from making that decision. That’s why we are where we are. That's why we're struggling financially. That's why we're struggling with our performance on the pitch.

'There are two choices – we either continue to struggle, we'll see further decline and we could see Wales drop out of the world’s top 12. With promotion and relegation potentially coming into the Nations Championship in 2031, that becomes cataclysmic for us as a nation. The national team funds the rest of the game, so that would have a big impact.

'The other choice is the plan to go from four to three and none of that has changed.

‘I look myself in the mirror every day and ask myself if is this the right thing for Welsh rugby. Can somebody show me another credible plan that's out there? I haven't seen anybody else produce one, other than a big document produced by ChatGPT.’

Addressing Parsons and Co directly, Tierney continues: ‘It's interesting that that same small group of people have also been involved in previous situations. There's been a long-standing issue there with the WRU. If I step down, I'll be OK.

'But whoever comes into this role, they’ll be faced with the same decision in another year or two, if not sooner. It’s about being brave to do the right thing.

'The style of the campaign really worries me. The personal attacks are unjustified and not OK. The decision has been made and we’ve got a plan to get there. They’re trying to get that decision overturned by saying it isn’t justified.

'These are toxic tactics to stop a decision that our board has not taken lightly. If I left now and then looked back and Welsh rugby has declined, I would carry that really heavily for the rest of my life and think that we should have stuck at that.’

Wales are now ranked 10th in the world and Tierney fears they could drop out of the top 12

Wales were wooden spoon 'winners' at this year's Six Nations, their sole win coming against Italy

In 2019, Wales were Six Nations Grand Slam champions, World Cup semi-finalists and briefly, World Rugby’s No1-ranked side. But since then, the country’s national game has struggled badly both on and off the field and Wales are now ranked tenth in the world.

Tierney’s detractors say they want to see further evidence to back-up the three-team proposal. The WRU plans on releasing more, independently assessed data in the coming months. How it will move to three sides remains unclear. The Ospreys and Scarlets – bitter rivals – have said they have no plans to merge.

‘The criticism I hear is it's taking too long,’ Tierney adds. ‘The counter argument to that is this is people's livelihoods. Putting stability in the system, doing it right, and having consideration for the impacts it has is also really important.’

Tierney has been director general of the passport office working on significant British government and international political projects including immigration proposals surrounding the wars in Ukraine and Afghanistan. Tierney has also undergone treatment for cancer while heading up the WRU but she admits the WRU challenge is enormous.

‘This is the hardest job I've ever done,' she says. 'The politics, passion and how much people care make it the best job in the world. It also makes it the hardest job in the world.’

Asked if she thought the WRU had lost the belief and trust of the Welsh rugby public amid the ongoing political wranglings, Tierney defends the level of rugby expertise on her board.

‘That trust is being eroded every single day by those small minority of very loud critics,’ she counters. ‘That's what's eroding our ability to sell tickets and to secure sponsorship because it's damaging the brand so much. It's difficult. They're part of the cause and effect because they're saying things that are unjustified and aren't true.’

Ospreys supporters protest against the WRU and the plan to reduce the number of Welsh clubs from four to three

Wales fans are also up in arms about the performances of their national team

Welsh rugby remains at a crucial juncture. A new full-time chair is planned to be in place by November following the departure of Richard Collier-Keywood and a whole host of other work remains ongoing in the background, chiefly around improving the country’s academy structures.

It is likely that the governing body’s next set of financial results will sharpen the focus as to why moving to three teams is required. The big question is how the WRU will get there.

‘Our turnover varies but it’s just over £100million. Once we've covered costs, we’re left with £20million to invest in the professional game,’ Tierney says. ‘That would have four teams on about £5million each with costs going up and commercial deals and media deals going down. If you compare that to teams in PREM Rugby and others in the United Rugby Championship, we’d be way behind them. We’ll see a continuing decline if we have clubs funded at that level.’

Asked what her message is to the Welsh rugby public, Tierney responds: ‘Try to put the noise to one side and come out and support our teams in the next few months. I wouldn't stay if I didn't think we could thrive again.'

Sports.title: RIATH AL-SAMARRAI: Aston Villa and Unai Emery want you to believe that Ollie Watkins is to blame for the most depressing transfer of the summer. Here's why they're wrong - and how years of chaotic spending pushed him out
Sports.content:
There were two phrases that Paul Tisdale often repeated to a younger version of Ollie Watkins. This is going back a few years, to a period between 2016 and 2017, when they were together at Exeter City and long before the melodrama of Watkins’ decision to cash out on Aston Villa for Saudi Arabia.

The key point is that Watkins was once one of those raw, emerging talents who struggled to make the step up from the academy at a League Two club. He had pace to burn, his attitude was spotless, but the rest was a bit of a jumble – systems and structured roles were tougher for him to grasp. As the son of a woman who sang soul ballads for a living, Watkins was at his best when feeling the music. In short, he needed a manager with patience and, in Tisdale, he had one.

Gradually, through many rough patches and many conversations, everything began to make more sense. And after making sense, it made money – so much money was raised from Watkins’ sale to Brentford, and again with the sell-on cash when he joined Villa, that Exeter upgraded from wooden buildings to concrete at their training ground.

I remember speaking about some of this with Tisdale a couple of years ago, when that same lad was selected by Gareth Southgate to play for England at Euro 2024, and went on to score the last-minute winner in the semi-final. Tisdale’s pride was fluorescent, but he also discussed the ‘anxieties’ and ‘difficulties’ Watkins encountered along the way, and the two points he kept drumming into his player: ‘Less is more’ and ‘make yourself selectable’.

Those instructions have returned to mind in the past fortnight, because Watkins wasn’t especially selectable for Villa at the start of the season. The fact that no one at the club has challenged the assumption he went on strike to force his proposed £52million move to Al Hilal seems quite revealing. For that matter, no one from Watkins’ management has disputed it either.

Less is more? In our assessments of players who sell out for Saudi Arabia, I tend to see it as accepting more money for less relevance. At 30 years old, fresh off a World Cup, Watkins making that journey feels like a waste; it is his decision to make and our prerogative to be disappointed. Soulless? A little of that, too.

Ollie Watkins is heading for the exit at Aston Villa after making himself unavailable for selection last weekend

Watkins was once one of those raw, emerging talents who struggled to make the step up from the academy at a League Two club - in his case at Exeter City

Personally, I see this move as the most depressing of the window, and for a variety of reasons that veer from Saudi sportswashing to the apparent death of ambition in an elite player.

But Watkins isn’t a bad sort – too many well-placed sources say the exact opposite. He is a good guy, a hard worker, and unfussed by the showy options of a footballer’s life. From Exeter to Villa, he has been a grafter; one who is easy to like and admire.

I have often thought the same about Villa as a club. But I would also suggest this window says more about them than Watkins.

It says something about a spending policy in recent seasons that allowed a club to thrive, but also contributed heavily to the systematic dismantling of an excellent squad, in part by choice and in part by consequence of their actions.

We should be clear on two things at this point – Villa did not want Watkins to go, felt no imperative to sell him, and his mind has been on Saudi possibilities for the better part of 18 months. But let’s talk about push factors. If you’re sat in that Villa dressing room, what does it tell Watkins when the likes of Morgan Rogers, Ezri Konsa, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne have all gone for varying reasons in the same window?

They were four of the 11 who started against Freiburg in the Europa League final three months ago. Adding the imminent departures of Emiliano Martinez and Watkins, and the spine has been torn out. For all the money spent on replacements, none of it fosters the feeling of an evolving project so much as the start of a substantial rebuild. And rebuilds take time that a 30-year-old would be less inclined to give.

To study Villa’s chaotic window is to better understand a club that has needed to sell in order to buy under the constraints of spending rules imposed by the Premier League and UEFA. We might find those rules anti-competitive and weighted in favour of the status quo – hard to dispute any of that – but we cannot deny their existence. The problem there is that Villa lived fast and loose for an awfully long time. That was a choice and increasingly across the past two years the chickens have come home to roost.

I remember a conversation with a key figure at a Premier League club early last year, when we were discussing Tottenham’s frugality on the subject of wage expenditure. He agreed that Spurs lacked ambition, but then pointed to the other, more dangerous extreme – Villa. The prognosis was stark, because their excellent progress under Unai Emery had also moved them closer to a financial cliff edge.

Six of the 11 who started against Freiburg in the Europa League final three months ago will be gone before long

Hard as it is to knock Emery, a superb coach who has done great work at Villa, we should acknowledge that he is no better than average as an operator in the transfer market

The Deloitte Football Money League from 2025 told of a club that had the 18th biggest revenues in world football but had spent 94 per cent of their turnover on wages in two of the previous three seasons. Those absurd levels fell to 72 per cent in the 2026 report, but for context, Liverpool were at 60 per cent, Manchester City 57 per cent, Manchester United 51 per cent and Arsenal 49 per cent. Only Chelsea matched Villa’s level.

Is it the cost of keeping up? Yes. Is it also a case of pride before a fall? It looks that way.

Hard as it is to knock Emery, a superb coach who has done great work at Villa, we should acknowledge that he is no better than average as an operator in the transfer market. He has more say than all other Premier League managers in those matters, with the exception of Mikel Arteta, and his fingerprints exist on the deals that have left Villa churning through masses of playing staff.

On balance, it was probably worth it – a European trophy and top-four finishes at home are a stunning return. Watkins, for one, owes him a lot. But we shouldn’t sugarcoat that Villa’s summer of chaos is about far more than a striker lining his own pockets.

Sports.title: How Arsenal overhauled their academy to produce a new wave of world-class Hale End talent: The two experts leading aggressive recruitment, the Folarin Balogun template and fighting back when rivals poach their top young stars
Sports.content:
It’s all change in the Arsenal academy after a period of flux.

Per Mertesacker left the top job over the summer after eight years to become the German FA's managing director, a role he starts in January. Following the former Arsenal captain out of the door was Under 21s head coach Max Porter, who was appointed Stoke City assistant manager.

That left a void in the heart of Hale End, at a time when academy production lines are more important than ever in a world of pure profit and homegrown talent.

But now, with a new hierarchy in place headed up by Mertesacker's replacement Pascal de Maesschalck, the Gunners are looking to reassert their status as an academy goldmine.

Hale End’s proud history stands strong, having produced the likes of Tony Adams, Ashley Cole and Jack Wilshere over the years.

The most recent gems, Ethan Nwaneri, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Max Dowman, have all shone in Mikel Arteta's first team, where they join the jewel in Hale End's crown, Bukayo Saka.

New Arsenal academy director Pascal De Maesschalck with academy operations manager Lee Herron

Arsenal are looking for the next gem off their production line, which has recently produced Max Dowman, Ethan Nwaneri and Myles Lewis-Skelly

But the output masked problems within. The Under 21s won just eight of their 21 matches last season in the Premier League 2 competition, including a 7-0 thrashing at the hands of Liverpool in January.

When the Under 19s beat Bayern Munich 4-2 in the UEFA Youth League in November 2025 – helped by Dowman dropping back down to that level and scoring twice after already making a handful of first-team appearances – it snapped a 16-game winless streak across the Under 18s, 19s and 21s.

And while the academy teams foundered with uncertainty over who would replace Mertesacker, rivals took advantage.

First, Manchester City hijacked a move for promising Leicester City winger Jeremy Monga, whom Arsenal had been close to signing. Then, Tottenham beat the Gunners to West Ham’s Under 15s midfield star Isaac Allen. Talented youngsters such as Kyran Thompson and Mishel Nduka chose to continue their careers elsewhere, at Newcastle United and Manchester City respectively.

But in recent weeks, the balance has been wrestled back under new academy director De Maesschalck, the 52-year-old Belgian who was previously technical director at Chelsea's sister club Strasbourg, following ten years as Club Brugge academy head and three years leading Monaco's youth development.

Each of those clubs is renowned across the continent for producing world-class talents. At Brugge he became highly regarded for making academy players ready for the first team, while at Monaco he brought through golden boys such as Eliesse Ben Seghir, Maghnes Akliouche and Soungoutou Magassa, who all became first-team stars before earning the club sizeable sums when joining Bayer Leverkusen, Paris Saint-Germain and West Ham respectively.

And it’s understood that he’s been tasked at Arsenal to make the academy more aggressive in recruitment and recoup more money in player sales.

That drive is already in effect. Arsenal have previously brought in players under 18 from Scotland and Ireland, like Callan Hamill, Evan Mooney and Ceadach O’Neill.

Arsenal lost two of their top talents this summer in Mishel Nduka (left, to Manchester City) and Kyran Thompson (right, to Newcastle United)

Defender Elijah Upson, 18, the son of ex-Arsenal centre back Matt, joined from Spurs

And of late, there’s been a push to raid other clubs across England for their best talent. Arsenal sporting director Andrea Berta hinted towards this in his quotes around the appointment, praising De Maesschalck's knack for ‘identifying the best emerging talent to join Arsenal on a journey towards professional football’.

Defender Elijah Upson, 18, the son of ex-Arsenal centre-back Matt, joined from Spurs. Midfielder Axel Donczew, 16, has signed from Cardiff City, while Crystal Palace’s Mylo Bernard, 16, has also joined, and Arsenal are also set to beat multiple clubs to the signature of highly rated Blackburn Rovers striker Igor Tyjon, 18.

And then on the selling front, there’s been a move under Pascal to have produce more cases like Mika Biereth and Folarin Balogun who, while not quite good enough for an Arsenal team pushing to be the best in Europe, help out on the financial side.

London-born Denmark striker Biereth was snapped up from Fulham's academy in 20212 and sold to Sturm Graz for £4million three years later. The Austrian side then sold Biereth to Monaco in January 2025 for £12.8million, earning Arsenal more money as a result of their 30 per cent sell-on clause.

Balogun, meanwhile, was sold to Monaco for £34.3million in August 2023 after not quite making it in Arteta's first team. After a breakout World Cup with the US national team, he has been linked to the likes of Tottenham, and has a 17.5 per cent sell-on clause. Arsenal want more of this to continue during De Maesschalck's reign.

There’s been change in the coaching setup, too. David Horseman has stepped up from his roles as Under 19s manager and Under 21s assistant to replace Porter as Under 21s head coach, in an appointment overseen by Arteta, assistant manager Albert Stuivenberg and De Maesschalck.

It’s understood they liked Horseman's balance of having extensive academy experience, as well as both managing and coaching in the Football League, specialising in player development.

Just two years younger than Arteta, Horseman has already spent nearly 15 years working in professional academies. He started at Bristol City, spending eight years across different positions including Under 18 manager, head of academy coaching and academy manager.

‹ Slide me › Arsenal poached Mika Biereth from Fulham's academy in 2021 and three years later without making a first-team appearance, he was shipped off to Sturm Graz and then Monaco

‹ Slide me › Folarin Balogun couldn't quite make the grade at Arsenal but after a breakout World Cup, his 17.5 per cent sell-on fee in the £34.3m deal that took him to Monaco could pay dividends

Under 21s head coach David Horseman leads his team through pre-season training

His forays into senior management and coaching have been more challenging. In July 2023, Horseman was appointed head coach of Forest Green Rovers but lasted just six months, winning only two of his first seven matches. He returned to Bristol City as caretaker manager alongside Lee Cattermole after Matt Taylor was sacked in December 2024, but the team were relegated at the end of the season and Horseman left.

But it’s academy expertise which the Gunners are tapping into. Before joining Arsenal in September, he had a short spell at Manchester United as a professional development phase coach. That gave him an insight into how another enormous academy operates from the inside.

For Arsenal, the overall aim is clear: produce more first-team players by raiding their English rivals, while ensuring those who don’t make the first-team grade are of the quality to be sold for worthwhile sums.

After a period of uncertainty, the academy is entering a new era under De Maesschalck with the Gunners determined to stand above the rest.

Sports.title: Moses Itauma and Filip Hrgovic weigh-in descends into chaos as British star PUSHES rival off stage - before being SLAPPED
Sports.content:
See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Moses Itauma and Filip Hrgovic had to be pulled apart by security after their heavyweight weigh-in descended into chaos when Hrgovic was pushed off the stage before slapping his British rival.

The two heavyweights exchanged heated words during their face-off before lining up for one final set of photographs.

But when Hrgovic stepped in front of Itauma, the Brit shoved him forward, sending his opponent tumbling off the stage.

A furious Hrgovic immediately climbed back up and slapped Itauma, who then went berserk as both men attempted to fight before security rushed in to drag them apart.

The extraordinary scenes came just 24 hours before Itauma's first shot at becoming heavyweight world champion.

It was a notable change from the 21-year-old, who has remained largely calm throughout the build-up despite Hrgovic's repeated attempts to get under his skin.

Moses Itauma and Filip Hrgovic had to be pulled apart by security after their heavyweight weigh-in descended into chaos

Itauma started the chaos when he pushed Hrgovic off stage before his rival slapped him

Itauma had previously dismissed his rival's insults as 'schoolground banter', while Hrgovic has tried to provoke him at almost every opportunity during fight week.

The British heavyweight had even told his manager not to nibble at Hrgovic during Thursday's press conference, seemingly determined not to be drawn into any of the mind games.

But after keeping his composure throughout the week, it was Itauma himself who finally snapped at the weigh-in.

And while it offered a side to the unbeaten heavyweight that few have seen before, those watching appeared to love it.

Hrgovic was still furious when he spoke after the confrontation and vowed to 'smash' Itauma when the pair meet in the ring tomorrow night.

Itauma, meanwhile, admitted that he had been unable to resist the temptation to react.

'I had a scratch to itch and I had to do that today,' he said.

Sports.title: Sky Sports forced to apologise for Rayan Cherki's x-rated interview after he called his performance 's***' - despite scoring TWICE - as Erling Haaland smirks alongside him following Man City's win at Palace
Sports.content:
Rayan Cherki left fans confused and in stitches after he described his match-winning display in Man City's victory over Crystal Palace as 's***'.

Cherki starred at Selhurst Park by scoring twice in the second half, with Erling Haaland also adding a brace in the 4-1 victory.

The result means Enzo Maresca has two Premier League wins from two matches since replacing Pep Guardiola after his side overcame some testing moments in the first half against the Eagles.

Cherki was awarded the Player of the Match award but his post-match interview with Sky Sports certainly got supporters talking, with the broadcaster forced to apologise after he swore.

'My performance is so-so,' he said. 'In the first half, we didn't find the space, and I played so s***.

'When I see Enzo (Maresca) wants to change (substitute) me, I don’t like that, and I need to show them I want to play, I want to score, I want to give an assist to Erling.

Sky Sports were forced to apologise after Man City star Rayan Cherki said he 'played s***'

Cherki's comments came despite him scoring twice in City's 4-1 victory over Crystal Palace

'Because today I didn't give a lot of balls for him so next time I want to give him a lot of balls.'

Cherki's first goal saw him poke home after he demonstrated superb skill and quick feet to take the ball past several Palace defenders, before his second was a long range strike that took a slight deflection.

And when pressed for thoughts on his first strike, Cherki showed his humility and instead outlined his desire for the club to have a memorable campaign.

He added: 'I'm very happy for the win, see you next week. Pep [Guardiola] was a big story, we will start another story. We want to prove it and we are here for that.'

Enzo Maresca disagreed with Cherki's assessment of his display, although admitted he perhaps wasn't playing at his peak in the first period.

'He’s happy,' the City boss said of Cherki after the game. 'His performance was very good, not because of the two goals but how he worked off the ball.

'He has to press. He was in charge of Wharton when Palace had the ball. His game was a complete game on and off the ball.

'He loves football. So it is much more easy to work with him. Then he is Rayan. We know how good he is, the quality he has. In this moment, he is helping the team with his assists and goals and there is no doubt he will help the team in the future.

'He was probably not playing at his level in the first half but overall I was happy with his performance off the ball. In the second half, he scored twice and he is much more happy.'

Haaland, who smirked as Cherki swore on TV, joined the plaudits for the attacking midfielder and added: 'It's been a short pre-season. Rayan [Cherki], five weeks ago was at the World Cup. Game by game, we'll be back, we just need a few games.

'We played well, it's a new manager but we've been playing together, with the addition of a few new players, for a long time.'

'We know what to do, and we just need to trust Enzo. This is the right step in the right direction for everyone.'

On Cherki's first goal, midfielder Elliot Anderson said: 'I'm just sat back watching. I see this every day since I've joined, him, Phil (Foden)... they've got so much talent. It's no surprise, to be honest. The talent they have is scary.'

City made it two Premier League wins from two games under Enzo Maresca with the victory

Meanwhile, Jamie Redknapp was similarly full of praise for Cherki following the game, with the Sky Sports pundit labelling the Frenchman a 'genius'.

'After Rayan Cherki painted a masterpiece - an incredible goal - City started to play and got a real hold on it,' he said. 'Cherki felt like the difference because his two goals came at such an important time.

'He just had such an amazing effect on the game and it was absolutely wonderful to see him. He is a genius, the things he can do with a football are absolute genius.'

City, who are still hoping to add more players before the transfer window closes on Tuesday, return to action next Saturday when they entertain Coventry City.

Sports.title: Atletico tell Julian Alvarez to join Arsenal or stay at the club, Aston Villa confirm £65m Nicolas Jackson signing and Spanish club joins race for Man United star Joshua Zirkzee: WINDOW WATCH
Sports.content:
It's that time of the year again – the transfer window is now open until September 1 and it's sure to be a busy period as clubs look to make big signings ahead of the new season.

Here are today's latest developments from Simon Jones and the Daily Mail Sport team...

Atletico set Alvarez deadline amid Arsenal interest

Atletico Madrid have given Julian Alvarez until Sunday to make a decision over his future.

The Spanish side have told the ex-Man City star to move to Arsenal or stay at the club.

Alvarez is missed Atletico Madrid training for a third day running on Friday, but later trained alone.

Alvarez has been absent citing illness since Atletico told the Argentina striker they would not sell him to Barcelona.

Club CEO Gil Marin told Spanish media: ‘I’ve been in the football world for more than 30 years. My word is one of the few things I have. As long as I am CEO, Julián Alvarez will NOT be transferred to FC Barcelona. That is absolutely certain.’

Arsenal are willing to pay up to £128m for Alvarez if he opts to join them now.

With Atletico refusing to sell him to LaLiga rivals Barcelona, Arsenal are viewed as the only destination for Alvarez if he wants to leave Atletico.

Julian Alvarez missed training for the third day in a row as he pushed to leave Atletico Madrid

Hutchinson set for Milan switch

Nottingham Forest will listen to offers for Omari Hutchinson with AC Milan considering a loan offer for the winger.

Hutchinson became Forest’s record signing a year ago when he joined from Ipswich for nearly £40million but boss Oliver Glasner does not see the 22-year-old as a regular starter.

Milan have an interest in Hutchinson, who would be open to the move, but are unlikely to offer a permanent deal.

A loan with an obligation to buy is the likeliest offer at this stage.

TOM COLLOMOSSE

Emotional Emery reveals Watkins goodbye - as Jackson is confirmed

Unai Emery revealed Ollie Watkins impending move to Al Hilal had reduced him to tears as he leapt to the defence of the under-fire forward.

Watkins infuriated Aston Villa fans when he did not appear in last weekend’s 4-0 defeat at Brighton, even though he was the club’s only fit centre-forward.

At the time, Emery did nothing to protect Watkins when asked about his absence. But on Friday he delivered a lavish tribute to the England man and said the £50m fee for the 30-year-old was too good to turn down, while confirming Nicolas Jackson would replace him.

Emery said: ‘I told him goodbye with a huge hug and a few tears. After the Brighton game he was sorry and told us he made a mistake, that he was wrong.

‘We accepted it and so did the players. He was always very committed and behaved well with us and with me. He’s a fantastic guy, even more than he is a player. Now it’s a new chapter here with Nicolas Jackson and we wish Ollie all the best in Saudi Arabia.

Reunited. This time in claret & blue.



Aston Villa is delighted to announce the signing of Nicolas Jackson from Chelsea 🇸🇳 pic.twitter.com/s2P8j6uKJa — Aston Villa (@AstonVilla) August 28, 2026

‘Ollie had fantastic years here always scoring and playing even when he was injured. Last week I was a little disappointed but we spoke about it. One mistake does not cancel all the good things he did here for the supporters.

‘It’s crazy that for a 30-year-old we can have £50m.’

Nicolas Jackson has joined for £65m from Chelsea having taking his formative steps in the professional game under Emery at Villarreal.

Emi Martinez was also on the brink of sealing a move to Chelsea – the fourth transfer deal between these clubs in less than six weeks.

TOM COLLOMOSSE

Atletico monitoring Zirkzee

Manchester United striker Joshua Zirkzee is on Atletico Madrid’s radar as they anticipate a late bid from Arsenal for Julian Alvarez.

Zirkzee has an offer from Fiorentina, while Juventus and Napoli are interested and some Premier League clubs are also weighing up late offers.

SIMON JONES

City and Spurs battle for Gakpo

Manchester City continue to rival Tottenham for Liverpool winger Cody Gakpo.

Liverpool have maintained they must have two more forward players in place before they contemplate selling the Netherlands international and even then it would have to be a substantial fee.

Liverpool have yet to receive an official approach from either club.

City are also pushing to sign Enzo Fernandez from Chelsea. Despite links with Liverpool’s Alexis Mac Allister as a back-up option, no contact has been made.

City are also pursuing parallel negotiations for Everton winger Iliman Ndiaye who has three years on contract and would cost around £80million.

SIMON JONES

Liverpool have yet to receive an official approach from any club for Cody Gakpo despite links

Ward-Prowse is a Saint... again!

Southampton have confirmed the signing of James Ward-Prowse from West Ham for a fee understood to be £800,000.

Ward-Prowse rejoins the Saints on a two-year deal, having previously made 410 appearances for the club.

Ward-Prowse joined West Ham in a £30m deal in 2023, and also spent time on loan at Nottingham Forest. However, he fell out of favour with boss Nuno Espirito Santo.

'It feels a bit surreal. The last couple of days have been pretty intense, but I’m delighted to be back, and to be wearing the red and white again is truly special,' Ward-Prowse said.

SIMON JONES

Lights, Camara, action for Chelsea as they brace for Enzo bid

Chelsea are weighing up a move for Monaco midfielder Lamine Camara as they anticipate Manchester City's bid for Enzo Fernandez.

Chelsea are considering bringing in two midfielders with City expected to pay over £120m for Fernandez.

Talks were held between the clubs yesterday, as reported by Daily Mail Sport, over Camara who also attracted a £40m offer from Crystal Palace this summer and various enquiries.

Monaco are interested in Tottenham's Pape Matar Sarr on loan but face competition from Nottingham Forest.

SIMON JONES

Spurs join race for Ndiaye

Tottenham have joined Manchester City by showing interest in Iliman Ndiaye of Everton.

Both Spurs and City are in for Liverpool's Cody Gakpo also, should the Anfield club agree to sell.

Ndiaye has three years left on contract and is valued around £80m.

Spurs want to add more quality to their new-look attack before the deadline.

Gakpo has been their priority but City's presence means they will need alternative options also.

SIMON JONES

Tottenham Hotspur are showing an interest in Everton's star man Illiman Ndiaye

Collyer collared by Baggies

West Brom have agreed a £3million deal for Manchester United midfielder Toby Collyer.

The total package is potentially worth up to £7.6m for the 22-year-old.

United have also inserted a 40 per cent sell-on clause for any future sale.

SIMON JONES

Overy travelling to Sydney

Manchester United youngster James Overy will fly to Australia tonight as he closes in on a permanent switch to Sydney FC.

The 18-year-old, who moved to United’s academy set-up in 2024, has featured across Under-18s and Under-21s but did not break through to the first team.

Daily Mail Sport understands that he is in line to get a three-year deal with Sydney FC, who are not paying a fee. Overy will complete his move following a medical on Monday.

EXCLUSIVE BY NATHAN SALT

Valencia interested in Liverpool's Elliott

Liverpool winger Harvey Elliott is being targeted by Spanish side Valencia.

The 23-year-old has interest from a number of clubs with Lazio and Napoli among them but Valencia are hopeful they can tempt the England U21 international to link up with coach Carlos Corberan, the former West Brom boss.

Liverpool have still to receive an official approach but are aware of the interest.

Elliott had a tough time at Aston Villa last season where he was on loan with an obligation to buy at £35m following 10 games.

Clubs are exploring another loan.

SIMON JONES

Valencia are on of a number of clubs interested in Liverpool midfielder Harvey Elliott

Bolton confirm signing of Bazunu

Bolton have confirmed the signing of goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu from Southampton. Bazunu has signed a three-year deal at the club.

The 24-year-old said: 'It's a club with massive history. I see it as a place where I can come and progress my personal career, while helping the team with their ambitions of getting back to where they belong.'

SIMON JONES

Sports.title: Roberto De Zerbi holds transfer summit with Tottenham owners after £400m spend - as Spurs boss reveals aims for final days of the window
Sports.content:
Roberto De Zerbi is planning to include Dejan Kulusevski in his Premier League squad as the Tottenham winger closes in on a return to full fitness.

Kulusevski, 26, has been out for more than 15 months after suffering a serious knee injury in May 2025.

His recovery has been littered with complications and setbacks and the disappointment of missing the World Cup, but the Swede finally seems to be making steady progress.

'I hope and I will be very happy to see Kulusevski inside [the squad],' said De Zerbi. 'I want to put Kulusevski in the list because he is working very well, very hard. He's a good guy and he's a different player.

'If he feels good like now, he's improving day by day, it's great watching him. He deserves it because he has suffered too much for his career for his age. I'm not speaking of him as a player but as a human. He deserves to be inside the list.'

Kulusevski's inclusion in the 25-man list to be confirmed after Tuesday's transfer deadline would restrict De Zerbi in other areas with a limit of 17 overseas senior players.

Roberto De Zerbi revealed he is set to include Dejan Kulusevski in his Premier League squad

De Zerbi also shed light on a transfer summit he held with the club's hierarchy earlier this week

Wilson Odobert and Xavi Simons, also recovering from serious knee injuries, are unlikely to be named in the squad.

'Odobert is injured for a long time,' said De Zerbi. 'Before February, March, he is not available. Xavi Simons before March, April, he's not ready.'

Spurs have signed eight players this summer and are still searching for a left winger before the deadline, with Cody Gakpo of Liverpool a top target.

Pape Matar Sarr is most likely to leave as things stand although, after completing the signing of Omar Marmoush, Spurs would entertain interest in Richarlison, who has one year remaining on his contract plus a one-year option.

Meanwhile, De Zerbi picked up the bill as Tottenham's powerbrokers met for dinner to plot their final moves of the summer transfer market.

The Spurs boss and his assistant Enrico Venturelli were joined by members of the ruling Lewis family, chief executive Vinai Venkatesham and sporting director Johan Lange at an Italian restaurant in London on Thursday.

They have invested close to £400million in new players since flirting with relegation last season and will not rule out more business, with Cody Gakpo of Liverpool a top target as they try to reinforce on the left wing.

'I think we can do one player more and in one specific position,' said De Zerbi, ahead of the first home game of the Premier League season against Newcastle. 'We went for dinner and we are all on the same page. There is a very good connection.

'I am not pushing. It's the first time I didn't push to complete the squad. I didn't push. They pushed to build it with the top players. It's not my business the transfer market. I didn't expect one transfer window like we have done.'

Spurs have signed eight new players and recouped almost £150m with sales, a figure which can increase with bonus add-ons.

It is the first summer transfer window since Daniel Levy was ousted as chairman. Transfer activity was led by Lange, Venkatesham and director of football operations Rafi Moersen. Nick Beucher, son-in-law of Vivienne Lewis, has become increasingly influential since the power shift, almost a year ago.

They have twice broken the club's transfer record to sign Mateus Fernandes from West Ham for £85m and Sandro Tonali from Newcastle for £100m.

'Johan was brilliant in terms of ideas to make solutions,' said De Zerbi. 'Vinai, when we closed the Tonali deal, made a video call to me when I was on holiday and he had a big smile, very happy.

'We went for dinner before the Chelsea game last season with Vinai and Johan, and it's a part of our job to organise and make the last plans in the last days of the transfer market, to speak about the condition of the players and the transfers we can do in the next three or four days. There is seriously a great relationship with all of them.'

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan

Semi-final: Wales vs Bosnia and Herzegovina
