World.title: García Luna corruption case wins $5.8M for Guerrero schools: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

💰 García Luna case yields $5.8M for Guerrero schools : UIF chief Omar Reyes Colmenares said Mexico received US $5.8 million this week from its civil suit victory over the Weinberg family — ex-Security Minister García Luna’s alleged frontmen — in a Miami-Dade court. Sheinbaum said the funds will go to schools in Guerrero’s disadvantaged Montaña region.

: UIF chief Omar Reyes Colmenares said Mexico received US $5.8 million this week from its civil suit victory over the Weinberg family — ex-Security Minister García Luna’s alleged frontmen — in a Miami-Dade court. Sheinbaum said the funds will go to schools in Guerrero’s disadvantaged Montaña region. 🇲🇽 Mexico is ‘Doing very well,’ Sheinbaum says ahead of second report: Sheinbaum declared Mexico is “doing very well” almost two years into her six-year term. Her positive assessment of the current state of affairs came ahead of the presentation of her second annual government report next Tuesday.

Sheinbaum declared Mexico is “doing very well” almost two years into her six-year term. Her positive assessment of the current state of affairs came ahead of the presentation of her second annual government report next Tuesday. 🚣 Gold for rower Kenia Lechuga: Sheinbaum congratulated Nuevo León native Kenia Lechuga on her gold medal in the women’s lightweight sculls at the 2026 World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam, saying that as a former rower herself she felt “special affection” for the win. Mexican rowers also won gold in the women’s lightweight double sculls and bronze in the men’s lightweight sculls.

Why today’s mañanera matters

Today’s mañanera was significant as the federal government was able to demonstrate that its successful civil suit against former Security Minister Genaro García Luna — now imprisoned in the United States — is reaping monetary rewards.

Also of note was President Claudia Sheinbaum’s positive assessment of the current state of affairs in Mexico almost two years into her six-year term. Her favorable evaluation of the prevailing situation came four days before she is scheduled to present her second annual government report (segundo informe de gobierno) in a speech in Mexico City.

Sheinbaum: US $5.8 million recovered in García Luna case to go to schools in Guerrero

Omar Reyes Colmenares, head of the federal government’s Financial Intelligence Unit (UIF), told reporters that on Tuesday of this week, Mexico received US $5.8 million in funds recovered in the case involving García Luna, who in 2024 was sentenced to 38 years in prison in the United States after he was found guilty of collusion with the Sinaloa Cartel.

He noted that the UIF filed a civil suit in Florida aimed at recovering public money that was diverted out of Mexico in a corruption scheme involving García Luna and members of the Weinberg family. Members of the Weinberg family have been identified as frontmen for García Luna, who served as security minister during the 2006-12 government led by former President Felipe Calderón.

Reyes highlighted that a court in Miami handed down a ruling in May in favor of the Mexican state and against the Weinberg family. As part of the ruling, Judge Lisa Walsh in Miami-Dade County ordered members of the Weinberg family and related companies to pay US $578.5 million in damages to the Mexican state for losses incurred as a result of their involvement in corruption schemes.

“As a result of this process,” said Reyes, “the Mexican state received US $5.8 million on Aug. 25, 2026.”

The UIF chief said the money was obtained from the recovery of a surety bond and “the liquidation of 12 properties located in Florida, United States, and linked to the Weinberg family.” He noted that Mexico is awaiting the liquidation of other assets in order to recover additional funds diverted out of the country by García Luna.

Later in the press conference, Sheinbaum said that the $5.8 million in recovered funds that Mexico received this week would be allocated to schools in the Montaña region of the southern state of Guerrero.

“It’s around 100 million pesos that is going to be used in [one of] the most disadvantaged areas in the country,” she said.

Mexico is doing ‘very well,’ Sheinbaum says ahead of her second annual report

A reporter reminded Sheinbaum that in her first annual report speech — delivered at the National Palace on Sept. 1, 2025 — she said that Mexico and her government were “doing well” and would do “even better.” He subsequently asked the president how her administration is doing 12 months later.

“Mexico is doing better, Mexico is doing well,” Sheinbaum said.

“We’re doing very well — with the difficulties that any country can face, but we’re doing well,” she said.

@Claudiashein afirmó que México progresa positivamente en economía, reducción de la violencia y bienestar social, rumbo a su Segundo Informe de Gobierno. Algunos spots de campaña serán difundidos en radio, televisión y redes sociales. Las piezas muestran sus giras de… pic.twitter.com/pu8YEMBrT4 — Nota Central (@notacentralmx) August 28, 2026

Sheinbaum said she is “very optimistic” about Mexico’s economy and declared that Mexicans’ quality of life is improving. She also pointed out that violence has declined — a statement supported by a 30.8% annual reduction in homicides in the first seven months of 2026.

Sheinbaum subsequently spoke about her government’s raison d’être, saying that the reason why “we’re here” is to “create well-being for the people of Mexico.”

On Wednesday, the president presented economic data that she said was indicative of the strength of the Mexican economy. She highlighted the record foreign direct investment Mexico received in the first half of 2026, quarter-over-quarter economic growth of 1.4% in the second quarter of the year and the USD:MXN exchange rate, which at the time was below 17.

Sheinbaum congratulates world champion rower

The president congratulated Mexican rower Kenia Lechuga, a Nuevo León native who on Thursday won gold in the women’s lightweight sculls at the 2026 World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam, Netherlands.

“Many congratulations,” Sheinbaum said, adding that as a former rower herself, she reserved “special affection” for a victory by a Mexican rower.

Lechuga, who had previously won silver and bronze medals at World Rowing Championships, wasn’t the only Mexican rower to win gold in Amsterdam on Thursday. Aylin Ibarra and Melissa Márquez won the women’s lightweight double sculls, while Aléxis López placed third to secure the bronze medal in the lightweight men’s sculls.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: How Mexico City can solve its 400-year water crisis
World.content:
Following a bout of heavy rains in September 1629, water rose through the streets of Mexico City and did not recede. The city had just spent 22 years digging a drainage channel through the mountains, the Desagüe de Huehuetoca, meant to solve a problem the closed, mountain-ringed basin had faced for centuries: nowhere for excess water to go.

The project failed. Parts of the city stayed flooded for years and more than 30,000 people died, mostly from disease in the standing, sewage-laced water.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by ABC News (@abcnews)



The city kept making the same trade for four centuries after that: draining the water to survive and turning every success into a new, worse problem.

A city that traded its lake for a sinking foundation

Before the Spanish conquest, Tenochtitlán sat on an island in Lake Texcoco, its neighborhoods built with the lake rather than against it. Colonial and then Porfirian-era engineers kept draining it instead, culminating in the Gran Canal del Desagüe around 1900. Draining the lake solved flooding and erased the city’s water supply at the same time, so the city turned to pumping the aquifer beneath the old lakebed’s soft, clay-rich sediment.

Pumping that aquifer releases the pressure holding the clay open. The clay compacts, causing the ground to drop. A 2021 study published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth measured subsidence near 50 centimeters a year in the worst areas, and found the sinking no longer tracks current pumping rates: It is now driven by decades-old compaction that cannot be undone, even if every well stopped tomorrow.

That uneven sinking has warped the Gran Canal itself, leaving stretches of the drainage system sloping the wrong way. Mexico City has sunk roughly 30 feet across the lakebed zone, and engineers now run pumping stations just to lift sewage back up to where gravity can take over — the same 1607 trade, repeated at greater cost.

The newest version, the Túnel Emisor Oriente, finished in 2019 after 11 years of digging, carries wastewater 62.5 kilometers (39 miles) to Hidalgo state, where it irrigates the Mezquital Valley. Only about 36% of the city’s wastewater gets treated at all; the nearby Tula Valley region now draws 90% to 100% of its own aquifer from decades of Mexico City’s former runoff.

What survives to reach a kitchen tap

Mexico City’s water is treated properly at the source. What happens after is where the system fails.

Official figures from Mexico City’s water agency, the Sistema de Aguas de la Ciudad de México (SACMEX), put network-wide leak loss at roughly 40%, while researchers studying intermittent, low-pressure water systems in general have documented exactly how contamination gets in through a leaking network: a crack or joint, a nearby contaminant source, and a pressure gradient pulling inward.

Rooftop reservoirs, also known as tinacos, exist precisely because city pressure is not continuous, and a small pilot study in Guadalajara found contamination rates more than double after water sat in a home’s storage tank versus straight off the network.

Water contamination

Two boroughs carry a documented, more specific version of this.

In Iztapalapa, two named SACMEX/UNAM wells have shown arsenic and heavy-metal levels exceeding Mexico’s own drinking-water standard since they opened; separately, UNAM researchers found microplastics, Giardia muris and E. coli in the borough’s water.

SACMEX’s own 2020 data recorded arsenic violations across 28 wells in Tláhuac, Tlalpan, Coyoacán, Iztapalapa, Iztacalco and Azcapotzalco, signifying a documented national pattern: Only 1 in 10 Mexican treatment plants is even equipped to remove arsenic or fluoride.

Stressing the system

Meanwhile, large companies are also extracting from the same stressed basin. CONAGUA’s public registry shows Coca-Cola FEMSA holds a well concession in Cuauhtémoc, where it extracts 1.13 billion liters a year. PepsiCo’s bottler holds another in Iztacalco, extracting 511 million liters.

Nationally, Coca-Cola and PepsiCo’s Mexican bottlers have extracted roughly 14.7 billion and 25.7 billion liters, respectively, since 1994.

What none of the public record shows is what becomes of the 15% to 30% of that water any industrial reverse-osmosis system inevitably rejects as concentrate, a limit set by the physics of the membrane itself.

Where the hope is

The subsidence side of this cycle has already been broken elsewhere.

Tokyo sank roughly 4 meters before two laws, the 1956 Industrial Water Law and the 1962 Law on Regulation of Groundwater Use in Office Buildings, made new wells prohibitively expensive to drill while the government subsidized cheaper surface-water infrastructure as the replacement. Groundwater pumping in the city’s 23 wards peaked in 1964 and has fallen since; subsidence in the most heavily regulated districts was brought close to zero.

Venice stopped pumping groundwater entirely and now draws its drinking water from the Italian mainland instead, sinking at about 1 millimeter a year, down from a rate that once threatened the city outright.

Neither city undid the damage already on the books. Both proved the mechanism itself can be stopped, and both did it with a law, not a technology.

Legal remedies vs. a household fix

The legislative move mirrors Tokyo’s. Sustained public pressure on regulators, not new technology, is what got its fix passed. Here, that looks like contacting a local representative directly, and backing investigations like “Veneno en mi agua,” or “Poison in my water,” that keep this issue on the public record instead of letting it fade after one news cycle.

A household’s own move is smaller and immediate: A fix goes under the sink.

An ultrafiltration membrane, at roughly 0.01 microns, physically blocks the bacteria and parasitic cysts responsible for most water-borne illness here, the exact risk documented above. It runs on the building’s own water pressure: no pump, no electricity and a 100% water recovery rate, so there is no reject stream at all. The water that enters the membrane is the water that leaves the tap, only cleaner. That combination — no pump, no electricity, no wasted water — also makes it the cheapest of these options to buy and run.

Reverse osmosis, run at home, sends roughly 3 liters down the drain for every liter it produces, a smaller version of the same tradeoff bottlers make at industrial scale. Given how much of this city’s wastewater exits the basin rather than getting treated and returned, that reject water is likely gone from the Valley of Mexico’s own water cycle for good, unlike ultrafiltration, which never enters that path at all.

Ultrafiltration

Garrafón delivery carries its own documented risk: Independent testing found the majority of samples in one Mexico City study contaminated with coliform bacteria, and nearly a quarter with E. coli, in an industry that grew 85% between 2012 and 2018.

Ultrafiltration is the one choice in this entire chain that does not ask the aquifer for anything extra to keep a household safe. It does not fix the leaking network, the sinking ground, or the four centuries of trades that got the city here. It is the one piece of the cycle a single kitchen can opt out of today, without waiting on a General Water Law that has been stalled in Congress for eight years, or a recharge program that exists as exactly one working pilot against a documented crisis.

Andrew D. Daily lives in Roma Norte, where he runs a water filtration company and mexicocitytravel.com, a simplified guide for visitors. Before meeting his wife and relocating to CDMX, he worked 11 years in Los Angeles, CA, as a television Production Manager on shows like Shark Tank, The Voice, and Miss Universe.

World.title: Meet Jacinto Canek, the Maya rebel who rose against Spanish rule in Yucatán
World.content:
The people of Cisteil were tired. After years as a Spanish district, they depended heavily on the municipality of Yaxcabá, located in what is now the state of Yucatán. Despite being a relatively small town, it had a fiery population that wanted to free itself from the Spanish yoke.

Cisteil lasted no more than eight years under this abusive regime. Little did the Spanish know that this small Yucatecan town would spark a major Maya anti-colonial uprising, led by a Maya man named Jacinto Canek.

From student and Maya physician to revolutionary leader

Long before Miguel Hidalgo began the Mexican independence revolts in Dolores, in what is now the Bajío region, southeastern Maya communities were already seeking to rid themselves of Spanish invaders.

Despite his standing as a prominent figure of Maya resistance, little is known about the early life of Jacinto Uc de los Santos Canek. Born in the 18th century, he led the “most important Maya rebellion in Yucatán during the colonial era,” according to the Great Maya Museum in Yucatán.

Documentary evidence shows he was born around 1731 to a poor family in the southeastern state of Campeche. Historical records indicate he studied Latin, history and Christian doctrine at the Convento Grande in Mérida before being expelled for his rebellious nature. Canek had a strong knowledge of Christian doctrine, joined a religious organization in his hometown of San Francisco de Campeche and practiced traditional Maya medicine learned through oral tradition.

After the 1761 rebellion, “Jacinto Canek chose a name of historical significance for the Maya,” according to a study by Robert W. Patch from the University of California, Riverside. He proclaimed himself king of the movement to reclaim “political and religious domination of the Yucatán Maya.”

Thousands of Indigenous people recognized his authority and viewed him as an incarnation of Kukulkán, the sacred serpent of the Maya pantheon. Researchers note the movement sought to revitalize Maya culture after two centuries of colonialism, with revolutionaries believing the days of Spanish rule were numbered.

Jacinto Canek: Kukulkán and Christ, embodied in a Maya revolutionary

No other significant anti-colonial movement had taken place in present-day Mexico to this point. However, as a review of a criminal trial resulting from the rebellion emphasizes, “it was a highly serious rebellion, with a strong anti-colonialist content.”

Beyond establishing stronger trade ties with former Maya chiefdoms, the people of Cisteil wanted to reclaim their culture, traditions and religion. “The Maya continued to believe in a cyclic version of history,” the study points out, “which led them to think that one day in the future they would overthrow the Spaniards.”

Canek took a name sacred to two religious traditions: Maya and Christian. From 1761 onward, he was known as Jacinto Uc de los Santos Canek Chichán Moctezuma. He embodied the man-god myth of Mesoamerican tradition, presenting a syncretic Maya-Christian figure blending Jesus Christ and Kukulkán. Under that name, he summoned the highest rulers of Cisteil to wage revolution.

How the Maya remember Jacinto Canek

Yucatán Governor José de Crespo y Honorato ordered the arrest of the revolt’s leaders to quell the movement. Spanish forces captured Canek and took him to Mérida, where he was condemned to be “broken alive” — having his limbs broken with iron bars — before being executed on Dec. 14, 1761. His body was burned to ashes after his death.

Many followers were killed alongside him. Following the execution, Spanish commanders suppressed the rebellion before it could spread beyond central Yucatán.

The Spanish then launched a campaign to delegitimize the revolutionaries, framing the event as a “drunkards’ riot,” according to UNAM records. Among the Maya, however, it remained “a noble uprising against colonial exploitation.”

Today, Canek is remembered as “one of the most significant figures in the history of Yucatán” and as someone who “lives in the hearts of the women and men of the Maya people.”

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: Colombia: Barranquilla Confirms IndyCar Race for April 2028 on Magdalena River Circuit
World.content:

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

COLOMBIA · MOTORSPORT

Key Facts —What happened: Barranquilla mayor Alejandro Char confirmed IndyCar will race in the Colombian city in April 2028. —The stage: The street circuit will run along the Gran Malecón and Vía 40, with the Magdalena River as backdrop. —How long: The planned layout covers about 4.3 kilometres, mixing the riverside promenade with city avenues. —The catch: The series raced in São Paulo from 2010 to 2013, so “first outside North America” needs a footnote. —The bigger dream: Char says Formula 1 is watching the project too, but only the US series has a confirmed date. —The backdrop: Colombia is now a top-five Latin American car market, with first-half sales up about 50 percent.

Barranquilla has a date: April 2028, when IndyCar will race on a street circuit along the Magdalena River. It is the first confirmed international round for the US series in more than a decade, and it lands in Latin America’s fastest-growing car market.

What the mayor announced

Alejandro Char, the mayor of Barranquilla, made the announcement on Thursday 27 August. He chose the launch of a Magdalena River tourism event as his stage.

“IndyCar is going to race with us,” Char said. “In April 2028 it will race here, in front of the river.”

He framed it as a first for the series. The championship, he said, will leave North America for the first time to hold a race.

For foreign readers: IndyCar is the top single-seater championship in the United States. Its signature event is the Indianapolis 500, held every May.

The circuit by the river

The track will be a street circuit of about 4.3 kilometres. Char first described the layout in July, with sectors on the Gran Malecón and the Vía 40.

The Gran Malecón is Barranquilla’s riverfront promenade, the centerpiece of the city’s recent urban renewal. The Vía 40 is its main north–south artery.

The Magdalena is Colombia’s great river, its Mississippi. Racing beside it is the point of the whole project.

An earlier draft of the layout measured 3.92 kilometres, according to local media. The design work involves Tony Cotman, the veteran track designer behind several American street circuits.

How a Colombian city sold itself to the US series

The pitch began in earnest at the Indianapolis 500 in May. A Barranquilla delegation met the series’ chief executive Mark Miles there.

Miles was publicly cautious at the time. A 2027 race, he said, was unrealistic, though he called the city well-funded and eager.

The project also has a famous godfather. Juan Pablo Montoya, Colombia’s IndyCar champion and two-time Indy 500 winner, is the race’s ambassador.

Days before the announcement, Barranquilla staged a show run with Montoya and his son Sebastián. The event, backed by the mayor’s office, was a deliberate warm-up.

The fine print behind the headline

The “first outside North America” line deserves a footnote. The series raced in São Paulo, Brazil, every year from 2010 to 2013.

April 2028 would still be the series’ first international round in 15 years. It would also be the first championship race ever held in Colombia.

There is no track yet, only streets and a plan. Contracts, safety certification and paddock construction all sit between today and race day.

Char also floated a Formula 1 “Caribbean Grand Prix” as the next prize. Nothing on that front is confirmed, and F1 has announced no such race.

Why Colombia can sell this now

The commercial logic runs through the showroom. Colombia is now a top-five car market in Latin America, according to regional industry rankings.

It trails only giants like Brazil and Mexico in volume. In growth, it leads: January sales rose 38.9 percent year on year, the region’s fastest rate.

The momentum held through mid-year. Dealers registered 157,620 new vehicles in the first half of 2026, up about 50 percent, say trade groups Fenalco and Andi.

Strikingly, the country’s best-selling car this year is electric. The Tesla Model Y topped the first-half charts, ahead of the locally assembled Renault Duster.

What to watch from here

The first marker is the final circuit design. A 4.3-kilometre layout mixing promenade and arterial road will need serious safety work.

The second is the sanctioning paperwork. The series has not yet published the race on an official calendar.

The third is Formula 1. If Barranquilla delivers this race cleanly in 2028, the Caribbean Grand Prix talk gets harder to dismiss.

Frequently Asked Questions

When will IndyCar race in Barranquilla? In April 2028. Mayor Alejandro Char confirmed the date on 27 August 2026, at the launch of a Magdalena River tourism event. Where will the circuit run? Along the Gran Malecón riverfront and the Vía 40 avenue, on a street layout of about 4.3 kilometres beside the Magdalena River. Is this really IndyCar’s first race outside North America? The mayor said so, but the series raced in São Paulo, Brazil, from 2010 to 2013. Barranquilla would be the first since then, and the first in Colombia. Is Formula 1 coming to Barranquilla too? Not confirmed. Char says Formula 1 is watching the project, but only the IndyCar race has an official date. How big is Colombia’s car market? Colombia is a top-five market in Latin America, behind leaders like Brazil and Mexico. New-vehicle registrations grew about 50 percent in the first half of 2026, according to Fenalco and Andi.

Sources: Pulzo on the mayor’s announcement; RACER via Daily Motor Culture on the IndyCar pitch and Mark Miles; Semana and El Colombiano on Colombia’s car market ranking and growth; Fenalco/Andi registration data.

World.title: Ecuador Orders 119 Investment Funds and Administrators to Raise Their Capital
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

ECUADOR · ECONOMY

Key Facts —What happened: Ecuador has ordered fund and trust administrators to hold more of their own capital, scaled to what they manage. —Who it hits: The rule touches 85 active investment funds and 34 administrators, 119 entities in total. —The formula: A fixed US$400,000 plus a variable slice of assets under management, up to about US$6.9 million. —The catch: The money protects the administrator’s operations, not the saver’s investment directly. —The deadline: Firms get two years to comply, but must file a regularisation plan within the first month. —Also in Quito: The four Andean Community countries met this week to push regional energy integration.

Ecuador is forcing its fast-growing investment funds industry to put more of its own money on the line, with a new capital rule that reaches 119 funds and administrators as the sector’s assets hit a record US$3.1 billion.

What the new rule demands

The measure came from the Junta de Política y Regulación Financiera y Monetaria. That is Ecuador’s top financial policy board, and it approved the rule on 20 August as Resolution JPRFM-2026-034-V.

The rule is already in force. It covers the companies that run investment funds and trusts in Ecuador’s securities market, supervised by the Superintendencia de Compañías, Valores y Seguros.

Each administrator must now hold capital equal to a fixed US$400,000 plus a variable component. The variable part is a percentage of the money the firm manages for clients.

The percentage falls as the firm grows. It runs from 1.81 percent for administrators of up to US$50 million down to 0.88 percent for the largest players.

What that means in real money

Financial lawyer Grace Chiriboga walked through an example for local outlet Primicias. A firm managing US$50 million would need about US$1.3 million of its own capital.

That is the US$400,000 fixed part plus roughly US$905,000 from the variable part. At the top end, the variable component alone can reach about US$6.93 million.

Firms that fall short face a sharp sanction. They cannot distribute profits or return capital to their shareholders until they comply.

One detail helps foreigners read this story. Ecuador uses the US dollar as its official currency, so every figure here is already in dollars, with no exchange-rate guesswork.

Why regulators moved now

The sector has exploded. Assets managed by Ecuador’s investment funds grew 411 percent in seven years, from US$609 million in 2019 to US$3,115 million in July 2026.

More than 400,000 savers now participate in investment funds, according to Gregorio Moreno of Fideval, one of the administrators. That is a lot of trust placed in a young industry.

Investment funds pool money from many contributors and invest it for a return. The administrator runs the portfolio and is supposed to manage the risks.

The logic of the rule is simple. The more client money a firm handles, the deeper its own pockets should be if something goes wrong operationally.

The honest limit of the protection

Here is what the headline does not tell you. The required capital is not insurance for the saver, and it does not guarantee anyone’s investment.

Its purpose is to keep the administrator itself standing. The money backs technology, cybersecurity, processes and operating capacity, Moreno explained.

The market will likely consolidate. Chiriboga expects smaller firms that cannot raise the capital to seek partners, merge or leave the business.

Entry will also get more expensive. A newcomer now needs the same US$400,000 plus the variable slice from day one.

The calmer backdrop: a falling country risk

The rule lands in a brighter macroeconomic moment. Ecuador’s country risk index, the premium investors demand to hold its bonds, has fallen steeply.

The index stood near 2,000 points in 2023, a level that signals real fear of default. Local reports this week put it around 419 points, the lowest in years.

For context, anything below 500 is considered manageable for an emerging market. Ecuador last saw such levels before its 2020 debt restructuring.

Cheaper risk perception means cheaper borrowing for the state. It also tends to pull more savings toward formal vehicles such as the investment funds now facing the new rule.

Meanwhile, the Andes talk electricity

The same week, Quito hosted the Andean Forum on Regional Energy Integration. The four members of the Andean Community attended: Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru.

Ecuador currently holds the bloc’s rotating presidency, and it chose energy as a headline topic. The forum, opened on Thursday 27 August, ran for two days.

Officials from the Inter-American Development Bank, the International Atomic Energy Agency and the Latin American Energy Organization joined the talks. The theme was shared grids, resilient supply and a sustainable energy transition.

There was concrete news too. Ecuador has resumed buying electricity from Colombia after a suspension of almost seven months, a reminder that integration is already a lived reality.

Energy matters deeply here. Drought in 2024 forced blackouts across Ecuador, and a better-connected Andean grid is the country’s insurance policy against the next dry year.

What to watch from here

First, watch the regularisation plans. Within a month of the rule, every administrator below the new minimum must tell the supervisor how it will get there.

Second, watch for mergers. A wave of consolidation among the 34 administrators would confirm the smaller players are feeling the squeeze.

Third, watch the energy agenda. The Andean Community wants Chile to join its regional electricity market, and Ecuador’s presidency runs through 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Ecuador order investment funds to do? Fund and trust administrators must hold more of their own capital: a fixed US$400,000 plus a variable percentage of the assets they manage. The rule took effect on 20 August 2026. How many firms does the new capital rule affect? It covers 85 active investment funds and 34 fund and trust administrators, 119 entities in total. Firms have two years to comply. Does the extra capital protect savers directly? No. It is not insurance and does not guarantee investments. It is meant to keep the administrator operating, funding technology, security and processes. What is Ecuador’s country risk now? The index stood near 2,000 points in 2023 and has fallen steeply since. Local reports this week put it around 419 points, the lowest in years. What happened at the Andean energy forum in Quito? Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru discussed deeper energy integration on 27 and 28 August. Ecuador also confirmed it resumed buying electricity from Colombia after a seven-month suspension.

World.title: Brazil’s Minas-Rio Rail Corridor Goes to Auction as ANTT Approves Tender Notice
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · INFRASTRUCTURE

Key Facts —What happened: Brazil’s land transport regulator ANTT approved the final tender notice for the Minas-Rio rail corridor on 27 August. —The asset: The corridor covers about 733 kilometres, linking interior Minas Gerais to the coast at Angra dos Reis. —Who runs it now: Ferrovia Centro-Atlântica, known as FCA, operates the tracks today and must hand them to the winner. —The money: The minimum grant is a symbolic R$1, about US$0.19, because the winner’s real cost is rebuilding the line. —The catch: No auction date is set, and rules give bidders at least 100 days after publication to submit proposals. —Why it matters: It is the first tender for existing tracks under Brazil’s 2021 Railway Law, a test case for the sector.

Brazil’s transport regulator has approved the tender notice for the Minas-Rio rail corridor, clearing the way for an auction of 733 kilometres of freight track. The winner takes over from today’s operator and must commit to rebuilding the line.

What the regulator approved on Thursday

The board of ANTT, the National Land Transport Agency, approved the definitive tender notice on Thursday 27 August. The document governs the auction of the Minas-Rio rail corridor.

The corridor will be offered in two lots. The first joins Iguatama, in Minas Gerais, to Barra Mansa, in Rio de Janeiro state, plus a branch between Varginha and Lavras.

The second lot runs from Barra Mansa down to Angra dos Reis, on the Atlantic coast. Together the two lots total about 733 kilometres.

Directors also adjusted the auction’s live-bidding rules. Up to three bidders will all advance to the open outcry round, whatever the gap between their offers.

The corridor, and why foreign investors should care

Minas Gerais is Brazil’s mining and coffee heartland. Moving its output to port by rail rather than truck is one of the country’s oldest logistics dreams.

Barra Mansa, the corridor’s hinge point, sits beside Volta Redonda, home of the CSN steelworks. Angra dos Reis gives the line an Atlantic outlet west of Rio de Janeiro city.

Today the tracks are run by Ferrovia Centro-Atlântica, or FCA, the rail arm of logistics group VLI. The tender transfers that operation to a new operator.

The winner takes on duties of maintenance, recovery and modernization. Within two years of takeover it must present a full plan to rebuild and upgrade the railway.

Why the entry ticket costs one real

The minimum grant for the Minas-Rio corridor is a symbolic R$1 (US$0.19). The real price is the investment the winner must commit to.

That symbolism bothered the TCU, Brazil’s federal audit court. It demanded a simplified technical study showing the economics of recovery, operation and freight demand.

The court cleared the project on 20 August, with conditions. ANTT told its board on Thursday that every determination had been met.

One condition sets the calendar floor. At least 100 days must pass between publication of the notice and the receipt of proposals.

Another protects competition law quirks of the 2021 Railway Law. Neighboring concessionaires may hold a right of first refusal, and the notice must document who was asked.

A test case for Brazil’s new railway model

The 2021 Railway Law let private firms build lines under simple authorizations. Almost all deals since then have been greenfield projects, built from scratch.

The Minas-Rio tender is different. It puts tracks that already exist, and already run under an old-style concession, into the new regime.

Marcelo Fonseca, the director overseeing the process, called it a lead case. His board colleagues expect it to shape every future rail tender of this kind.

Others are already queued. The Malha Oeste corridor, with about R$29 billion (US$5.63 billion) in planned investment, is moving through the same pipeline.

What to watch from here

The next step is formal publication of the notice. Only then does the 100-day clock for bidders start running.

Watch who shows up. Mining groups, steelmakers and existing rail operators all have reasons to want a rebuilt route to Angra dos Reis.

Also watch FCA. The current operator must split off the tendered stretches, a separation the audit court ordered documented in detail.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did ANTT approve for the Minas-Rio corridor? The final tender notice, approved on 27 August 2026. It clears the way for an auction of about 733 kilometres of freight railway in Minas Gerais and Rio de Janeiro states. What exactly is for sale? Two lots. The first links Iguatama to Barra Mansa plus a Varginha–Lavras branch, and the second runs from Barra Mansa to the port of Angra dos Reis. Who operates the railway today? Ferrovia Centro-Atlântica, or FCA, the rail arm of logistics group VLI. The auction winner takes over with maintenance and modernization obligations. Why is the minimum grant only R$1? The symbolic R$1 (US$0.19) reflects that the winner’s real cost is recovering and modernizing the line. The federal audit court required a study to justify it. When will the auction happen? No date has been set. Regulation requires at least 100 days between publication of the notice and the receipt of proposals.

World.title: Uruguay Wants a Beef Market in Vietnam as Mercosur Opens Trade Talks
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

URUGUAY · TRADE

Key Facts —What happened: Mercosur and Vietnam held their first in-person round of trade talks, led on the bloc’s side by Argentina. —Uruguay’s stake: Montevideo wants Vietnamese sanitary approval for its beef before the end of 2026. —The catch: A signed deal is years away; the beef market opening runs on a separate, faster track. —Why Vietnam matters: Vietnam is already Argentina’s sixth-largest export market, with about US$4 billion in annual trade. —Also this week: A survey found 67 percent of Brazilians are interested in doing business with Uruguay. —What comes next: Technical teams will keep negotiating toward a preferential agreement compatible with WTO rules.

Mercosur has opened formal trade negotiations with Vietnam, and Uruguay is moving on a parallel track to get its beef into the Southeast Asian country of 100 million people before the year ends.

What Mercosur and Vietnam just started

The first in-person negotiating round between Mercosur and Vietnam took place this week. Argentina, which holds the bloc’s technical lead, hosted the working teams.

Argentina’s foreign minister, Pablo Quirno, announced the start publicly. He said he had the satisfaction of receiving the teams for the first face-to-face round.

The process was formally launched in late December. Mercosur, made up of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, agreed with Vietnam to negotiate a preferential trade deal.

The goal is to cut tariffs and tackle non-tariff barriers on both sides. Any agreement must be compatible with World Trade Organization rules, the standard framework for global trade.

Why Uruguay cares more than most

For foreigners new to the region, Uruguay is a small country that punches far above its weight in food. Its 3.4 million people share the land with roughly 12 million cattle.

Beef is the country’s signature export, and about 80 percent of production is sold abroad. Every new market matters, and Asian markets pay the best prices.

Weeks before this round, an official Uruguayan mission travelled to Vietnam. Its main goal was to speed up the sanitary authorization of Uruguayan beef.

Sanitary authorization is the veterinary approval that lets a country sell meat at all. Without it, no tariff cut in the world helps, because the product simply cannot enter.

The government in Montevideo wants to close that process before the end of 2026. It then sees the bloc negotiation as the vehicle to improve tariff conditions later.

The two tracks, explained

This is the part that confuses many readers. Trade deals and market access run on separate clocks, and Uruguay is working both at once.

Track one is sanitary. Vietnam’s authorities inspect Uruguay’s slaughterhouses, disease controls and traceability systems before letting a single steak in.

Track two is commercial. The bloc negotiation will eventually decide how much tariff Vietnamese consumers pay on top of the beef’s price.

Uruguay’s strategy is to finish track one bilaterally and fast. Track two, slower by nature, can then follow through this channel.

How big is the Vietnam opportunity

Quirno offered a sense of scale from the Argentine side. Vietnam is already Argentina’s sixth-largest export destination.

Two-way trade runs at about US$4 billion a year. Argentina enjoyed a surplus of roughly US$1.4 billion in 2025.

Vietnam has around 100 million people and one of Asia’s fastest-growing middle classes. Meat consumption rises quickly when incomes do.

Uruguay already sells heavily into Asia, with China as its top beef buyer. A Vietnamese opening would diversify that concentration, a long-standing goal in Montevideo.

The Brazilian neighbour is watching too

A separate survey released this week added colour to Uruguay’s commercial moment. It found that 67 percent of Brazilians are interested in doing business with Uruguay.

The study, reported by El Observador in Montevideo, showed high Brazilian willingness to visit, invest in and buy products from Uruguay. More than half of respondents said they would even consider moving to Uruguay for work.

Brazil is Uruguay’s giant neighbour and a fellow member of the bloc. Strong Brazilian interest underlines the country’s reputation as a stable, easy place to do business.

That reputation is the same asset Uruguay is selling in Asia. Predictability, full traceability of every animal and grass-fed production are its calling cards.

What to watch from here

The first milestone is the Vietnamese sanitary decision. If approval lands before year-end, first shipments could follow quickly.

The second is the pace of the negotiating rounds. Preferential deals of this kind typically take years, not months.

The third is Uruguay’s parallel push in other Asian markets. The country has long sought wider access in Japan and South Korea, where it already holds niche approvals.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Mercosur and Vietnam agree to do? They opened negotiations for a preferential trade agreement, holding their first in-person round this week. The talks aim to cut tariffs and non-tariff barriers under World Trade Organization rules. Why does Uruguay want access to Vietnam? Uruguay exports about 80 percent of its beef and wants new Asian markets beyond China. Vietnam has 100 million consumers and a fast-growing middle class. When could Uruguayan beef reach Vietnam? The government aims to secure Vietnamese sanitary approval before the end of 2026. Tariff improvements would come later through the Mercosur negotiation. How important is Vietnam to South American trade already? It is Argentina’s sixth-largest export destination, with about US$4 billion in annual two-way trade. Argentina ran a surplus of roughly US$1.4 billion with Vietnam in 2025. What did the survey about Brazilians and Uruguay find? It found 67 percent of Brazilians are interested in doing business with Uruguay. More than half said they would consider moving to the country for work reasons.

World.title: Brazil: Rio’s Santos Dumont Airport Closes After Business Jet Skids Off Runway
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · AVIATION

Key Facts —What happened: A business jet skidded off the runway at Rio’s Santos Dumont airport while landing on Thursday 27 August. —Who was aboard: Only the pilot and one crew member were on the Embraer Phenom 100, and nobody was hurt. —The shutdown: Operator Infraero suspended all takeoffs and landings while firefighters lifted the jet off the grass. —The fallout: At least 53 flights were canceled and 15 diverted to Galeão, stranding passengers for hours. —The catch: The runway reopened on Thursday night, but the cause of the excursion is still unknown. —What comes next: Cenipa, Brazil’s air accident investigation center, has opened an inquiry into the landing.

A small business jet ran off the runway at Rio de Janeiro’s Santos Dumont airport on Thursday afternoon, closing one of Brazil’s busiest domestic terminals for hours. Nobody was hurt, but dozens of flights were canceled or diverted.

What happened on the runway

The incident took place at 4:10 p.m. on Thursday 27 August 2026. A small jet, registration PS-VEE, left the runway during its landing procedure.

The aircraft was an Embraer Phenom 100, a very light business jet built in Brazil. It came to a stop on the grass beside the tarmac.

Infraero, the state-owned company that operates the airport, activated its emergency plan immediately. Only the pilot and one crew member were aboard, and both walked away unhurt.

Firefighters removed the aircraft with a crane and placed it on a trailer. The runway was released for traffic again on Thursday night.

Hours of chaos for passengers

While the jet sat on the grass, nothing could land or take off. Infraero confirmed 53 canceled flights and 15 diversions by Thursday evening.

The diverted flights went to Galeão, Rio’s international airport, about 20 kilometres north of downtown. Later news counts put the number of cancellations at 71.

Videos sent to CNN Brasil showed long queues inside the terminal. One passenger reported waiting more than four hours without boarding.

The timing made things worse. Late afternoon is the peak window for the Rio–São Paulo air shuttle, one of the busiest routes in South America.

Its Defense & Security segment develops and produces military aircraft and…

The airport that sits in the middle of Rio

For foreign readers, Santos Dumont is not just any airport. It sits on the edge of Guanabara Bay, a ten-minute taxi ride from Rio’s business district.

It is named after Alberto Santos-Dumont, the Brazilian aviation pioneer. Brazilians take his claim to have flown before the Wright brothers very seriously.

The airport is famous for its scenic approach between Sugarloaf Mountain and the bay. It is also known for short runways that demand precision from pilots.

Because of that geography, it handles mostly domestic flights within Brazil. It normally operates from 6 a.m. to 11 p.m.

The terminal opened in 1936 on land reclaimed from the bay. That makes it one of the oldest major airports still operating in the country.

Its capacity has been politically contested for years. Federal restrictions introduced in 2023 already limit operations, part of a plan to push more flights toward Galeão.

The Rio–São Paulo shuttle that dominates its schedule is a national institution. Brazilians call it the ponte aérea, the air bridge, and it regularly ranks among the world’s busiest routes in industry league tables.

Why one small jet can close a whole airport

Santos Dumont effectively runs on one main runway for its scheduled traffic. A stranded aircraft anywhere near it stops the entire operation.

Removal is slow by design. Investigators must document the scene before heavy equipment drags the wreck away.

In this case the closure lasted several hours, from mid-afternoon into the evening. Airlines then had to rebuild their schedules flight by flight.

What investigators will look at

Technicians from Cenipa, the Brazilian Air Force’s accident investigation center, were at the airport on Thursday. They have opened a formal inquiry into the cause of the runway excursion.

Cenipa investigations in Brazil do not assign legal blame. They exist to prevent the next accident, and their findings typically take months.

For now, the cause is simply unknown. Weather, braking, runway condition and pilot action are all standard lines of inquiry in cases like this.

Travelers with flights from Rio this weekend should check with their airline. Residual delays often outlive the reopening itself.

Later news counts put cancellations at 71. Who investigates runway excursions in Brazil? Cenipa, the Brazilian Air Force’s Center for Investigation and Prevention of Aeronautical Accidents. World.title: Itaú BBA Cuts Chile’s CMPC to a New Floor Over Its US$6 Billion Natureza Megaproject
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

CHILE · MARKETS

Key Facts —What happened: Itaú BBA cut its CMPC price target to 1,030 pesos (US$1.12), the lowest of 15 analysts tracked by Bloomberg. —The worry: The planned US$4.6 billion Natureza pulp mill in Brazil could overload an already stretched balance sheet. —The catch: Itaú actually raised its profit forecast for the company; the problem is debt, not the business. —The damage: The shares have lost more than 20 percent in 2026, and the average analyst target is 1,500 pesos (US$1.63). —Also in Santiago: ENAP’s chairman denied the state oil firm hid pollution data at its Aconcagua refinery. —What comes next: A decision on approving Natureza is expected in the coming months.

Brazilian broker Itaú BBA has slashed its target for Chilean pulp and paper group CMPC to a new psychological floor, blaming uncertainty over the company’s US$4.6 billion Natureza megaproject in Brazil and a balance sheet already at its limit.

What Itaú BBA actually said

The broker kept its underweight recommendation on the stock, meaning it tells clients to hold less of the stock than the index. It then cut the price target to 1,030 Chilean pesos (US$1.12) per share for the end of next year.

That is the lowest target among the 15 estimates compiled by Bloomberg. The average sits around 1,500 pesos (US$1.63), though that average has been falling for 12 months.

The report came from an analyst team led by Daniel Sasson and was published on Wednesday 26 August. Diario Financiero first reported the details in Santiago.

The team wrote that it sees a challenging medium-term outlook for market pulp prices. Uncertainty over the possible approval of the Natureza project adds risk, they said, given the company’s current leverage.

The paradox: better profits, worse debt

Here is the part that surprises. Itaú BBA actually raised its 2027 profit estimate for the pulp group slightly, to US$1.24 billion in EBITDA, the standard measure of operating earnings.

Better trends in the Softys tissue business and in Biopackaging more than offset weaker prices for short-fibre pulp. The company, in other words, is performing reasonably well.

The problem is what Natureza would do to the balance sheet. Itaú projects net debt at about 4.8 times EBITDA by the end of 2026, even before counting the project.

That ratio falls to about 4.2 times if only half of the hybrid bonds, worth roughly US$1.3 billion, count as debt. Either way, the analysts called the enterprise value multiple of 6.4 times between fair and elevated.

The Pulp segment produces and markets pulp, forestry, and lumber products to the industrial pulp mills, remanufactured products, and plywood plants. This segment also offers sawn…

Why Natureza scares the rating agencies too

Natureza is a planned US$4.6 billion pulp mill in Brazil, one of the largest investments in Chilean corporate history. The company is the forestry arm of the Matte group, one of Chile’s richest families.

All three major rating agencies have already reacted. S&P cut the company to BBB-minus in February, Fitch trimmed its local rating in April, and Moody’s turned its outlook negative in June.

Moody’s warned that building Natureza without extra measures could push leverage above five times at the peak of construction. First-quarter net profit had already fallen 50 percent to US$24.8 million.

Itaú did offer one positive note. Management has signalled that selling forest assets could speed up deleveraging and free up money for future growth investments.

The pulp market behind the downgrade

Short-fibre pulp, the raw material for tissue and printing paper, has fallen to about US$560 per tonne. Itaú believes that is a floor and prices could rebound in the short term.

The longer view is darker. New supply from China, Indonesia and Latin America, including Indonesia’s giant OKI plant, meets weak demand growth toward 2030.

In the same report the broker kept its buy call on Suzano, the Brazilian pulp giant. It rated Empresas Copec, parent of its rival Arauco, at market return.

Meanwhile, ENAP fights a pollution-data scandal

Across Santiago’s corporate world, another Chilean heavyweight had a rough week. Cristián Muga, chairman of state oil company ENAP, denied that the firm hid information about pollution episodes at its Aconcagua refinery.

The refinery, in the coastal town of Concón near Valparaíso, is under internal investigation for irregularities in its environmental reporting. The anomalies involve sulphur dioxide emissions and sulphur recovery calculations.

Muga rejected any cover-up and said the company itself detected the anomalies. The case is sensitive because environmental watchdog SMA filed charges against the same refinery in December over liquid waste discharges into the sea.

The mining paradox hanging over it all

Chile’s wider business mood was captured this week by Jorge Riesco, president of mining association Sonami. Speaking at the group’s annual summit, he summed up a strange year.

“We have never earned so much producing so little,” Riesco said, pointing to record copper prices alongside stagnant output. State copper giant Codelco just reported a sixfold profit jump for the first half while producing less copper.

For CMPC, the lesson cuts both ways. High prices saved the miners this year, but pulp prices are falling, which is exactly why the Natureza gamble worries Santiago’s market.

What to watch from here

The first milestone is the Natureza approval decision, expected in the coming months. A green light without asset sales would likely trigger fresh rating pressure.

The second is the promised forestry divestment plan. Its size and speed will show how serious CMPC is about protecting its investment-grade rating.

At ENAP, watch the internal investigation into the Aconcagua reporting anomalies. Any finding of deliberate misreporting would turn a corporate story into a political one.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Itaú BBA cut its CMPC price target? The broker sees weak pulp prices ahead and uncertainty over CMPC’s US$4.6 billion Natureza project in Brazil. It cut the target to 1,030 pesos (US$1.12), the lowest of 15 analysts tracked by Bloomberg. What is the Natureza project? It is a planned US$4.6 billion pulp mill in Brazil, one of the largest investments in Chilean corporate history. All three major rating agencies have already warned about CMPC’s debt because of it. How much debt does CMPC carry? Itaú BBA projects net debt of about 4.8 times operating earnings by the end of 2026, before Natureza. That falls to 4.2 times if only half of its US$1.3 billion in hybrid bonds counts as debt. What is happening at ENAP’s Aconcagua refinery? The state oil firm is investigating irregularities in environmental reporting on sulphur emissions at the Concón plant. Chairman Cristián Muga denied the company concealed any information. What did Sonami’s president mean by earning more and producing less? Jorge Riesco pointed to record copper prices lifting mining profits while Chilean output stagnates. State miner Codelco’s first-half profit rose sixfold even as it produced less copper.

World.title: Argentina’s FIT 2026 Travel Fair in Buenos Aires Will Be the Largest in Its History
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

ARGENTINA · TOURISM

Key Facts —What happened: Argentina officially presented FIT 2026, the 30th edition of Latin America’s international tourism fair. —How big: Organizers project over 20,000 square meters, more than 350 exhibitors and delegations from 60 countries. —The headline claim: Tourism secretary Daniel Scioli said this will be the largest FIT in the fair’s history. —The catch: The record numbers are still projections, because the fair only opens on 26 September. —Guest of honor: The Dominican Republic is Guest Country, after a 120 percent jump in its tourists visiting Argentina. —What comes next: FIT 2026 runs 26 to 29 September at La Rural, with a first International Sports Tourism Forum on the 29th.

Buenos Aires will host the 30th edition of FIT, Latin America’s biggest tourism trade fair, from 26 to 29 September 2026. Organizers say it will be the largest ever, with 60 countries and a guest-of-honor role for the Dominican Republic.

What FIT is, and why this edition matters

FIT stands for Feria Internacional de Turismo de América Latina. It is the region’s leading travel trade fair, held every year in Buenos Aires.

The venue is La Rural, the historic fairground in the Palermo neighborhood. Argentina’s farm society built it in the nineteenth century, and it now serves as the city’s main exhibition center.

FIT 2026 will be the fair’s 30th edition. The official presentation took place this week, one month before opening day.

The fair mixes two audiences. Weekend days are open to the general public, while Monday and Tuesday cater mainly to tourism professionals.

The numbers behind “largest in history”

Organizers expect more than 20,000 square meters of exhibition space. They project over 350 exhibitors, with some trade reports putting the target near 360.

Delegations from 60 countries are expected to attend. Daniel Scioli, Argentina’s national secretary of tourism, said the edition will be the largest in the fair’s history.

The presentation drew the sector’s top names. Andrés Deyá, president of FIT and of FAEVYT, the Argentine federation of travel agencies, led the event.

Valentín Díaz Gilligan, head of the Buenos Aires Tourism Board, and Adrián Manzotti of the city’s travel agency association AVIABUE also attended. President Javier Milei has been invited to open the fair.

Worth noting: these are organizer projections made a month out. The final exhibitor count will only be known once doors open on 26 September.

The Dominican Republic takes the guest-of-honor slot

Each year FIT names a Guest Country, and for the anniversary edition the honor went to the Dominican Republic. The Caribbean nation will showcase beaches, historic cities, gastronomy and music.

The choice follows a striking statistic. Officials cited a 120 percent increase in Dominican tourists visiting Argentina, the fastest growth of any source market.

There is a policy story behind it. Scioli said the Milei government implemented visa exemptions for citizens of the Dominican Republic, China and India.

Jennifer Elias Franjul, tourism marketing director at the Dominican ministry, promised surprises. Her country plans a full gastronomic and cultural offering at its pavilion.

What is new inside the fair

FIT 2026 introduces themed spaces that mirror how the industry is changing. The list includes FIT Tech, FIT Food & Market, FIT Outdoor, FIT Cruises, FIT Fashion & Travel and FIT B2B.

The traditional Business Rounds remain the commercial core. They are pre-scheduled meetings where buyers and sellers negotiate contracts face to face.

The biggest new feature lands on the final day. The first International Sports Tourism Forum will take place on Tuesday 29 September.

FIT, the City of Buenos Aires and UN Tourism, the United Nations tourism agency, are organizing it together. The forum will examine how major sporting events reshape destinations.

Why Argentina is pushing tourism this hard

For foreign readers, the context is economic. Tourism is one of the few sectors that brings fresh US dollars into Argentina’s chronically currency-short economy.

The Milei government has bet on deregulation and cheaper red tape to attract visitors. The visa waivers Scioli celebrated are part of that strategy.

A record fair is also a shop window for the regions. Argentine provinces use FIT to sell everything from Patagonian glaciers to Mendoza’s wine country to international buyers.

Practical details if you plan to go

FIT 2026 runs from Saturday 26 to Tuesday 29 September at La Rural. The venue sits in Palermo, close to the city’s main hotel districts.

On Saturday and Sunday the fair opens to the general public from 2 p.m. to 9 p.m. Monday and Tuesday run from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m., aimed at trade visitors.

Travelers looking for Argentine holiday deals should come on the weekend. Industry deals, however, will be made in the Business Rounds on the professional days.

World.title: Mercado Libre to Triple Its Logistics Network in Chile by 2027
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

CHILE · BUSINESS

Key Facts —What happened: Mercado Libre will triple its logistics capacity in Chile, from 140,000 to 450,000 square metres by 2027. —The jobs: The expansion will create more than 2,500 new jobs across Santiago and 14 regional cities. —Where it grows: New capacity runs from Antofagasta in the north down to Puerto Montt in the south. —The catch: This is a two-year build-out, so the full 450,000 square metres arrive only by the end of 2027. —Why it matters: Chile’s network already moves over one million packages a week, 55 percent within 24 hours. —The money: Trade publication Modaes put the investment behind the plan at US$240 million.

Mercado Libre, Latin America’s biggest e-commerce company, will triple its logistics network in Chile over the next two years, growing from 140,000 to 450,000 square metres of warehouse and distribution space and adding more than 2,500 jobs.

What Mercado Libre announced

The announcement came on Thursday 27 August at Mercado Libre Experience. That is the company’s flagship e-commerce event, billed as the largest of its kind in Latin America.

Between 2026 and 2027, the company will expand its storage and distribution infrastructure in Chile from 140,000 to 450,000 square metres. The plan covers Santiago and 14 cities in the country’s regions.

It includes new and enlarged storage centres, distribution hubs and service centres. Together they will stretch the company’s operational footprint from Antofagasta in the far north to Puerto Montt, more than 1,000 kilometres south of Santiago.

The build-out will generate more than 2,500 new jobs, according to the company. Spanish trade publication Modaes reported the investment behind the expansion at US$240 million.

Three big warehouses around Santiago

The story starts in Colina, a fast-growing commune on the northern edge of Santiago. In 2022 the company opened Chile’s largest e-commerce warehouse there, with 100,000 square metres and room for up to 15 million products.

A second centre of the same size is now under construction in Colina. Announced in 2025, it is due to start operating at the end of this year.

For 2027, the company plans a third distribution and storage centre of 50,000 square metres. It will sit in Santiago’s northern zone, close to the other two.

Five new last-mile centres will add another 90,000 square metres. Last-mile centres are the small urban depots where parcels begin their final trip to your door.

The company operates Mercado Libre Marketplace, an online commerce platform that can be accessed through mobile app or website; and Mercado Pago, a financial technology solution platform, which offers comprehensive set of financial technology services to users and other users…

The regions get the bigger leap

Outside the capital, the growth rate is even steeper. Regional capacity will jump 174 percent, from 40,000 square metres to more than 110,000.

Fourteen cities will see new or expanded facilities. The list runs from Antofagasta, Copiapó, La Serena and Coquimbo in the north through Talca and Concepción in the centre to Temuco, Valdivia and Puerto Montt in the south.

The practical result is speed. The company says the expansion will bring same-day delivery to 26 more cities, including Arica, Iquique, Calama, Viña del Mar, Rancagua and Chillán.

For a country almost 4,300 kilometres long but barely 180 kilometres wide, that is no small promise. Distance has always been the tax on Chilean e-commerce.

Why the company is betting on Chile

Rafael Lira, the company’s marketplace director for Chile, Peru and Ecuador, framed the move as a vote of confidence. The expansion, he said, shows deep trust in Chile’s growth and in job creation.

He also made the inclusion argument. E-commerce, in his words, only fulfils its purpose when it reaches everywhere, including regions with less access to the digital economy.

The numbers suggest the bet is already paying off. Its Chilean network delivers more than one million packages a week.

Of those, 55 percent arrive within 24 hours and more than 80 percent within 48. The company says small businesses selling through its fulfilment network can sell up to twice as much.

What this means if you live in Chile

For foreigners in Chile, Mercado Libre is the local Amazon. It runs the marketplace, the payment app Mercado Pago and the delivery network Mercado Envíos.

Faster regional delivery changes daily life outside Santiago. A shopper in Temuco or La Serena will increasingly get the same next-day service a shopper in the capital takes for granted.

For small Chilean businesses, the pitch is reach. A workshop in Chillán can store products in the network and ship to the whole country within two days.

The jobs matter too. Warehouse and delivery work has become one of the main entry points into formal employment in Chile’s regions.

What to watch from here

The first milestone is the second Colina centre, due to open before the end of 2026. Its start-up will show whether the timeline holds.

The second is the competitive response. Rivals such as Amazon, Falabella and the Chinese platforms Shein and Temu all want the same Chilean shopper.

The third is the 2027 warehouse and the five last-mile depots. Only when those are running will the promised 450,000 square metres actually exist.

What did Mercado Libre announce for Chile? It will triple its logistics capacity from 140,000 to 450,000 square metres between 2026 and 2027. The plan covers Santiago and 14 regional cities and creates over 2,500 jobs. How much is Mercado Libre investing in Chile? The company did not publish a figure in its announcement. The trade publication Modaes reported an investment of US$240 million behind the expansion. Where will the new warehouses be? World.title: Belize City man fined $1,500 for taking common-law wife’s money and wounding her but somebody beat him up and sent him to court with ‘batty eye’
World.content:
Belize City man fined $1,500 for taking common-law wife’s money and wounding her but somebody beat him up and sent him to court with ‘batty eye’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man has been spared jail but ordered to pay a $1,500 fine after pleading guilty to wounding his common-law wife during a domestic dispute on Central American Boulevard. He showed up to court on Friday with two “batty eye” local slang for both his eye being swollen from an apparent beating.

Thirty-four-year-old construction worker Alton Nicholson appeared unrepresented before Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison in Court #6 on Friday, where he pleaded guilty to wounding his 51-year-old common-law wife.

The charge arose from an incident on Tuesday, August 25, 2026.

According to the police account, the woman was on Central American Boulevard at around 11:45 a.m. when Nicholson approached her while she was with a friend and asked for $10. She reportedly gave him a $20 bill, expecting him to return with her change.

When he did not return, the woman went looking for him. She told police that when she found Nicholson, he accused her of having a sexual relationship with one of his friends and threatened to hurt both of them.

Nicholson allegedly began dragging her toward an abandoned house. She managed to break free and run, but Nicholson chased after her and she fell, sustaining injuries.

Police arrived and later escorted the woman to the hospital, where a doctor classified her injuries as wounding.

Nicholson was also observed with swelling around both eyes and reportedly told police that he had been beaten by another man during the incident.

At his arraignment, Nicholson admitted to the offence and asked the court for leniency, telling the magistrate that he is the sole provider for his family.

As a first-time offender, Nicholson was spared an immediate prison sentence and fined $1,500 plus $5 cost of court. He has until December 31, 2026, to pay the fine or face six months in prison in default.

World.title: Free after 92 days: Trinidadian says failed Belize job arrangement left him with $11,470 Golden Bay Hotel bill
World.content:
Free after 92 days: Trinidadian says failed Belize job arrangement left him with $11,470 Golden Bay Hotel bill

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Trinidadian national Rubindra Dale Rampersad walked out of the Belize City Magistrate’s Court a free man on Friday after spending 92 days behind bars over an unpaid $11,470.24 hotel bill, and is now telling his side of the story.

The 46-year-old had been charged with making off without payment after allegedly leaving Golden Bay Hotel on May 29 without settling the bill accumulated during a month-long stay.

On Friday morning, a representative of Golden Bay Hotel confirmed to the court that the outstanding amount had been paid in full. Following a criminal mediation agreement, the charge against Rampersad was dismissed.

Rampersad, who appeared with attorney Kimberly Wallace of Lavenders Chambers, emerged from court shortly after midday and began his first interview as a free man by apologizing to our court reporter, whom he had treated disrespectfully during two previous court appearances.

He then sought to explain how he ended up in Belize and ultimately behind bars.

Rampersad said he travelled to Belize expecting to work in connection with the Millennium Challenge Account-Belize (MCA-Belize) programme. According to him, he had been promised approximately US$5,000 along with reimbursement of expenses, including his travel to Belize, but said the arrangement did not materialize as he had expected.

“I am no scam,” Rampersad said, maintaining that he travelled to Belize intending to work but found himself stranded without the financial support he expected.

His account is consistent with claims he made earlier in the case. News 5 reported in June that Rampersad alleged a procurement-related work arrangement included up to US$5,000 in relocation support, but that after he arrived he was told the reimbursement was not guaranteed. Police, meanwhile, said Golden Bay Hotel reported that a credit card used for the stay repeatedly failed and that Rampersad was intercepted at the airport after leaving the hotel without settling the bill.

MCA-Belize is the independent entity established to implement Belize’s US$125 million Millennium Challenge Corporation Compact, which focuses on education and energy. The organization has been publicly recruiting personnel for various positions throughout 2025 and 2026.

Rampersad was initially denied bail because the court considered him a flight risk, citing his lack of established ties to Belize. At subsequent hearings, the Chief Magistrate indicated bail could be considered if he secured a Belizean surety and confirmed prepaid accommodation, while his attorney, Darrell Bradley, pushed for the matter to be resolved through criminal mediation.

That mediation eventually succeeded, with Golden Bay agreeing to the settlement once its outstanding bill was paid.

Rampersad said he believes some of his constitutional rights were violated during his lengthy detention, though no court finding to that effect has been made.

Despite describing his incarceration as a difficult experience, Rampersad also spoke warmly about Belizeans and the people he met inside the Belize Central Prison.

“There are great people in prison,” he said, adding that he made friends during his more than three months behind bars and remains grateful to those who treated him well.

Rampersad leaves the ordeal without a criminal conviction in Belize and says he is simply happy to be free after 92 days in custody.

World.title: Police await CCTV after 77-year-old woman killed crossing Philip Goldson Highway
World.content:
Police await CCTV after 77-year-old woman killed crossing Philip Goldson Highway

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are awaiting surveillance footage as they investigate Thursday’s fatal traffic accident that claimed the life of 77-year-old Burrell Boom resident Erlene Gillett.

The accident occurred shortly before 11:30 a.m. on August 27 in the vicinity of Mile 2 on the Philip Goldson Highway.

Police say Gillett was attempting to cross the highway when she was struck by a Dodge Caravan being driven by a man whose name has not been released.

The vehicle has since been impounded as part of the investigation, while a sample was obtained from the driver and he was served with a Notice of Intended Prosecution.

During Friday’s police press briefing, Assistant Superintendent Stacy Smith said investigators have received assurances that surveillance footage from an establishment in the area may have captured the accident. That footage is expected to help police establish the exact circumstances surrounding the collision, including whether other motorists may have stopped to allow Gillett to cross.

Smith urged pedestrians to use designated crossing areas where available, but stressed that motorists also have a responsibility to remain alert, even when travelling within the speed limit.

Local media reports say Gillett was crossing the highway in front of My Lights when she was struck by a southbound minivan.

The investigation continues.

World.title: Police indicate inmate has died following apparent suicide attempt while in police custody
World.content:
Police indicate inmate has died following apparent suicide attempt while in police custody

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have indicated that an inmate who reportedly attempted to take his own life while in custody has since died, though police say further details on the case are still being gathered.

The matter arose during Friday afternoon’s police press briefing when reporters sought an update on the condition of the inmate.

Assistant Superintendent Stacy Smith indicated that her understanding was that the inmate had died, but said she had not yet received a complete briefing on the investigation.

Smith also indicated that a post-mortem examination was expected and said police hope to provide additional information on the matter by Monday.

Reporters raised concerns about the circumstances because the deceased was in the custody of the state at the time of the incident, placing a duty of care on the institution responsible for him.

Police did not provide the inmate’s identity, the facility where the incident occurred, or further details surrounding the apparent suicide attempt during Friday’s briefing.

The investigation remains ongoing.

World.title: International News: Missing persons near 2,000 in Nepal flood disaster
World.content:
International News: Missing persons near 2,000 in Nepal flood disaster

By Zoila Palma: The number of people reported missing after devastating flash floods in Nepal has surged to 1,924, according to the country’s disaster relief agency, as rescue teams continue searching areas devastated by a massive flood wave.

At least 517 foreign nationals are among those reported missing, although authorities have issued varying figures as the situation continues to develop, BBC reports.

Nepal’s reported death toll has risen to 579, while at least five people have died in Tibet, where 558 others are reported missing. Information from Tibet remains limited, with reports largely coming from Chinese state media as rescue and recovery operations continue near the Nepal-Tibet border.

The disaster has left widespread destruction in its wake, with one rescue worker describing the scene near the border as “nothing but ruins.”

Rescue teams are now working in extremely difficult terrain near Gyirong Port, where roads have been destroyed and dense forests and steep cliffs have hampered access.

China’s state broadcaster CCTV reported that firefighters from Tibet and Sichuan reached the area on Friday, including six Tibet fire and rescue personnel, 15 members of a Sichuan rescue team and a rescue dog.

World.title: Belize and regional partners strengthen Agricultural Disease surveillance
World.content:
Belize and regional partners strengthen Agricultural Disease surveillance

By Zoila Palma: Belize and other member countries of the International Regional Organization for Agricultural Health (OIRSA) have agreed to strengthen regional surveillance and coordination to protect agricultural production and trade from emerging diseases and pests. The agreement was reached during the 97th Extraordinary Meeting of the International Regional Committee for Agricultural Health (CIRSA) held today in Guatemala City.

The meeting brought together Ministers of Agriculture and other senior representatives from Mexico, Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Panama and the Dominican Republic.

Belize was represented by Luis Alex Balona, Minister of State in the Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and New Growth Industries. The meeting was chaired by Guatemala’s Minister of Agriculture, Livestock and Food, María Fernanda Rivera.

Among the major agricultural health threats discussed were African Swine Fever, Fusarium Wilt Tropical Race 4 and Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza. Regional authorities noted that these diseases can cross borders and cause significant impacts on agricultural production and international trade. To address the risks, countries agreed to maintain constant surveillance and strengthen standardized prevention and response protocols, particularly at borders, ports and airports.

The meeting also examined the growing impact of extreme weather events on agricultural health. Changes in rainfall patterns and rising temperatures can create favourable conditions for the emergence and spread of pests and diseases, making regional cooperation increasingly important. Authorities emphasized that coordinated action is essential to protect farmers and the communities that depend on healthy and resilient agricultural systems.

CIRSA members also reviewed efforts to strengthen OIRSA as a regional institution, including progress toward approving its 2026–2036 Strategic Plan, a new Investment Policy and updated organizational regulations. These measures are intended to improve the capacity of member countries to detect, prevent and respond to agricultural health threats while protecting food production and regional trade.

World.title: Belize hosts regional Fruit Fly meeting as 50-year Medfly Control programme reaches milestone
World.content:
Belize hosts regional Fruit Fly meeting as 50-year Medfly Control programme reaches milestone
