Poland’s government has approved a draft budget for 2027 that keeps defence, healthcare and the energy transition among its spending priorities, while projecting another year of heavy borrowing. The deficit is forecast at 7.1% of GDP, unchanged from 2026 but well above the level of 3.7% the government had committed to reach by 2027 after Poland was placed under the European Union’s excessive deficit procedure in 2024. Rada Ministrów przyjęła projekt ustawy budżetowej na 2027 rok. Projekt odpowiedzialnie łączy finansowanie bieżących potrzeb państwa i przedsięwzięć wzmacniających jego bezpieczeństwo oraz potencjał rozwojowy.#BudżetPolaków 🔗 https://t.co/SjWyBUwi8U pic.twitter.com/X9ue6cw5ns — Ministerstwo Finansów (@MF_GOV_PL) August 28, 2026 The budget – which must still be consulted with business and trade union representatives before being approved by parliament and then signed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki – sets total expenditure at 977.6 billion zloty (€225.4 billion), 58 billion zloty more than this year. Revenues are projected to rise by 68.4 billion zloty to 695 billion zloty, leaving a nominal budget deficit of 282.6 billion zloty, the highest on record and 10 billion zloty more than this year. Defence spending will remain high, at 198.1 billion zloty, equivalent to 4.5% of GDP, one of the highest levels in NATO. The healthcare budget will reach 274.1 billion zloty, up 26.3 billion zloty from 2026. Spending on energy security and transformation will rise 8.3% year-on-year to reach 19.7 billion zloty. The government expects GDP growth to remain strong, at 3% in 2027, while average inflation is forecast at 2.8%, within the central bank’s target of 2.5%, plus or minus one percentage point. Average wages are expected to rise by 5.9% next year in nominal terms, slightly slower than the 6.4% forecast for this year. The government expects that unemployment, measured according to the national methodology, will stand at 6% at the end of 2027, broadly unchanged from its current level. Poland’s gross borrowing needs are projected at 565 billion zloty in 2027, below the 688 billion zloty budgeted for this year. Debt-servicing costs, however, are expected to rise to 107 billion zloty, up 17 billion zloty from this year. Finance minister Andrzej Domański said that the rise in debt-servicing costs is driven by an increase in the overall volume of debt and the need to refinance bonds issued in 2020 and 2021 at very low interest rates. Poland's debt has been growing at the second-fastest rate in the EU this year, and is set to continue rising. What is behind this trend – and should we be worried – asks Alicja Ptak in the latest of her series of articles and podcasts on Poland’s economy https://t.co/1pvnb2ZxoY — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 30, 2025 The projected deficit leaves Poland under continued pressure to bring its public finances into line with EU fiscal rules. In 2024, the country was placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure after its deficit exceeded the bloc’s limit of 3%. Warsaw pledged at the time to bring the deficit below 3% by 2028. However, last year the deficit actually rose, from 6.4% of GDP in 2024 to 7.3% in 2025, which was the second-highest level among all EU member states. This year, Poland’s public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time on record. “The 2027 budget represents a continuation of expansionary fiscal policy, and Poland is making no progress in correcting its excessive deficit and is taking no action to bring it below 3% of GDP,” wrote analysts at ING Bank Śląski today. “The result is a further increase in public debt.” Poland’s public debt has passed 60% of GDP for the first time, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. The country is already under the EU's excessive deficit procedure, requiring it to take steps to bring public finances under greater control https://t.co/LNJ0YrP2Ge — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2026 Efforts to reduce the deficit have also been complicated by political stalemate between the government and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who has vetoed several fiscal measures, including tax increases. Nawrocki did, however, approve a new levy on banks that came into force this year. The situation has led two of the big three rating agencies, Fitch and Moody’s, to shift Poland’s credit outlook to negative. This year, Fitch warned that the political gridlock between Nawrocki and the government was making tackling the deficit and debt more difficult. However, speaking today, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that the 2027 budget reflects Poland’s position at a time when war is being waged across its eastern border and other conflicts are weighing on the country’s finances. Meanwhile, 2027 will also see pivotal parliamentary elections, at which Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, will seek a second term while the right-wing opposition, supported by Nawrocki, will attempt to win power. Ratings agency Fitch has again warned that the "political gridlock" between Poland's government president – such as the current clash over EU defence loans – is hindering efforts to tackle "large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt" https://t.co/JSqwwayTdm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 18, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish “vampire” burial sheds light on 17th-century efforts to keep the dead in their graves
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Researchers investigating an unusual 17th-century burial in northern Poland, in which the remains of a teenage girl were found with a padlock fastened to her toe and a sickle placed across her neck, believe the measures may have been intended to stop her returning from the dead. The burial, discovered in 2022 at an unmarked cemetery in the village of Pień, is an example of what archaeologists describe as “anti-vampiric” or “anti-demonic” burial, in which precautions were taken to protect the living from a deceased person believed to pose a danger. In a newly published academic paper, a team of researchers led by Dariusz Poliński, an archaeologist at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, say that the girl, whom they have named “Zosia”, may have been blamed by her contemporaries for misfortunes such as disease and famine. The unusual combination of objects that Zosia was buried with – a triangular padlock attached to her left big toe and an iron sickle laid across her throat, with the blade facing towards her neck – immediately attracted archaeologists’ attention when they were discovered. Poliński and his colleagues have used radiocarbon dating, DNA sequencing, isotope analysis and X-ray and microscopic imaging to investigate the burial. Their findings have now been published in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports. The researchers have established that Zosia, who was aged between 17 and 19, died around the mid-17th century, most likely between 1620 and 1674. Her grave appears to have been secured in two stages, with analysis of soil layers showing that it was reopened after the initial burial and the sickle added later. “It was unusual that there were two precautions, two methods of showing that this skeleton should be kept in the grave – so the fear of the body coming back to life was greater,” Poliński told CNN. The researchers say the padlock had several possible meanings in funerary symbolism. It could mark the end of earthly life and the transition to the world of the dead, prevent contact between the living and the dead, break a run of bad luck, or protect the community from the deceased returning. “In some interpretations, it was also believed to help halt the spread of epidemics,” Poliński told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The sickle had a more direct purpose: if the deceased tried to rise from the grave, it was positioned to sever the head or slit the throat, preventing her from returning to the world of the living. However, the latest findings suggest there may have been a third protective element. Researchers found “a distinct green discolouration” in the oral cavity, suggesting that an object containing a high proportion of copper had been placed in the girl’s mouth. Given the extent of the discolouration, they have largely ruled out the possibility that it was simply a coin. “The protective measures taken at the time of the original burial and subsequently after the grave was opened clearly demonstrate the immense fear of Zosia,” said Poliński, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. The grave of a "vampire child" – who was turned face down and secured with a padlock to ensure he could not rise from the grave – has been discovered in Poland Researchers believe the site was a cemetery for those excluded or feared by the local community https://t.co/Ez2QgvMnuX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2023 Poliński believes that the woman may have been ill or had a physical or mental disability, leading her neighbours to treat her badly while she was alive and fear that she would haunt them after her death. However, the researchers found no skeletal evidence of trauma, violence or disease that might explain her treatment, and her cause of death remains unknown. The Pień cemetery, which has not been marked on maps, contains several other unusual burials, including a child buried face down with a padlock beneath the foot and skeletons weighed down with rocks. This has led researchers to suggest that the cemetery may have been located on unconsecrated ground, away from a church or chapel, and used for people who were poor, disgraced, feared, or otherwise excluded from the community. Zosia’s burial, however, appears to have been unusual in another respect. Analysis suggests she was of relatively high social status. Traces of silk and gold-and-silver thread near her skull suggest she wore an expensive cap, a luxury item generally associated with nobility or wealth. Two years ago, sculptor and artist Oscar D. Nilsson unveiled a 3D facial reconstruction of Zosia, based on measurements of her skull and skeletal clues about her age, weight and health. The reconstruction shows a young woman with blue eyes, light brown hair and a broad nose. “It’s really ironic, in a way,” Nilsson told Reuters at the time. “These people burying her, they did everything they could in order to prevent her from coming back from the dead…We have done everything we can in order to bring her back to life.” A team of scientists has reconstructed the face of a 400-year-old woman, once believed by her neighbors to be a vampire, revealing the human story buried by supernatural beliefs https://t.co/Q6sipo7h4O pic.twitter.com/0gLVIEfaZi — Reuters (@Reuters) October 30, 2024 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. A dispute has emerged between Poland’s government and the office of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki over whether Poland would be willing to host allied nuclear weapons. Deputy defence minister Paweł Zalewski announced on Thursday that Poland wants to participate in the US-led NATO nuclear sharing programme, but without actually hosting warheads. That prompted criticism from Nawrocki’s senior foreign policy aide, Marcin Przydacz, who says Poland should host such weapons. Afterwards, he was asked by reporters if an expanded future US military presence in Poland might include nuclear weapons. “No. I would like to say this very clearly and openly: Poland does not want nuclear warheads on its territory,” replied Zalewski, quoted by broadcaster TVN. The minister added that Poland still wants to be part of NATO’s nuclear deterrence programme. However, he said that this could be achieved without hosting the weapons themselves. Those remarks triggered criticism from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party. Former PiS defence minister Mariusz Błaszczak said that refusing to host warheads “in practice means renouncing participation in nuclear sharing”. “Poland should strive for full participation in nuclear sharing,” added Błaszczak. “This is not a matter of Poland possessing its own nuclear weapons, but of strengthening NATO’s nuclear deterrence on the eastern flank.” Criticism also came from other sources, including retired Brigadier General Stanisław Koziej, who served as head of the National Security Bureau (BBN) of former President Bronisław Komorowski, who is an ally of the current government. Koziej called Zalewski’s announcement “an incomprehensible strategic mistake in the field of deterrence”. He rejected Błaszczak’s claim that refusing to host warheads would effectively exclude Poland from nuclear sharing. “We want to participate in NATO’s nuclear deterrence programme without wanting the stationing of nuclear weapons in Poland,” he wrote. “Thanks to our efforts, NATO has opened up precisely such a possibility.” In response to Koziej, Zalewski argued that “intentions do not deter, real capabilities do…above all, those whose use we ourselves decide upon”. Meanwhile, defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz also weighed in, declaring that “Poland remains strongly interested in participating in the NATO nuclear sharing programme” and is also “conducting talks regarding the proposal for participation in a European nuclear protective umbrella”. Przydacz added that “it is not true” the country wants to participate without actually hosting warheads. “Poland also wants to have warheads on its territory,” he said. Nawrocki, who is a close ally of President Donald Trump, has made clear his support for Poland seeking a nuclear sharing arrangement with the United States. A ban on the use of fireworks that was introduced last year by Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has been withdrawn after the local authorities decided not to appeal against a court decision revoking it. Kraków had argued that the ban would boost the safety and health of both humans and animals. However, opponents of the measures, including the provincial governor, who launched the legal challenge against it, argued that it was excessive and undermined constitutional freedoms. Kraków bez zakazu fajerwerków. Miasto nie zaskarży wyroku WSAhttps://t.co/rPEYNhEMAQ — Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) August 25, 2026 In November 2025, Kraków’s city council adopted a resolution banning fireworks, firecrackers, sparklers and other pyrotechnic materials being set off “for entertainment purposes”. The ban, which carried an exemption for last year’s New Year’s celebrations, applied in public spaces as well as private properties where the use of fireworks was deemed to impact public places. The city said the ban aimed to “protect the life, health and peace of residents” and “ensure public safety”, adding that the discharge of pyrotechnics created noise and air pollution and could pose a threat to the health and life of humans and animals. Some councillors also argued that a ban would benefit residents suffering from trauma, including World War Two veterans and Ukrainian refugees. The city’s then mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, cited a city poll finding that 67.5% of respondents supported a year-round ban on fireworks and 31.2% opposed it. However, the measures were criticised by the head of the Association of Pyrotechnic Importers and Distributors, Marta Smolińska, who told news service Puls Krakowa that the ban was an “extreme solution” that would hurt local businesses. She called instead for “promoting the responsible use of pyrotechnics”. In December, Krzysztof Klęczar, the government-appointed governor of the Małopolska province, of which Kraków is the capital, announced that he would challenge the ban in the Provincial Administrative Court. Klęczar argued that the measures may “violate the principle of proportionality of limiting constitutional freedoms and rights as well as the freedom…to conduct business activity”. National parks in Poland have appealed to revellers to refrain from using fireworks this New Year’s Eve to avoid awakening wild animals from their winter slumber. A number of cities have also called on residents to abandon the tradition to protect petshttps://t.co/T6RQHdsF9P — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 29, 2022 His arguments were endorsed by the court, which, in a ruling in late June, deemed the resolution introducing the ban “invalid” and ordered that the city of Kraków pay legal costs. The court said the ban “went beyond the competence of the city council” and “violated the principle of proportionality of the protection of constitutional freedoms and rights”. It added that it “was not necessary to protect health, life or public order”. While Kraków could have appealed against the ruling at the Supreme Administrative Court, it has decided not to take that step. An appeal “would probably have little chance of upholding the resolution,” spokeswoman Dominika Jaźwiecka-Bujalska told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Poland's largest opposition group has proposed a law banning fireworks, arguing that they cause distress, and even death, among domestic pets and wild animals https://t.co/UVzFMv3IEn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 23, 2021 At the national level, in 2021, Civic Coalition (KO) – which was then the largest opposition party and is now Poland’s main ruling party – proposed a law that would have banned the use of most fireworks and firecrackers to protect domestic and wild animals. While that legislation did not proceed beyond a parliamentary commission, two further bills seeking to limit the use of fireworks to protect animals are currently proceeding in parliament, reports local news service Portal Samorządowy. Several Polish cities have introduced their own restrictions, which in some cases have also faced legal challenges. Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city, also introduced a ban in January, which was likewise revoked in an administrative court after facing opposition from the provincial governor, reports PAP. Year-round bans remain in place in the Baltic resort town of Sopot, where there is an exemption for 31 December and 1 January, and the southern mountain resort town of Zakopane, a popular destination for New Year’s revellers, where the New Year period is included. The president of the Polish Olympic Committee (PKOl), Radosław Piesiewicz, has been detained as part of a criminal investigation into Zondacrypto, a cryptocurrency firm that collapsed earlier this year and was a major sponsor of Poland’s Olympic team. The development comes a day after Waldemar Żurek, Poland’s justice minister and prosecutor general, revealed that prosecutors are investigating possible crimes relating to Zondacrypto’s financing of various individuals and organisations, including PKOl, Piesiewicz, and figures from Poland’s right-wing opposition. Dziś w ramach śledztwa w sprawie ZondaCrypto zatrzymany został Radosław P. Prokuratura będzie przekazywała dalsze informacje po zakończeniu czynności z jego udziałem, prowadzonych w Śląskim Wydziale PZ PK. — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) August 27, 2026 On Thursday afternoon, Żurek announced that Piesiewicz had been detained and would be charged. He said he was unable to reveal what the charges would be, but confirmed that prosecutors are investigating a €40,000 watch reportedly given to Piesiewicz by the former head of Zondacrypto, Przemysław Kral. Under Piesiewicz’s leadership, PKOl signed an agreement in 2025 with Zondacrypto that made the crypto firm the main sponsor of the Polish team at this year’s Winter Olympics in Italy. However, in April, Zondacrypto began to come under scrutiny after customers began reporting being unable to access their funds. The firm subsequently collapsed and Kral went into hiding abroad. Prosecutors estimate losses to its clients of at least 350 million zloty (€81.4 million). At a press conference today, Żurek confirmed that Piesiewicz had been detained in connection with the investigation into Zondacrypto, which concerns suspected large-scale fraud and other criminal activity. The development comes days after two leading media outlets, Wirtualna Polska and TVN, published a joint investigation in which they alleged that Piesiewicz received a watch worth €40,000 and other gifts from Kral. The gifts were allegedly given in exchange for Piesiewicz intervening on behalf of Zondacrypto with Poland’s consumer protection authority, UOKiK. Piesiewicz denies the allegations and says he bought the watch with his own money, with Kral simply helping facilitate the purchase. 🔴Szef Zondacrypto, prezes PKOl i złoty zegarek za 40 tysięcy euro Prezes Polskiego Komitetu Olimpijskiego Radosław Piesiewicz dostał od szefa Zondacrypto Przemysława Krala zegarek Patek Philippe wart 40 tysięcy euro oraz inne prezenty – wynika z ustaleń wspólnego śledztwa… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) August 24, 2026 Piesiewicz, who became head of PKOl in 2023 under Poland’s former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, has long been a controversial figure. In 2024, after PiS had lost power, he publicly clashed with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s new government following Poland’s poor performance at the Paris Olympics, where the Polish team finished with its lowest medal haul since 1956. This year, as Zondocrypto fell into crisis, it emerged that the company had failed to provide promised bonuses to Polish athletes following the Winter Olympics. In May, 82 of the 106 members of the Polish Olympic Committee supported a motion calling for an extraordinary meeting at which the sole item on the agenda was the dismissal of Piesiewicz from his position. He has so far refused to convene the meeting. Poland has finished @Paris2024 with just one gold and 10 medals in total – its worst result since 1956. The prime minister has suggested there are failings in how Polish sport is managed. But the head of the Olympic committee has blamed the government https://t.co/iS9OqF1RuB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2024 On Wednesday, Piesiewicz and PKOl were among a list of individuals and organisations Żurek announced were being investigated by prosecutors over potential crimes relating to financing they had received from Zondacrypo. Most of them are linked to Poland’s right-wing opposition. They included the foundations of Zbigniew Ziobro, a deputy leader of PiS, and Przemysław Wipler, a former PiS politician now associated with the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja); conservative broadcaster Republika and its head, Tomasz Sakiewicz; and the Polish version of the American CPAC conference. Earlier this year, Tusk claimed that Zondacrypto’s financial success was “rooted not only in Russian money linked to…one of Russia’s most powerful mafia groups, but also to the Russian security services”. His ruling coalition has three times passed a bill to introduce tougher regulation of the crypto market. However, each time, it has been vetoed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who argues that the measures are too restrictive. Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a collapsed crypto firm, of organisations and individuals linked to the right-wing opposition, including the Polish version of US conservative conference CPAC https://t.co/swceV864nA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 26, 2026 On Wednesday, Tusk wrote on social media that “we now know why Nawrocki and PiS have blocked the cryptocurrency bill like maniacs”. “Cash for watches worth €40,000 euros, [financing] for media, election parties, foundations of right-wing politicians,” he continued. “And the ‘Zonda’ show is just getting started.” PiS figures have, however, denied any wrongdoing in relation to Zondacrypto. “I’m outraged by the suggestion that PiS was involved in anything illegal,” one of the party’s MPs, Piotr Kaleta, told news website Interia. He noted that no evidence had been presented and no indictments made against PiS politicians. “Instead, we have ministers threatening to hold others accountable, and nothing has happened. This is simply meant to cover up the incompetence of the current government.” Teraz już wiemy, dlaczego z uporem maniaka @NawrockiKn i PiS blokowali ustawę o kryptowalutach. World.title: Poland asks EU to fine Meta €250m over scam Facebook ads

Poland has formally requested that the European Commission fine Meta, the owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, €250 million (1.1 billion zloty) for failing to tackle fraudulent advertising on its platforms. Its decision follows a high-profile campaign by Rafał Brzoska, the billionaire owner of Polish delivery giant InPost, over scam adverts on Facebook that exploit fake images of him and other prominent Polish public figures, including President Karol Nawrocki. Platformy cyfrowe muszą ponosić pełną odpowiedzialność za swoje działania i dlatego zawnioskowałem o nałożenie na Metę kary w wysokości miliarda złotych. Po analizie materiałów, w tym tych otrzymanych od Meta, a także kolejnych doniesień medialnych o braku kontroli nad… pic.twitter.com/1zSZg8MGf4 — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) August 27, 2026 On Thursday morning, digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski announced that he had sent a request to the European Commission to take action against Meta, including fining it €250 million. “Inaction and ineffectiveness in combating harmful s and fraudulent content targeting Poles will not be tolerated,” wrote Gawkowski. “I expect the European Commission to conduct the proceedings swiftly and impose the fine. There is more than enough evidence.” The minister also called on Meta itself to “immediately introduce effective tools to eliminate scams, fake s, and the promotion of illegal applications. This Wild West on the platform must come to an end”. Gawkowski shared an image of the first page of a letter he had sent to Henna Virkkunen, the European commissioner for technological sovereignty, security and democracy, in which he argued that Meta’s failure to combat fraud may violate the EU’s Digital Services Act. He pointed to a study by CERT Polska, a Polish state IT security body, which found that, of 122 adverts reported to Meta as being fraudulent, in 106 cases the company rejected requests to remove them. Gawkowski noted that the European Consumer Organisation has reported similar concerns to the EU. On Wednesday, Gawkowski also shared copies of correspondence he had exchanged with Meta earlier this month. In response to the minister’s concerns, the tech firm had argued that it “does not seek to profit from” fraudulent advertising and outlined steps it was taking to address the problem. Meta disclosed that, between July 2025 and June 2026, it had, in Poland alone, removed 380,000 examples of content and 137,000 adverts for violating its policies on fraudulent practices. It noted that the vast majority were removed before users even reported them. Meta przesłała odpowiedź o działaniach związanych ze zwalczaniem scamów i wskazuje, że niektóre dane przekazuje z zachowaniem ścisłej poufności. W państwie szanującym obywatela takie dane muszą być jawne i dlatego podjąłem decyzję o ujawnieniu treści pisma. W piśmie Meta… — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) August 26, 2026 Gawkowski’s intervention follows a high-profile campaign by Brzoska, one of Poland’s richest people and who, along with his wife, former TV presenter and businesswoman Omenaa Mensah, is a prominent public figure. Brzoska and Mensah have long complained about the unauthorised use of their likenesses in fraudulent social-media advertising, especially on Facebook. In 2024, Poland’s data protection authority ordered Meta to stop displaying adverts that featured false reports of Mensah’s death to promote scams. Earlier this month, Brzoska renewed his campaign, highlighting an example of a scam on Facebook that used a fake image of him being handcuffed by police in his home. Tak działa koncern @Meta w Polsce-nieustająco tolerując fake newsy na mój i wiele innych publicznych osób temat… Może innym to nie przeszkadza, ale jeśli moje małoletnie dzieciaki wysyłają mi te screeny pytając "o co chodzi Tato?", to jak się polskiemu zarządowi tej gównianej… pic.twitter.com/rp4CUscah1 — Rafał Brzoska (@RBrzoska) August 14, 2026 Brzoska – who also pointed to examples of Facebook running fake adverts featuring other prominent Polish figures, including President Nawrocki – launched a petition calling for platforms that run scam adverts to be fined 150% of the revenue they received from them. The petition – which, at the time of writing, has been signed by almost 91,000 people – cited leaked data, reported by Reuters last year, indicating that Meta estimated 10% of its sales in 2024, around €16 billion, came from advertising scams or illegal products and services. In comments to Reuters, Meta said at the time that the estimate was “rough and overly inclusive” and that the actual figure was lower. But it declined to provide an updated figure. Nowy dzień i nowy scam serwowany bez żadnych oporów przez @Meta z Prezydentem @NawrockiKn w roli głównej. Ale to managerowie Meta (Robert Bednarski, Jakub Turowski,Tomasz Parfjanowicz i Ewa Tumanow) mówią,że nic nie mogą w tej sprawie. Jeśli chcemy temu powiedzieć stanowcze… pic.twitter.com/ZVZl04yYY1 — Rafał Brzoska (@RBrzoska) August 24, 2026 This week, Brzoska welcomed Gawkowski’s moves against Meta. He also noted that, while the minister’s letter to Meta had been addressed to Jakub Turowski, Meta’s director of public policy for Central and Eastern Europe, the firm’s response to him was unsigned. “First-class cowardice,” declared Brzoska, who has repeatedly published the names of four of Meta’s senior Polish managers, including Turowski. The United States has donated $2.1 million worth of equipment for border protection, including drones and thermal imaging cameras, to Poland under an agreement signed on Tuesday. The Polish border guard says that the package is part of a wider US programme, worth an estimated €12 million, to support Poland and the Baltic states in response to the migration crisis engineered by Russia’s ally Belarus on their borders. Stronger border security strengthens our shared security. Today in Warsaw, the United States and Poland marked the donation of more than $2 million in U.S.-funded equipment to the Polish Border Guard @Straz_Graniczna . The donation, funded by the State Department’s @StateINL and… pic.twitter.com/8Mh1eHLo0t — US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) August 25, 2026 “Stronger border security strengthens our shared security,” declared the US embassy in Warsaw, announcing the donation of equipment, which includes 45 drones and nine advanced thermal imaging cameras. “This is just the next step in our security partnership,” they added. “Additional equipment, training, and expertise will follow.” The Polish border guard also confirmed that the support includes training packages and bilateral study visits, as well as the delivery of 15 snowmobiles to Poland next year. On Tuesday, it also hosted a delegation of senior figures from the US Border Patrol and US Customs and Border Protection for talks on “exchanging experiences, strengthening cooperation, and implementing advanced technologies in response to migratory pressures”. Since 2021, Belarus has been encouraging and assisting migrants – mainly from Africa and Asia – to attempt to irregularly cross into the European Union over its borders with Poland, Lithuania and Latvia. Tens of thousands of attempted crossings have been reported each year. In response, Poland has strengthened physical and electronic barriers along the border with Belarus. It has also eased rules on the use of firearms by uniformed officers to protect the border, and has temporarily banned asylum applications by people who irregularly cross from Belarus. As a result of such efforts, attempted illegal crossings are down 98% so far this year, while Poland also claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who do manage to cross. The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98% Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 After meeting with American officials on Tuesday, the Polish border guard said that the head of the US delegation, Jason E. Schneider, acting chief patrol agent for the US Border Patrol’s Rio Grande Valley sector, had praised Poland as a “model and benchmark” for dealing with migratory pressures. It also noted that Stephanie Holmes, the deputy chief of mission at the US embassy, had noted Poland’s role “protecting the entire eastern flank of NATO and [acting] as a guarantor of transatlantic security”. Belarus is a close ally of Russia, and the migration crisis engineered by Minsk on the EU and NATO’s eastern flank is seen as one element of the so-called “hybrid warfare” being waged by Moscow against the West. 🤝 Polska i USA wspólnie dbają o bezpieczne granice i stabilność całego regionu! 🇵🇱🇺🇸 W Warszawie odbyło się spotkanie kierownictwa polskich i amerykańskich służb, w tym U.S. Border Patrol. Wydarzeniu towarzyszyło podpisanie umowy z Departamentem Stanu USA, dzięki której na… pic.twitter.com/rN9umTfPfU — Straż Graniczna (@Straz_Graniczna) August 25, 2026 The Polish border guard reported that, as well as donating equipment, the US has since 2024 been providing and funding “advanced tactical and technical training”, including “courses in border protection tactics”, for Polish officers. Next month, they will provide training in operating the newly donated drones, which are being provided as part of a broader $12 million US programme to support Poland and the Baltic states in “direct response…to the situation on the Belarusian border”, said the Polish border guard. In January this year, Polish officials also conducted study visits to El Paso and Detroit in the United States to “learn about methods used for counteracting illegal migration on the US borders with Mexico and Canada”. A further visit to the southern US border is scheduled for November. Poland says that “specialists from the Middle East” have been brought to Belarus to dig tunnels under the border for migrants to cross into Poland. Four such tunnels have been discovered this year, including one last week that was used by 180 migrants https://t.co/4ConkQnj8z — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 In 2024, the EU itself announced that it would allocate €170 million to help member states neighbouring Russia and Belarus “counter hybrid threats from the weaponisation of migration”, which it said was being used “as a political tool to destabilise EU society”. Poland was allocated the largest share of the fund, with €52 million. Last year, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Poland’s border with Belarus, where she thanked Warsaw for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” being orchestrated by Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom she called a “predator”. Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a cryptocurrency firm that collapsed earlier this year, of organisations and individuals linked to Poland’s right-wing opposition. Meanwhile, a lawyer representing Przemysław Kral, who was Zondacrypto’s head when it collapsed, has revealed that his client is cooperating with prosecutors. In a statement published on Tuesday, Żurek said investigators had secured extensive evidence, questioned numerous witnesses, and carried out proceedings involving suspects who have already been formally charged, though he declined to identify them or disclose the charges. However, he added that there had now been a “breakthrough in the investigation”, including “looking into illegal financial flows towards politicians and entities associated with them”. CPAC and the Olympic committee were previously sponsored by Zondacrypto, while Republika sold extensive advertising space to the crypto firm. Żurek also said they were investigating potential financing by Zondacrypto of actions taken by individuals who helped fugitive former PiS deputy justice minister Marcin Romanowski. World.title: Slavia Prague to Face Bayern Munich, Arsenal and Porto in Champions League
World.content:
Slavia Prague have learned their eight opponents for the 2026/27 UEFA Champions League league phase following Thursday’s draw in Monaco.

Slavia will play four matches at home at Eden Arena and four away.

At home, Slavia will welcome Arsenal, Aston Villa, Villarreal and Lens. Their away fixtures will take them to Bayern Munich, Porto, Fenerbahçe and Sabah Baku in Azerbaijan.



The most high-profile home fixture will be against Arsenal, the reigning Premier League champions. Slavia also faced the London club in last season’s Champions League campaign, making the return meeting at Eden Arena particularly notable.

The toughest away assignment is likely to come in Munich, where Slavia will face six-time European champions Bayern at the Allianz Arena. The team will also travel to Portugal to meet Porto and to Istanbul for a match against Fenerbahçe.

The longest trip of the league phase will be to Baku to face Azerbaijani champions Sabah, who are making their debut in the Champions League league phase.

How the Champions League league phase works

The 2026/27 competition is being played under UEFA’s new league-phase format for the third consecutive season. Instead of a traditional group stage, all 36 teams are placed in one league table.

Each club plays eight matches against eight different opponents, with two opponents drawn from each of the four seeding pots. Every team has four home and four away games.

The top eight teams in the final standings will advance directly to the round of 16. Teams finishing ninth to 24th will enter a knockout playoff for the remaining eight places, while clubs finishing from 25th to 36th will be eliminated.

The league phase begins on September 8–10, with six rounds taking place before the end of 2026. The final two matchdays will be played in January, with the league phase concluding on January 27. UEFA will announce the exact dates and kick-off times for each individual match later.

World.title: MINT Market Returns to Prague’s Náplavka with More Than 130 Local Brands
World.content:
MINT Market returns to Prague’s Rašín Embankment on Sunday, September 6, bringing more than 130 independent brands and makers to the Vltava riverbank.

From 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., visitors can browse a wide selection of independent fashion, jewellery, ceramics, natural cosmetics, illustrations and original accessories, with many of the products made by small Czech and Prague-based businesses.



The popular design market is also known for its relaxed atmosphere, food stalls and chill-out area. Admission is free, and the riverside venue is fully accessible. The event is suitable for visitors of all ages.

MINT Market has been supporting independent and local creators since 2010.

Over the past 16 years, the project has grown from a small market into a nationwide platform, hosting more than 450 events in over 20 Czech cities and bringing together a community of more than 1,500 designers and makers.

For visitors, the September event offers a chance to discover products that are often made locally and in small quantities, while meeting the people behind the brands directly.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The best design markets in CZ (@mintmarket.cz)

“Supporting small and local brands has been one of the core ideas of our project from the very beginning,” says MINT Market organizer Lenka Šašková.

“We provide creators with a place where they can showcase their products and meet their customers, because nothing can replace a personal meeting.”

The full list of vendors and further information about the September market can be found on the MINT Market website. Updates are also available through the Facebook event and Instagram.

World.title: Historic Invalidovna Building in Prague Begins Major Reconstruction
World.content:
The long-awaited reconstruction of Prague’s Invalidovna has officially begun.

The Baroque complex in Karlín will undergo a major renovation costing CZK 2.15 billion, with work scheduled for completion in 2030.

The project is the largest investment in the history of the National Heritage Institute (NPÚ). Alongside the restoration of the historic building, two new extensions will be constructed on the southern side of the complex.



One will provide facilities for the Prague Philharmonic Choir, while the other will house technical infrastructure needed to operate the site.

Much of Invalidovna will remain open to the public

Once the reconstruction is complete, the NPÚ will use part of the complex for restoration workshops, laboratories, archives and study rooms.

An underground garage with space for 50 vehicles is also planned.

Around 80 percent of the complex is expected to remain accessible to the public. The restored site will include exhibition and conference spaces, visitor routes through the Baroque interiors, a café and facilities for children’s groups operated by Prague 8.

A new multi-purpose hall in one of the extensions will be suitable for concerts, conferences and other events. The modern section will also contain technical facilities that cannot be accommodated inside the protected historic building.

The courtyard and gardens will be opened through the original entrances.

A Baroque complex with a long military history

Invalidovna was built between 1731 and 1737 based on plans by Kilián Ignác Dientzenhofer, one of the leading architects of the Czech Baroque. The institution provided accommodation and care for war veterans and their families until 1935.

The original complex was designed at a time when European armies were beginning to develop more systematic forms of care for soldiers who had been wounded or disabled in war.

Military campaigns were often accompanied by outbreaks of diseases such as cholera and typhus, which could kill even soldiers whose battlefield injuries were not life-threatening. Separate psychiatric institutions were later established for veterans suffering severe mental trauma after their military service.

World.title: PIZZA! PIZZA! POP-UP Returns to Holešovice Market on September 3

World.title: Manifesto Market’s Craft Beer Returns for Its Third Edition

World.title: More Czechs Are Living Paycheck to Paycheck, New Survey Finds
World.content:
The number of Czechs who have nothing left from their paycheck at the end of the month is rising.

This year, 13 percent say they have no money left after covering their expenses, up from 9 percent last year. Meanwhile, 84 percent have at least a small amount left over, five percentage points less than in 2025.

The findings come from a May survey conducted by loan provider Provident Financial among 1,000 respondents.



According to the survey, Czechs’ ability to save is declining. Only 43 percent of respondents have at least 20 percent of their monthly income left after covering their expenses, down nine percentage points from last year. Almost half of Czechs nevertheless regularly set aside part of their paycheck each month.

At the same time, their overall financial resilience appears to be improving. More than a quarter of respondents have enough savings to cover their expenses for more than a year, compared with just 15 percent last year. The share of people with no financial reserve at all has also fallen, from 18 percent in 2025 to 13 percent this year.

The gap between men and women in the amount of money left at the end of the month has also narrowed. This year, 45 percent of men have at least 20 percent of their paycheck left after expenses, compared with 59 percent last year. Among women, the figure has fallen from 45 percent to 39 percent.

The share of Czechs with enough savings to cover 12 months without their main source of income has increased sharply this year, rising by 11 percentage points compared with 2025. At the same time, the proportion of respondents whose savings would last less than three months fell to 12 percent, down from 17 percent a year earlier.

Men are considerably more likely than women to report having enough savings to cover at least six months of expenses. The figure is 63 percent among men, compared with 39 percent among women.

Education also appears to play an important role in financial preparedness. Seven in ten respondents with a university degree say they have enough savings to cover at least six months, compared with 43 percent among people with lower levels of education.

World.title: Not Ready for Summer to End? 3 Places to Take the Kids Before August Ends
World.content:
The end of the summer holidays is in sight. While school supplies, pencil cases and sports shoes are already making their way onto shopping lists, there are still a few days of summer left to enjoy.

Before the September school routine kicks in, here are three ways to make the most of the final days of August with the family.



Letni Letna

When: 12–31 August

Where: Prague, Letenské sady

Letenské sady is taking on a new look until 31 August, transforming into a colourful festival village. The Letní Letná Festival isn’t just about evening acrobatics for adults. It also offers a programme for younger visitors called Letní Letná for Children.

From morning until late afternoon, the huge children’s tent comes alive with fairy-tale performances and other activities. Kids can take part in creative and juggling workshops, explore an interactive play area made from recycled materials or take a ride on the iconic hand-carved wooden carousel.

Most of the children’s activities take place under the festival tents, so an unexpected rain shower won’t disrupt the day.

The festival also offers a “Night Watch” childcare service for children aged four and up. Parents can enjoy the evening programme while experienced entertainers look after their children.

When: 24–29 August

Where: Liberec and the surrounding area

Fancy a trip beyond Prague at the end of August? Head north to Liberec from 24 to 29 August, when the city hosts Crystal Valley Week, a celebration of Czech glassmaking and jewellery.

This year’s theme focuses on the interconnection of cultures, with the Czech glass bead at the centre of the programme. Children can also enjoy a free ride aboard the special Crystal Tram, which has been decorated this year to resemble a long-distance train.

There are plenty of opportunities to make your own jewellery from glass beads, with workshops and craft sessions taking place throughout Liberec for both children and adults.

When: Sunday, 30 August, 11:00–19:00

Where: Prague, Ladronka Park

On the last Sunday of the summer holidays, skip cooking lunch and head to the F.O.O.D. Picnic in Prague’s Ladronka Park. The popular event returns for its 16th edition this year.

Entry to the festival grounds is free, with 120 food and farm stalls to explore, including food trucks. There is also a large children’s zone with games and creative workshops, as well as a raffle for younger visitors.

It’s a family-friendly way to spend the final Sunday of the holidays, combining food, activities and a relaxed atmosphere before the new school year begins.

World.title: Airbnb Accounts for 1 Percent of Prague’s Housing Stock, Analysis Finds
World.content:
Prague’s short-term rental market has grown into a professional business but Airbnb accounts for only a small share of the city’s housing stock, according to a new analysis.

In June 2026, around 7,878 entire apartments and houses in Prague were actively listed on Airbnb. With roughly 720,000 apartments across the capital, that represents about 1.1 percent of the total housing stock.

The situation is very different in individual parts of the city. In Prague 1, Airbnb-listed properties account for around one-fifth of all apartments, according to the Prague Institute of Planning and Development (IPR). In Prague 2, the share is around 7 percent, while in some outer districts it is below 0.5 percent.



The concentration of short-term rentals has also changed the nature of the market. IPR data show that hosts managed an average of two apartments in 2019. By 2024, that figure had risen to three, while more than half of Prague’s Airbnb listings were operated by hosts with at least five properties.

This means short-term accommodation is increasingly being run as a business rather than as occasional home-sharing.

Prague’s housing shortage is much larger

Despite the impact Airbnb can have in central neighborhoods, the analysis points to a much bigger problem behind Prague’s housing crisis — a long-term shortage of new construction.

Since 2006, Prague has accumulated a housing deficit of more than 91,000 apartments, according to the analysis. That shortfall is about 11.5 times larger than the number of apartments currently listed on Airbnb.

Even if every Airbnb property in the city were suddenly returned to the long-term rental market, Prague would still be short more than 83,000 homes.

The accumulated construction deficit reportedly became larger than the number of active Airbnb apartments around 2009 or 2010. Since then, the gap has continued to grow.

This suggests that Prague’s housing crisis began well before short-term rentals reached their current scale.

Tourism brings other concerns

Housing availability is also not the only issue surrounding short-term rentals.

Residents in central Prague have complained about noise, disruption and visitors staying in residential buildings.

The city also collects accommodation fees from short-term stays, although payment is not automatic because apartment owners must register and pay the fees themselves.

The debate over Airbnb in Prague therefore extends beyond housing. While short-term rentals can change the character of central neighborhoods and create problems for residents, the latest figures suggest that the city’s wider housing shortage is primarily the result of years of insufficient construction.

World.title: PM Magyar hits back at critics of Hungary’s new asset recovery office, his own supporters among others: ‘They are harming the country’
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has strongly defended the newly established National Office for Asset Recovery and Asset Protection (NVVH), accusing those who seek to undermine or discredit its work of opposing efforts to recover allegedly stolen public assets.

In a video posted on Facebook on Friday, Magyar said the new authority should certainly be criticised and scrutinised, and that its performance should be held to account. However, he argued that anyone who weakens, discredits or obstructs its work for political reasons is deliberately causing harm.

His comments came after the Hungarian Parliament elected Anna Unger as the NVVH’s president and Katalin Tasnádi as deputy president responsible for investigations.

Magyar: The new office must be judged by its results

Addressing supporters of the governing Tisza Party, Magyar said it was “extremely unfair and unjust” to question the commitment of MPs or government members to political change simply because of the parliamentary decision concerning the leadership of the new office.

According to the prime minister, those who genuinely support political change and want an effective asset recovery authority should judge its leadership based on its future actions and results. Magyar also insisted that the selection process had been professional and transparent.

He said he had recently spoken by telephone with Miklós Ligeti, legal director of Transparency International Hungary and one of the candidates considered for the position.

“He confirmed to me that he also considered the procedure constitutional, lawful and fair,” Magyar said.

The prime minister also urged public figures, including former MPs and former government officials, to reconsider their criticism of the authority and its newly appointed leadership.

“Those who try to trip up those responsible for recovering public assets right at the starting line will later find it difficult to explain whose interests they were actually serving,” Magyar said.

If you missed it: PM Magyar announces headquarters of new asset recovery office

‘The biggest Hungarian economic crimes ever seen’

Magyar described Tasnádi as one of Hungary’s best-prepared prosecutors and said her task would be to investigate what he called “the biggest Hungarian economic crimes ever seen” and identify those responsible. The prime minister also said the government wanted to speed up criminal proceedings.

He argued that it was unacceptable for criminal cases to take five to ten years to conclude and said the government would submit every necessary legislative amendment to Parliament to shorten the time required for investigations, prosecutions and court proceedings.

The NVVH is intended to play a central role in one of the Tisza Party’s key political pledges: recovering public assets that the government alleges were improperly taken and ensuring that those responsible face consequences.

NVVH leaders to receive 24-hour police protection

Magyar also highlighted the risks associated with investigating organised economic crime. He said that fighting and investigating the “mafia” was among the most dangerous tasks and confirmed that the leaders of the new authority would receive 24-hour personal protection from the police.

Magyar condemns Fidesz comparison with the ÁVH

The prime minister also sharply criticised the opposition Fidesz party for comparing the NVVH with the ÁVH, Hungary’s communist-era State Protection Authority. Magyar called the comparison “despicable” and said it was a shameful insult to the memory of the ÁVH’s victims and the legacy of the 1956 revolution.

He said he was not surprised that Fidesz was attacking the new authority and its leadership with what he described as low-level political tactics, claiming that the party had “plundered this wonderful country” over the past 16 years.

As a result, he argued, its representatives had something to fear and something to lose from effective asset recovery.

Magyar called on members of the public not to fall for what he described as personal and hurtful provocations. Instead, he urged Hungarians to support those taking on the task of recovering public assets and to defend them against what he called attacks without any factual basis.

‘Now something will happen’

Concluding his video, Magyar wished the new authority’s current and future employees success. “Work bravely, work freely,” he said, adding that he hoped that in a few years no Hungarian would again have to say, as people had so often said in previous decades, that “nothing ever happens in this country”.

“Because now something will happen,” the prime minister concluded.

World.title: Russia tells Hungary’s Péter Magyar to stop ‘hesitating’ over Paks II nuclear project
World.content:
A senior Russian senator has urged Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar to stop wavering over the controversial Paks II nuclear power plant project, warning that energy security and affordable electricity should not become the subject of “political games”.

Elena Perminova, first deputy chair of the International Affairs Committee of Russia’s Federation Council, issued the warning on Friday as tensions continue to grow between the Hungarian government and Russian state nuclear giant Rosatom over the future of Paks II.

“Prime Minister of Hungary Péter Magyar should stop hesitating and take the position of constructive, responsible work,” Perminova told Russian state news agency RIA Novosti. She argued that “security, energy sovereignty and affordable electricity for Hungarian citizens are not a field for political games”.

Have you heard? Russia threatens to cut oil and gas supplies to Hungary after Budapest labels Moscow a security threat

Russia defends Rosatom’s role in Paks II

Perminova also praised Russia’s nuclear industry, echoing President Vladimir Putin’s claim that Russia is the “absolute and undisputed world leader” in the nuclear power plant construction market. She said Russia possessed expertise covering the entire nuclear energy chain, from uranium mining and enrichment to fuel production, reactor design and construction, staff training and waste disposal.

According to the senator, the reliability of Russian nuclear technology has already been demonstrated, while Rosatom continues to build nuclear power plants around the world. Perminova also contrasted Russia’s position with what she described as the West’s energy crisis and dependence on external energy sources.

She claimed Hungary was already benefiting from cheap and reliable energy thanks to former prime minister Viktor Orbán’s pragmatic policies, and accused Magyar’s statements of posing “a direct threat” to Hungary’s own economy.

According to Perminova, continued cooperation with Rosatom on Paks II would serve Hungary’s “vital interests” and contribute to energy stability across Europe.

Budapest and Rosatom clash over the project

The latest Russian criticism follows increasingly sharp disagreements between the Hungarian government and Rosatom over the progress and cost of Paks II. On 13 August, Rosatom CEO Alexey Likhachev told Russian journalists that construction of the two new reactors had accelerated and that the company was following the timetable agreed with the Hungarian client.

Work on the foundation of the fifth reactor building is reportedly around 80 per cent complete, with more than 18,000 cubic metres of concrete already poured. Rosatom says preparations for the first concrete pour for the sixth unit are also progressing, while equipment for both reactors is being manufactured.

However, Magyar struck a very different tone the following day. Speaking at a press conference about the water-management measures around the existing Paks nuclear plant, the Hungarian prime minister questioned whether Rosatom had actually complied with its contractual commitments.

“If they had complied with the contract, Paks II would already have been operating in 2024,” Magyar said, while claiming that the project could now cost twice as much as originally planned.

He also famously argued that, after spending around HUF 1,000 billion (approx. EUR 2.75 billion), “there are only two large holes” at the site. Magyar has stressed that not all delays can be blamed on Rosatom, but said the Russian company nevertheless bears some responsibility.

Could Rosatom be pushed out of Paks II?

The dispute has raised the possibility that Hungary could seek major changes to the Paks II project — potentially even reducing or ending Rosatom’s role. At the same time, completely abandoning the existing project and starting again from scratch could prove extremely expensive, particularly given the work and equipment already in place.

Rosatom says the fifth reactor’s foundation is progressing, while excavation work for the sixth unit is also underway. Major equipment has already been produced or is being manufactured, including reactor components and a 730-tonne core catcher delivered to the construction site in 2024.

The project also involves companies from several countries beyond Hungary and Russia. French engineering group Alstom is supplying the turbines, while American, Czech, French, Dutch, German, Austrian, Swiss, Slovak and Turkish companies are also involved.

Rosatom currently says around 500 people are working on the project.

World.title: What’s the public’s problem with Unger? PM Magyar hits back at critics of Hungary’s new asset recovery chief
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar has hit back at criticism surrounding Anna Róza Unger, who was elected president of Hungary’s newly established National Asset Protection and Asset Recovery Office (NVVH) by Parliament on Friday.

Magyar responded to the criticism in several Facebook posts following Unger’s election, arguing that the performance of a public official should ultimately be judged by their actions rather than by the opinions of their critics.

“In a functioning and humane country, a leader’s work is judged by their actions, not by the opinions of pundits,” Magyar wrote. He added that choosing the head of a major public institution should not be treated as a popularity contest.

“The selection of the head of a serious institution is not an elimination show and not a vote on popularity,” the prime minister said.

Magyar takes aim at Ákos Hadházy

Magyar also appeared to respond directly to criticism from former MP Ákos Hadházy, who has questioned aspects of the selection process for the new office’s leadership. Hadházy announced that he would submit a public-interest data request to the minister responsible for the Prime Minister’s Office in an effort to obtain information about the evaluation system used in the recruitment process.

In response, Magyar wrote that the “so-called expert” was asking the Prime Minister’s Office for information even though Parliament had conducted the selection process. The prime minister also referred to Hadházy, writing:

“Many people wanted a veterinarian to be appointed to head the NVVH and the Prosecutor General’s Office, and now they object that we did not choose a lawyer.”

Magyar did not name Hadházy directly in the post. However, Hadházy then reacted to this post, writing:

“Dear Prime Minister, anyone who believes the government should not be criticised wants New Fidesz and NER 2.0. And they are working toward that end. I hope that is not what you want. Allow me—as a veterinarian—to oppose this by expressing my opinion. Of course, I will also request the scoring system from Parliament, and I very much hope you will support its release. I am turning to the Prime Minister’s Office because, to my knowledge, that is where these matters were decided.”

If you missed it: BREAKING: Hungary’s new asset recovery chief elected in secret vote

Unger’s lack of legal background questioned

One of the main criticisms of Unger’s appointment is that she is not a lawyer. Magyar addressed the issue at a press conference after Parliament’s vote, arguing that Hungarian law does not require the president of the NVVH to be a lawyer.

He pointed to the FBI as an example, saying that its director is not necessarily a lawyer either.

“What is important, and what it will be, is that the investigative deputy president, the deputy president responsible for prosecutions and the deputy president responsible for appeals should be lawyers and prosecutors,” Magyar said.

The new office is being established with a broader leadership structure, with specialist legal responsibilities assigned to its deputy heads.

Magyar also responds to criticism from within Tisza

The appointment has not been universally welcomed even among supporters of Magyar’s Tisza Party. In a comment beneath one of his posts, the prime minister addressed Tisza supporters who had expressed dissatisfaction with Unger’s election.

“It is perfectly fine to criticise and disagree, but I ask that we do not go below a certain level,” Magyar wrote.

Unger was elected by Parliament on Friday with 137 votes in favour, seven against and one abstention. Katalin Tasnádi was elected as investigative deputy president with 139 votes in favour, six against and one abstention.

The two officials subsequently took their oaths in Parliament. The new asset recovery office is expected to play a central role in the government’s efforts to recover allegedly misused public funds and protect state assets.

World.title: Budapest’s Britannica International School joins Ariston Education global network of schools
World.content:
Britannica International School, Budapest, today announced it had joined Ariston Education, a growing global group of premium Early Years – Year 13 schools and creator of the AQ = EQ + IQ framework for future-ready learning. The school now becomes part of the Ariston Education alliance of schools, extending the group’s international footprint and reinforcing its mission of creating “Pathways for Excellence” for students around the world.

A bigger network, greater opportunity

As part of a larger education network, Britannica International School will stand to benefit from increased richness and diversity across the wider Ariston Education network. Over time, this includes the addition of new schools to the group, strengthened central services and further investment in school improvement, systems, and services. The ambition is straightforward: to bring more resources, more expertise, and more opportunity to every Ariston Education school and the students and staff within it.

Active investment

Britannica International School, Budapest has already received the first initial investment destined to improving campus facilities and includes significant improvements to the school’s learning environment. Over the summer, key teaching and learning areas were refurbished, classrooms and shared spaces were enhanced, additional air conditioning was installed across the campus and outdoor play and learning facilities were upgraded. Continued investment has also been made in school infrastructure, safety and security systems, helping to ensure that students and staff benefit from a modern, comfortable and well-maintained environment that supports learning and wellbeing.

These improvements reflect a shared commitment to providing an environment where students can learn, develop and flourish.

Brian Rogove, CEO of Ariston Education, said:

“We are delighted that Britannica International School, Budapest has joined the Ariston Education alliance of schools, allowing the school to access wider resources in terms of investment, education and importantly a framework approach that best prepares their future ready students.”

Michael W. Clack, Principal of Britannica International School, Budapest said:

“Having spent time with Ariston Education’s leadership team and learning more about their vision and values, I am confident that this partnership represents a positive step forward for Britannica. What has impressed me most is the strong alignment between their educational philosophy and our own commitment to excellence, wellbeing, safeguarding and ensuring every student is known, valued and supported.

Most importantly, this is about building on strengths rather than changing who we are. The values, relationships and sense of community that have always defined Britannica remain at the heart of our school. At the same time, joining Ariston Education provides exciting opportunities for collaboration, investment and continued growth that will benefit our students, staff and families for many years to come.”

If you missed it: Outstanding A-Level results mark another success for Britannica International School Budapest

Business as Usual for School and Staff

Daily operations, teaching and learning, and school routines will continue as usual. Over time, investment from Ariston Education will support organic growth as schools become part of a larger education network.

The Principal will continue to report to the School Board and their Regional Head of Schools (RHoS) on a day-to-day basis, exactly as they do today. In addition, they will now also report to the Regional CEO of Ariston Education.

For employees, there are no immediate changes, and as the number of schools in the network increases, some roles and structures may evolve over time to support that growth, potentially bringing enhanced opportunities for professional development, career progression and investment in central support services.

The Britannica International School website britannicaschool.hu remains live and the school is also featured in the group’s website aristonedu.com.

World.title: FBI alert leads Hungarian police to arrest British fugitive wanted for 20 years, court makes questionable decision – video, UPDATE
World.content:
Hungarian police have arrested a 60-year-old British man who had been wanted internationally for more than two decades over alleged sexual offences committed in the United States. The arrest followed a tip-off from the FBI’s unit based in Hungary, which alerted the Hungarian National Bureau of Investigation (KR NNI) on 25 August that the fugitive might be travelling through the country.

According to Hungarian police, US authorities had been investigating the man since 2003 in connection with alleged offences involving a minor, including coercion and solicitation to engage in illegal sexual activity.

The man reportedly fled the United States in September 2004 and was believed to have travelled to England. US authorities charged him in 2004 and issued an arrest warrant that November. An international wanted notice was subsequently issued in 2006, with the Washington Interpol office also seeking his arrest.

FBI alert triggers Hungarian investigation

After receiving the information from the FBI, Hungarian investigators identified a vehicle with British registration that was being used by the wanted man. They established that he had entered Hungary from Romania on 26 August and then tracked his movements.

The KR NNI alerted the Hajdú-Bihar County Police Headquarters that the vehicle, believed to be carrying the fugitive, was travelling towards them on the M3 motorway from the direction of Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg County. Several police units were dispatched to intercept the vehicle.

If you missed it: Missing Hungarian football star Buzsáky breaks silence after 10 days

Fugitive arrested near Polgár

Officers caught up with the vehicle near Polgár and directed it into a motorway service area, where they stopped and checked the driver. The police’s suspicions were confirmed: the driver was the 60-year-old British national wanted by US authorities.

He was arrested and taken to the Hajdúnánás Police Station, where he was placed in custody. Hungary’s International Criminal Cooperation Centre (NEBEK) coordinated the necessary international cooperation and assisted in bringing the man before a court.

Court releases the suspect

The case took an unexpected turn after the arrest. The KR NNI requested that the man be placed in extradition custody pending further proceedings. However, the court rejected the request and released him, according to Hungarian police.

The authorities have not provided further details about the court’s decision. The arrest itself brought to an end more than 20 years of efforts to locate the man, who had been internationally wanted since 2006.

UPDATE: Here’s why the man was released

“According to the Budapest Metropolitan Court, no crime was committed, since the person on the other end of the ‘line’ during the British man’s chat was not a minor, but an American police officer,” Ferenc Levente Rab, deputy spokesperson for the Budapest Chief Prosecutor’s Office, told Telex.

World.title: EU Council President António Costa to meet Hungary’s Péter Magyar in Budapest
World.content:
European Council President António Costa will meet Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar in Budapest on Wednesday, 2 September, as part of a wider tour of EU member states. Costa announced the meeting in a statement on Friday, outlining the schedule for the second week of his tour of European capitals.

On Wednesday, the European Council president is due to meet Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden before travelling to Zagreb for talks with Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković. He will then continue to Budapest, where he is scheduled to meet Magyar.

The Budapest meeting will be one of a series of discussions Costa is holding with EU leaders as the bloc prepares for negotiations on its next long-term budget.

Costa touring EU member states

Costa announced on Monday that he would visit most EU member states between 25 August and 17 September. The tour is intended to give him an opportunity to discuss key European issues directly with national leaders, including the European Union’s next long-term budget, formally known as the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF).

The EU’s long-term budget sets spending priorities and funding levels for a seven-year period and is expected to be one of the bloc’s major political negotiations in the coming years. Costa’s meetings with national leaders are therefore aimed at gathering their views and building common ground ahead of the wider discussions at EU level.

If you missed it: Hungary sets 2030 euro target: Government reveals when budget deficit could fall below 3%

Budapest meeting comes amid major EU decisions

The meeting will be one of Magyar’s first high-level discussions with the president of the European Council since taking office as Hungary’s prime minister. The European Council brings together the heads of state or government of the EU’s member states and sets the bloc’s overall political direction and priorities. Costa has served as its president since December 2024.

His meeting with Magyar in Budapest is expected to provide an opportunity to discuss Hungary’s position on the EU’s future budget as well as European priorities. Costa’s tour will continue until 17 September, with the European Council president scheduled to meet leaders in most EU member states during the three-week diplomatic effort.

World.title: BREAKING: Hungary’s new asset recovery chief elected in secret vote
World.content:
Hungary’s Parliament has elected Anna Róza Unger as president of the country’s newly established National Asset Protection and Asset Recovery Office (NVVH) in a secret ballot.

Unger received 137 votes in favour, seven against and one abstention in Friday’s parliamentary vote. At the same time, MPs voted on the institution’s investigative deputy president. Katalin Tasnádi was elected with 139 votes in favour, six against and one abstention.

The votes mark a major step in the establishment of the new body, which is intended to play a key role in recovering and protecting public assets.

Unger and Tasnádi take their oaths

Following their election, Unger and Tasnádi both took their official oaths in Parliament.

Tasnádi briefly stumbled while repeating one of the particularly lengthy sections of the oath, which refers to the position of investigative deputy president of the National Asset Protection and Asset Recovery Office. Unger was seen smiling in the background, but Tasnádi subsequently completed the oath without further difficulty.

The two newly elected officials then signed their oath documents.

If you missed it: PM Magyar announces headquarters of new asset recovery office

Government figures congratulate the new leaders

Prime Minister Péter Magyar congratulated Unger and Tasnádi following their election, followed by Andrea Bujdosó, parliamentary group leader of the Tisza Party.

Most Fidesz and KDNP MPs were not present in the chamber at the time of the congratulations. Some representatives of the Mi Hazánk party were also absent, although István Apáti, a Mi Hazánk MP, congratulated the newly elected office holders.

The establishment of the NVVH has been one of the new government’s key institutional projects, with Magyar previously promising that it would have broad powers and a multi-member leadership structure.

The new office is expected to begin operating from the former Supreme Court building on Markó Street in Budapest, where it will initially use vacant offices after the Supreme Court moves to its renovated historic headquarters opposite Parliament.
