World.title: Meta settlement falls short on teen mental health protections, whistleblower says
World.content:
BEJAR. Arturo Bejar, a former Facebook safety engineer and Instagram consultant, leaves the courthouse as Meta faces a landmark trial in federal court over claims from 29 states that the company illegally collected and used children's data in violation of federal law, allegedly designed its social media platforms to keep young users hooked and misled consumers about their safety, in Oakland, California, U.S., August 19, 2026

'This agreement could simply codify much of the 'safety theater' that Meta has been doing in recent years,' says whistleblower Arturo Bejar, a former Meta safety engineer

A whistleblower whose testimony helped build a child safety case against Meta Platforms META.O said on Wednesday that the firm’s settlement with a coalition of US states does not meaningfully address harms from social media that he described in court.

Former Meta safety engineer Arturo Bejar told a judge and eight jurors last week that the firm had knowingly underreported the frequency with which teens were harmed on its platforms, pushed them toward content that made them feel bad about themselves and failed to correctly adjudicate reports of child predation.

On Wednesday, the states announced they and Meta had settled the case, with California Attorney General Rob Bonta declaring that the settlement “will make social media less dangerous for our kids.” However, Bejar said the proposed settlement does not meaningfully address the problems he was asked to testify about.

“This agreement could simply codify much of the ‘safety theater’ that Meta has been doing in recent years,” he said. “Instagram will be used a little less, but it will not be any safer.”

In announcing the settlement, Meta said it is “building on our longstanding efforts to empower parents and support teens.”

“We’re grateful for Mr. Bejar’s advocacy and for his testimony in our case,” Bonta said in a statement. “We agree that there is more to be done by legislatures and industry, but believe that the settlement we announced yesterday institutes real and enforceable change, real transparency, and real protections for children and teens across the country.”

Inconsequential remedies

The settlement involves Meta paying states up to $18 billion over the next decade and remedies such as limiting how teenagers use its Facebook and Instagram social media platforms.

In some instances, remedies secured by the attorneys general are measures that leaked documents showed Meta previously considered and rejected after determining them to be relatively inconsequential on both user well-being and business grounds.

For example, Meta has agreed to hide likes and reaction counts on posts to prevent young users from comparing their posts’ performance with those of peers.

Such an effort to address “negative social comparison” dates back to 2019, when Meta considered adopting the measure to address its researchers’ concerns that social media might be harming teenagers’ mental health.

Meta’s tests on the effects of hiding like counts, known as “Project Daisy,” found that the change had at most a modest impact on users’ experience.

“We didn’t observe movements in overall well-being measures,” Facebook employees wrote in a 2020 slide presentation to Mark Zuckerberg.

The effects on Meta’s business were similarly slight, with tests showing that daily user count would likely fall by around 0.09% if the change was adopted.

Meta ultimately allowed users to hide like counts as an opt-in feature.

Mixed reaction

Youth safety concerns about Meta’s products have been raised for years, with some of the most concerning material emerging from internal Meta research leaked by employees or obtained via legal discovery.

Broadly, Meta’s researchers have internally flagged algorithms’ tendency to recommend high doses of fitness and beauty content to teens with existing self-esteem issues and the intentional design of features that keep young users scrolling longer than they would independently choose. (READ: Teens a ‘top priority’: Documents show Facebook, platforms’ efforts to hook young users)

Other concerns focused on shortfalls in Meta’s handling of user reports and moderation of inappropriate content. Bejar, for example, oversaw work at Meta that concluded that users had bad experiences on Meta’s platforms at rates greater than the company’s official prevalence estimates.

Such allegations were central to the states’ case against Meta, but they are addressed only glancingly in the settlement. Instead, the remedies cited by the attorneys general focus on greater parental controls, time limits and boosting efforts to detect minors misrepresenting themselves as adults.

Meta’s ability to identify and remove underage users is itself far from guaranteed as users self-report their ages. In Australia, where the government banned social media use by teenagers under age 16, regulators have found that eight in 10 young teens remain on social media, prompting authorities to consider additional enforcement.

Reaction from teen mental health experts to the settlement was mixed. Dr. Jane Conron, a clinical psychologist at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine, said the settlement only requires Meta to offer a non-algorithmically curated social media feed to teens on an opt-in basis, a feature she predicted would go largely unused.

However, the settlement’s requirement that Meta cap the number of hours teens spend on Instagram and Facebook each day could be meaningful for some users, she said.

Some of her young patients are so “emotionally overwhelmed by leaving the app” that they cry when their parents attempt to restrict how much time they spend on it, Conron said. A built-in usage limit “will help,” she said, adding that she believes the settlement might also change the conversation around social media between teens and their parents.

While the deal did not require Meta to acknowledge fault or accept the claim that it built harmful products, Conron saw its existence as significant.

“I see changes because people will realize the gravity of the problem,” she said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Trump says US is taking partial control of Venezuela’s vast oil reserves
World.content:
TRUMP. US President Donald Trump participates in a Congressional Space Medal of Honor presentation to the Artemis II crew at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas, US, August 28, 2026

An analyst says it's unclear whether a US government lease would have a legal basis under Venezuela's constitution and its new hydrocarbons law, adding that there is 'no precedent'

President Donald Trump on Friday announced an unprecedented US push to take control of a fifth of Venezuela’s vast oil reserves, betting that American companies can revive the OPEC nation’s battered energy industry while delivering a new source of crude to help bring down US fuel prices.

Trump provided few details about the agreement, saying only that the US had secured majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves through a partnership with private business.

The South American nation’s leader welcomed the agreement, saying it would boost the economy and government revenue.

The new deal would represent a dramatic expansion of the US role in Venezuela’s oil industry as the Trump administration seeks to revive the country’s production and secure more crude for US refineries. Venezuela holds the world’s largest proven oil reserves but produces only about 1.25 million barrels per day, far below its potential after years of underinvestment, mismanagement and sanctions.

Rubio calls deal a win-win

“At my direction, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, working closely with Highly Respected Interim President of Venezuela, Delcy Rodriguez, and, through a partnership with private business, have secured majority US control of more than 65 BILLION BARRELS of proven Oil Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the American Taxpayer,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

The announcement followed weeks of US-Venezuelan negotiations over a deal that would give American companies long-term access to a group of Venezuelan oilfields and guarantee the resulting crude supply to the United States.

Venezuelan officials are preparing to sign agreements next week granting new oil exploration and production rights to a number of companies, particularly US firms.

Sources have told Reuters that a lease model was under consideration, with fields potentially auctioned to US producers, but the arrangement could face legal and constitutional challenges in Venezuela, where the state retains control over core oil industry activities.

Trump did not disclose the structure of the agreement, the fields or companies involved or how the United States would exercise majority control over the reserves. A list seen by Reuters shows the fields are in the Orinoco Belt and Lake Maracaibo regions.

Rubio described the agreement as a win for both countries, saying on X that it would secure stable, low-cost oil for the United States and help lower gasoline prices.

For Venezuela, Rubio said the deal would bring nearly $100 billion in private investment, support thousands of high-paying jobs and help rebuild the country’s economy.

Rodriguez, who became interim leader after the US seized President Nicolas Maduro in January, said late on Friday that the agreement would allow for a significant increase in production through the development of 17 strategic fields and result in tax revenue for the country totaling $209 billion.

“These investments will contribute not only to the recovery and modernization of our industry, but also to our country’s economic growth, the energy security of our hemisphere, and greater balance in international markets,” she said in a statement.

Legal basis, financial structure unclear

Analysts said they needed to see more details on the agreement’s legal and financial structure before assessing whether it could attract significant investment.

Also unclear is whether the deal will lower gasoline prices in the short term, as developing the infrastructure needed to produce, transport and refine Venezuela’s heavy crude could take years.

David Goldwyn, president of Goldwyn Global Strategies, said it was unclear whether a US government lease would have a legal basis under Venezuela’s constitution and its new hydrocarbons law, adding that there is “no precedent for having the US government enter into a lease to operate oil fields.”

Goldwyn also questioned whether the plan would address the obstacles that have deterred investment in Venezuela for years. “It is hard to see how this kind of arrangement would accelerate investment at any material scale,” he said, citing political uncertainty, an inadequate power grid, limited export capacity and government discretion over the industry.

Since removing Maduro, Washington has been trying to secure a stable flow of Venezuelan crude ​for US refineries while promoting American investment in the country’s oil industry.

The Trump administration is under pressure ahead of midterm elections in November to mollify consumer concerns over rising gasoline prices. Cheaper oil supplies and expanded output could help.

The US also has been looking for solutions to replenish its Strategic Petroleum Reserve, the nation’s oil stockpile, including the possibility of crude ⁠swaps with US ​producers.

Venezuela nationalized its oil industry in the 1970s, putting state-run PDVSA at its center. Under then-President Hugo Chavez, the government tightened control, forcing foreign producers into state-led joint ventures and later expropriating assets, including projects operated by ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips.

Under Maduro’s rule Venezuela’s production fell sharply. – Rappler.com

World.title: Ombudsman dismisses complaints vs UP officials over DiliMall
World.content:
PREMIER STATE UNIVERSITY. The main building of the University of the Philippines, Diliman, Quezon City

(1st UPDATE) UP officials welcome the Ombudsman's ruling that the complainants 'failed to establish a prima facie case with reasonable certainty of conviction' for alleged violations of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act

MANILA, Philippines – The Office of the Ombudsman dismissed the graft and administrative complaints filed against incumbent and former University of the Philippines (UP) officials over the development of DiliMall in its Diliman campus in Quezon City.

In its ruling dated June 22, a copy of which obtained from a Rappler source on Wednesday, August 26, the Ombudsman said it found that the complainants “failed to establish a prima facie case with reasonable certainty of conviction” for the alleged violations of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act of UP officials, specifically on the following:

Section 3(e) or causing any undue injury or giving any private party any unwarranted benefits through manifest partiality, evident bad faith or gross inexcusable negligence

Section 3(g) or entering into any contract or transaction manifestly and grossly disadvantageous to the same

Section 3(j) or knowingly approving or granting any license, permit, privilege or benefit in favor of any person not qualified for or not legally entitled to it or of a mere representative or dummy of one who is not so qualified or entitled

Substantial evidence to hold respondents administratively liable for violations of the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees was also not established, according to the ruling.

Those named respondents in the complaints were UP president Angelo Jimenez; former UP president Danilo Concepcion; UP vice president for development Daniel Peckley Jr.; former vice chancellor for planning and development Raquel Baltazar; CBMS Property Company OPC (also known as CBMS Consultancy); and JoseBizCo Incorporated.

Those who filed the complaints in December 2025 were the UP Shopping Center Stallholders Association, Samahan ng Manininda sa UP Campus Incorporated, University Student Council, UP Transport Group, and urban poor and affected residents.

Kristian Mendoza, one of the complainants, told Rappler that they filed a motion for reconsideration on Thursday, August 27. Rappler will update this story once complainants send their official statement.

Meanwhile, UP welcomed the dismissal of the complaints, adding that the ruling affirmed that no corruption, abuse of authority, or violation of law occurred.

It reiterated that its lands “are not for sale but for service.”

“The UP Shopping Center and Gyudfood facilities complement the academic environment by easing everyday burdens and allowing the community to focus on learning, research, and public service,” the country’s top state university said.

“Small vendors remain integral to campus life, while tenants displaced by the 2018 shopping center fire were invited to relocate in the new spaces at preferential lease rates. UP remains committed to transparency, fairness, and protecting traditions that make it a true public university.”

Allegations on failure to consult stakeholders, higher rental rates

Complainants alleged that UP officials failed to consult stakeholders prior to the execution of two master lease agreements (MLAs) for GyudFood Hub and Diliman Shopping Center, commonly known as DiliMall.

DiliMall is a commercial building that replaced the UP Shopping Center (SC), which was destroyed by fire in 2018.

They claimed that the MLAs imposed rental rates and other fees far higher than those previously charged at the old UP SC.

For the Ombudsman, the circumstances for Section 3(e) of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act were not shown by the evidence.

“At most, complainants disagree with the university’s decision to enter into the MLAs and the business model adopted for the redevelopment of former UP SC. However, disagreement with the wisdom of an official act does not, by itself, establish criminal liability under Section 3(e),” read part of the ruling.

The Ombudsman also said that records show that CBMS Consultancy, which was involved in the MLA for the DiliMall, has existed since 2018, as complainants accused that the company only existed after the contract was executed in January 2023.

“CBMS Consultancy also submitted business documents establishing its legitimacy, which was not controverted by complainants,” it said.

It also said there was no evidence that Concepcion acted with corrupt motives, personal interest, or deliberate intent to violate the law, adding that his participation was limited to approving and executing the contracts.

Complainants also failed to identify any law, rule, or regulation imposing upon Jimenez a ministerial duty to rescind the contracts, according to the Ombudsman. He assumed office in February 2023, after the execution of the MLAs.

“Absent such duty, his inaction cannot constitute manifest partiality, evident bad faith, gross neglect, or misconduct,” it explained.

In 2024, the UP Not For Sale Network protested the “commercialization” of the UP Diliman campus following the soft opening of DiliMall.

The group claimed that the new commercial building was “anti-student” and negatively affected small, local businesses, as DiliMall had paved the way for private big businesses to enter the campus.

In April, the UP System Administration said that the MLAs were “legally sound and in accordance with retail practices.”

“In the redevelopment of the Diliman Shopping Center, affected stallholders were given priority, with preferential rental terms and opportunities to reestablish their livelihood,” it also said. – Rappler.com

World.title: When school violence happens, the whole community needs to listen
World.content:
Psychologists say young Filipinos need safe spaces to be vulnerable without judgement — and that starts with listening to children and their families, and giving the support within their communities

This is Part 2 of a two-part story. Read Part 1: Psychologists want us to rethink what we ask about school violence

When it comes to school violence, psychologist Jannah Trixie Cuevas said it’s the whole community that must be held responsible for what could’ve been done differently.

“When we talk about the whole community, it’s the schools for not having interventions about it. It could be the parents for not seeing the warning signs right away. It could be a lot of pressures that we don’t see, that are being put on the children.”

Hannah Pellejo Jara, CEO and founder of Sapphire Clinics East Inc.’s Aura Health Rehab, a Filipino-owned rehabilitation and psychological services network where Cuevas works, also points out that the issue isn’t always about negligence.

Jara, who has heard many different stories of troubled kids and distressed families, said socioeconomic factors affect not only the mental health of the child, but of entire families and communities, especially caregivers and breadwinners.

“I think a lot of the fatigue of the families is because [of financial issues, like they think], ‘I have to earn, I can’t take care of my child’…. So, their economic state is still a factor, them being stressed about money, and then affecting the child as well.”

The conflicts parents go through because of money, work, or relationship difficulties affect how much they’re able to be attentive to their kids. The questions then expand from asking how supported the children are within the family, to how supported the family is within their community.

“I think the more complex route that may take a longer time to address are the family dynamics, even the community dynamics,” Jara said. “How supported are the families?”

“When I say this, for example, here in the Philippines, if I can’t take care of my child, my neighbor is there, or my mother is there, my brother is there who can help me carry this emotional burden. But for example, for single parents, everything is a burden on you, right? So, we have cases of single parents here that we’ve seen that they cry after. They’re like, ‘No one is supporting me. I’m all alone. I can’t take care of my child.’ They already have guilt because they have to work.”

Bridging the gaps

Aside from factors preventing parents from being there for their children physically, generation gaps tend to create emotional gaps within families as well.

“Based on the patterns that I’m seeing, parents have been comparing what’s happening to the kids nowadays to the time that they were kids,” Cuevas said. “There was a disconnection emotionally. Physically, most of the time they’re present, but emotionally, they’re absent.”

Fellow psychologist Arnel Sarte Jr. observed that this distance isn’t exactly because of a lack of trying on the parents’ part. The good intentions are there, but their expression of support and concern to their children can sometimes get lost in translation.

“Sometimes the support system thinks that they’re being helpful, with most parents telling their kids, ‘You can do it, just keep going.’ On the surface, when the child is doing okay, it’s a good validation. But for those kids that don’t even have the energy to keep moving forward, not knowing how they can do it, for them, it feels more like a responsibility when they hear, ‘keep going.’”

Dealing with kids struggling with depression and mental health issues also challenges parents to change how they make their kids feel loved. “It really depends on the state of the kids. They can take those words properly if they aren’t severely depressed, if they don’t feel like they’re completely alone, they can take that,” Sarte said.

“But what if they’re so severely depressed that just thinking already takes a toll on them? So if they’re told, ‘Don’t give up,’ they’re going to think, ‘How can I not give up? I don’t have the energy.’ So instead, make them feel that, ‘I’m here. You can lean on me.’ Ask them, ‘What do you want to eat? Is there anything you’re craving? Let’s eat.’ Simple ways like that can make them feel like they aren’t alone.”

That is ultimately what psychologists say young Filipinos need: safe spaces to be vulnerable without judgement, as well as support through loneliness.

“If the safe space is not available, if they don’t have a home, if they cannot communicate at their school, at least they should have someone inside the school or maybe someone that they can talk to, another person that they won’t feel judged,” Cuevas said.

“Now, everyone’s going through a lot of things already. Maybe just providing a safe space for a person, just listening to them without judging what they feel.”

Hand in hand with safe spaces, both children and family members would benefit from receiving psychoeducation on how to manage and regulate emotions and recognize difficult feelings.

Both Sarte and Jara also acknowledge how much damage bullying can inflict on a child and call on schools to intervene. Jara adds that social media usage significantly magnifies the impact of bullying on victims, and suggests that the Philippines follows the example of other countries like Australia to restrict the access of children below 16.

“It’s true what they say that social media contributes to mental health problems. For example, bullying. Before, when you were bullied in school, it was just in school. At home, it’s like, no matter what, you’re peaceful. Now, you’re being bullied in group chats or you’re being bullied on social media,” Jara said.

“So, all the time, it’s like the bullying is non-stop, and your outlet is also social media. It’s like this vicious cycle. At least for the parents, I think a low-hanging fruit will also be to really control the social media exposure of the children.”

So many questions, where are the answers?

But with all the questions that psychologists ask to look after the mental well-being of young Filipinos, their most pressing question is: what really happened during those school violence incidents? Why, after so long, do we know so little about the perpetrators and what drove them to commit fatal acts?

“And especially for the Tacloban case, it has been months, but there are no clear answers about what really caused those behaviors,” Cuevas said. “I think there was a lot of speculation, but no psychological evaluation right away. It was more of, okay, being told that a psychological evaluation needs to be done. But what was the result of the evaluation? That’s why there was no proper intervention set in place.”

With so many questions, where are the answers? Why is no one answering them?

“It happened once already, but the only resolution was to hire more school counselors. But what really happened there? The next step would have been to prevent incidents like this, because if there really is a group of people really targeting teenagers in the Philippines about having that sense of violence, how can we prevent it if we haven’t pinpointed who or what organization that is?” added Cuevas.

To protect and save Filipino children from future fatal incidents, it is not enough for conversations around the recent school violence incidents to be centered around what should have been done in hindsight. It requires serious follow through of psychological evaluations, the effort to understand more deeply our country’s youth, and the urgency to be truly attentive to the needs of the children and their families within the communities.

It requires the entire community to acknowledge the shared responsibility we have towards the children, and to be willing to change our ways and ask better questions for the sake of their futures. – Rappler.com

Elise Suarez is a Rappler intern from Puerto Princesa City and a Humanities student of the University of Asia & the Pacific.

World.title: ‘The only method I have found that relieved my illness is to keep creating art’: Remembering Yayoi Kusama
World.content:
ICON. Japanese avant-garde artist Yayoi Kusama speaks to journalists at her studio in Tokyo, Japan September 26, 2017.

She suffered from hallucinations from childhood and by the age of 10 had created paintings in watercolors, pastels, and oils using polka dot and net motifs that she encountered in her visions

In the history of the National Gallery of Victoria, their most successful ticketed exhibition did not feature the work of Vincent van Gogh, Claude Monet or Pablo Picasso. It was of the veteran Japanese artist, Yayoi Kusama, who has died aged 97.

Held over the summer months in 2024–25, the Melbourne exhibition attracted 570,537 ticketed visitors.

Kusama’s exhibitions throughout the world have attracted huge crowds. Her infinity mirror rooms, sprawling seas of polka dots, dancing pumpkins, and huge expanses of reflective surfaces have become some of the most photographed art objects in human history.

Her art has had a huge impact on many art movements of the 20th and 21st centuries, including pop art, performance art, minimalism, environmental art, video art, fashion, filmmaking, and feminism.

A difficult childhood

Kusama was born on March 22, 1929 in Matsumoto, Nagano Prefecture, Japan, to parents who were merchants and operated a plant nursery and seed farm.

She suffered from hallucinations from childhood and by the age of 10 had created paintings in watercolors, pastels, and oils using polka dot and net motifs that she encountered in her visions.

She described her childhood as traumatic, with a physically abusive mother and a womanizing father, and a time when her artistic endeavors were discouraged. She found refuge in her art.

Her childhood was overshadowed by World War II. By the time she was 13, she was sewing parachutes for Japanese soldiers and was aware of American bombers flying overhead and of constant air-raid sirens. She attended Arigasaki High School and, in 1948, studied Nihonga painting at the Kyoto Municipal School of Arts and Crafts.

By 1950, Kusama was exhibiting in Japan, to some acclaim, her sprawling paintings, mainly on paper, of abstracted natural forms and would cover all surfaces — floors, walls, ceilings and naked assistants with polka dots that she would term “infinity nets.”

Concerning her painting, Flower (D.S.P.S), 1954, she wrote:

One day I was looking at the red flower patterns of the tablecloth on a table, and when I looked up I saw the same pattern covering the ceiling, the windows, and the walls, and finally all over the room, my body and the universe. I felt as if I had begun to self-obliterate, to revolve in the infinity of endless time and the absoluteness of space and be reduced to nothingness.

The heart of the art scene

In 1957, Yayoi Kusama traveled to the United States and settled in New York. She was at the heart of the American post-war art movement where she exhibited to considerable applause large paintings, soft sculptures and environmental sculptures using mirrors and electric lights.

In the 1960s, she staged many happenings, such as body painting festivals, fashion shows and anti-war demonstrations.

It has been argued that her work had a profound impact on artists, including Claes Oldenburg and Andy Warhol.

Play Video

She was also involved in film productions and newspaper publication.

In 1968, the film Kusama’s Self-Obliteration, that Kusama produced and in which she played the leading role, won a prize at the Fourth International Experimental Film Competition in Belgium and the Second Maryland Film Festival and the second prize at the Ann Arbor Film Festival.

She held exhibitions and staged happenings in various countries in Europe and participated in the Venice Biennale in 1966, where she exhibited her Narcissus Garden comprising of hundreds of mirrored spheres.

(Narcissus Garden entered the collection of the National Gallery of Victoria in 2024, in its new iteration of 1,400 stainless steel balls, each 30cm in diameter.)

The artist’s physical and mental health deteriorated while she was in America and she attempted suicide.

For her, her art was the path to salvation.

A return to Japan

Kusama returned to Japan to live there permanently in 1973.

After experiencing a further suicide attempt, in 1977 she admitted herself into the Tokyo psychiatric institute, the Seiwa Hospital for the Mentally Ill, from which she was never discharged.

She lived in the hospital and made daily excursions to her studio where she maintained a frenetic pace of work.

Yayoi Kusama was one of the most acclaimed artists of her time. A major retrospective exhibition of her work held in 1998 at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art traveled to the Museum of Modern Art in New York, the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis, and the Museum of Contemporary Art in Tokyo.

There were also major retrospective exhibitions at the Whitney Museum, New York, and Tate Modern, London, in 2012, and at the Hirshhorn Museum in Washington, DC in 2017. In 2017, the Yayoi Kusama Museum opened in Tokyo.

Commercially, her work achieved record prices and she has received various awards for her novels, poetry, and films.

In an interview with Infinity Net in 2012, Yayoi Kusama said:

I fight pain, anxiety, and fear every day, and the only method I have found that relieved my illness is to keep creating art. I followed the thread of art and somehow discovered a path that would allow me to live.

If this article has raised issues for you, or if you’re concerned about someone you know, call the National Center for Mental Health Crisis in the Philippines at hotline number 1553.

– The Conversation/Rappler.com

Sasha Grishin is an Adjunct Professor of Art History at the Australian National University

World.title: What keeps Filipino political dynasties in power – a Rappler series
World.content:
Why do political dynasties endure in the Philippines? Rappler looks at the families behind them and the forces that have allowed their influence to last for generations.

The 1987 Constitution directs the state to “prohibit political dynasties.” But nearly four decades later, no enabling legislation has been enacted to set limits on the concentration of political power within families.

As a result, political families continue to wield significant influence across national and local politics in the Philippines. The same family names repeatedly appear on ballots and, after elections, on the lists of officials taking their oaths of office.

Why do Filipinos keep electing people from the same families? The answer is not always straightforward.

This Rappler series looks at the families that have held political power for generations, tracing how they built their influence, where such influence is strongest, and how it has endured over time. The profiles look at their family ties, political networks, how they rose to power, business interests, and roles in local and national government.

We chose these families based on the extent of their political presence, including the number of relatives who have held public office and cases where family members have simultaneously occupied multiple government positions. The selection was also shaped by the availability of contributors and reporting capacity in different provinces, so this series is not intended to be a definitive list or ranking of the country’s largest political dynasties.

The series draws on Rappler’s ongoing effort to map family connections among elected officials. Our team compiled and verified information from official government and public records, then used these data points to trace relationships and see how political power is passed, shared, and consolidated across generations.

Rappler will publish two profiles each week leading up to the 35th anniversary of the Local Government Code of the Philippines on October 10. Bookmark this page to catch the latest report.

It’s been 38 years since Davao City knew any other kind of governance but the Dutertes’.

What began with one man brandishing a local peace and order campaign in 1988 has expanded into a Philippine allurement to safety — a move that solidified the Dutertes’ political stronghold with three generations now being elected into city and national government positions.

Read the full story by Raizza P. Bello here.

More than three decades after Lilia “Nanay” Pineda first won the mayoralty of Lubao in 1992, the Pineda family remains firmly at the center of Pampanga politics, extending one of Central Luzon’s longest-running political dynasties.

Since 2010, the family has continuously occupied Pampanga’s two highest elective offices, with Lilia and her son Dennis “Delta” Pineda alternating between the governor and vice governor posts across successive elections.

Read the full story by Ahyenne Neleah Estacio here.

– Rappler.com

World.title: News Digest: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s Global Ties, Economic Outlook, Abai’s Legacy and More
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest covers Singapore-Kazakhstan relations, political and economic developments, energy expansion, cultural cooperation with Vietnam and more.

Singapore keen to build on goodwill, deepen ties with Kazakhstan: SM Lee

Singapore wants to build on the goodwill it enjoys in Kazakhstan and deepen ties in areas ranging from business to connectivity, Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong said as he wrapped up his first visit to the Central Asian country, reported The Straits Times on Aug. 28.

Lee said on Aug. 27 that Singapore’s relationship with Kazakhstan was “an account well worth cultivating”, with Singapore companies showing growing interest in the country and trade and investments increasing significantly in recent years

“We enjoy a lot of goodwill,” he told Singapore media in a doorstop interview at the St. Regis Astana Hotel, noting that Kazakhstan remembers warmly founding prime minister Lee Kuan Yew’s first visit in September 1991, three months before the country became an independent republic.

The Goethe of the Steppe: How Kazakhstan’s national philosopher shapes the bridge to the global economy

News Mark released an article on Aug. 10 exploring how Abai Kunanbayev’s philosophy, literary legacy and emphasis on education, honest work and openness to other cultures can help international investors understand Kazakhstan’s modern business culture and economic ambitions.

“Anyone wanting to invest in Central Asia’s dynamic market today cannot ignore one name: Abai Kunanbayev. What Johann Wolfgang von Goethe is to Germans, Abai (1845-1904) is to Kazakhs. He is not only the undisputed national poet, but also the ethical foundation of a country rapidly transforming from a former nomadic state into a global economic player. For international decision-makers, his work offers the key to understanding the mentality, business culture, and economic ambitions of modern Kazakhstan,” reads the article.

Kazakhstan after Kurultai elections: Expanding opportunities for co-operation with the European Union

EU Reporter published an article on Aug. 25 about parliamentary elections on Aug. 23 that completed the formation of Kazakhstan’s new legislature – the Kurultai – the central element of the country’s renewed political system following constitutional reform. Seven political parties took part in the vote. Turnout stood at 74%.

“The first convocation of the Kurultai has cemented the completion of the institutional transition and marked the country’s entry into a new political cycle.

The Aug. 23 elections have concluded the phase of institutional renewal in Kazakhstan and opened the period of practical implementation of reforms. For the European Union, this means a more predictable foundation for cooperation with Kazakhstan in the key spheres of energy, raw materials, and transport infrastructure. Kazakhstan enters a new political cycle with an updated institutional system, reinforcing its position as a strategic partner of the EU in Eurasia,” reads the article.

Astana Finance Days 2026 to bring global investors and financial leaders to Kazakhstan

More than 5,500 participants from over 80 countries are expected to gather in Kazakhstan’s capital on Sept. 9-10 for the ninth Astana Finance Days (AFD) 2026 forum, hosted by the Astana International Financial Center (AIFC), reads an EU Reporter article on Aug. 24.

The forum will bring together investors, representatives of the financial and technology sectors, regulators, government and quasi-state institutions, and international businesses.

Since its launch in 2018, Astana Finance Days has developed into one of the region’s major financial forums, providing a platform for discussions on capital markets, investment and financial cooperation. The 2026 program will focus on capital markets and investment products, regulation and market confidence, institutional innovation, financing the real economy, and regional and cross-border capital cooperation.

After ending power shortages, Kazakhstan can become electricity exporter

An EU Reporter article published on Aug. 25 covered Kazakhstan’s planned expansion of electricity generation in 2026-2027, the growing role of gas and renewable energy, and the government’s goal of moving from an electricity deficit to a surplus while building a reserve for the national grid.

“The expected 1.3 billion kilowatt-hour surplus by the end of 2027 marks an important shift in the government’s projections. The objective is no longer limited to covering immediate electricity consumption but also includes creating a reserve that could strengthen the reliability of the national grid. However, installed generation capacity and actual electricity output are not identical. The amount of electricity ultimately available to the system will depend on factors including the operating performance of new plants, fuel supply, grid infrastructure and, in the case of wind and solar projects, weather conditions,” reads the article.

Vietnam, Kazakhstan boost experience sharing in cultural industry development

Vietnam Pictorial released an article on Aug. 27 about Vietnam and Kazakhstan strengthening cooperation in cultural industries, tourism, education and other sectors while using cultural exchange as a tool to deepen bilateral ties and diversify economic relations.

During the meeting with Aida Balayeva, deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Culture and Information of Kazakhstan, Vietnamese Deputy Prime Minister Pham Thi Thanh Tra called for stronger people-to-people exchanges, local cooperation and tourism, noting that nearly 200,000 Kazakh tourists visited Vietnam in 2025 following the visa exemption policy for ordinary passport holders, according to the article.

Kazakhstan’s expanded Korea: A cultural legacy

The Chosun Daily published an article on Aug. 26 about Kazakhstan’s large Koryoin community and how Korea’s historical diaspora, cultural influence and growing popularity among Kazakh youth connect the two countries across generations.

“The ties between Kazakhstan and Korea date back much further than these cultural interactions. In 1937, the Stalinist regime forcibly relocated approximately 170,000 Koryoin from the Primorsky Krai region to Central Asia, citing fears they could become Japanese spies. Many of those transported by cargo trains settled in Kazakhstan, where around 120,000 of their descendants still live today. Kazakhstan is the country with the second-largest Koryoin population in the world, following Uzbekistan,” reads the article.

World.title: Experts Say Kazakhstan’s New Kurultai Leadership Reflects Diversity, Faces Heavy Legislative Agenda
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s new unicameral legislature, the Kurultai, elected its leadership and heads of eight standing committees during the first session of its first convocation on Aug. 28. Experts say the newly elected leadership reflects political and gender diversity and will face a significant legislative workload from the outset.

Aibek Dadebai, chairman of the Adilet party and former head of the Presidential Administration, was elected Kurultai Chairman. He thanked President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev for nominating him and deputies for supporting his candidacy, describing the position as a “great honor and responsibility.”

Adilet deputy and former Senator Nurlan Beknazarov, who represented Shymkent in the Senate from 2018 to 2026 and most recently chaired its Committee on Constitutional Legislation, Judicial System and Law Enforcement, and Ak Zhol party chairwoman and former Mazhilis Deputy Chair Daniya Yesspayeva were elected Deputy Chairs. Former Commissioner for Children’s Rights Dinara Zakiyeva, who served as a Mazhilis deputy from the Amanat party from 2021 to 2023, became the third Deputy Chair.

Political scientist Gaziz Abishev said the composition of the Kurultai’s leadership reflects broad political and gender representation.

“In other words, the composition of the Kurultai’s leadership is diverse with respect to both party affiliation and gender,” he said.

In an earlier interview with The Astana Times, Zhandos Aktayev, chairman of the Esti Bol Qory public foundation and Doctor of Law, said the new legislature would face a substantial workload from the outset.

“Although the Kurultai is a new institution, it will inherit legislation left unfinished by the previous Parliament, giving deputies an immediate and substantial workload,” Aktayev said.

Deputies also elected the chairs of the Kurultai’s eight standing committees. Serik Yegizbayev of the Auyl party was elected to head the Committee on Agrarian Affairs. Askhat Aimagambetov will chair the Committee on Social and Cultural Development, Unzila Shapak the Committee on Constitutional Legislation, Judicial System and Law Enforcement, Olga Perepechina the Committee on Finance and Budget, Amirbek Ospanbekov the Committee on Regional and Infrastructure Development, Marat Kozhayev the Committee on International Relations, Defense and Security, Darkhan Akhmediyev the Committee on Digitalization, Innovation and Science, and Natalia Godunova the Committee on Economic Policy, Energy and Industry.

The standing committees will review draft legislation before the full chamber considers it, making them central to the Kurultai’s legislative work.

Seven of the eight committees are headed by deputies from Adilet, the majority party. The new legislature has eight standing committees, compared with seven in the former Mazhilis and six in the Senate.

All 145 deputies took an oath to the people of Kazakhstan during the inaugural session, marking the formal start of the new legislature under the constitutional framework that took effect on July 1.

Speaking after his election, Dadebai said the scale of reforms requires “well-balanced decisions, professionalism and dedicated work,” adding that the Kurultai should contribute to the country’s modernization and constructive public dialogue.

“A lot of work lies ahead. I am confident that we will go through this responsible path together,” he said.

World.title: Why Data Is Becoming Next Fuel-Saving Tool for Central Asian Airlines
World.content:
ASTANA – Airlines are expected to spend around $350 billion on fuel this year, nearly one-third of their operating costs, as global industry profitability comes under pressure from higher energy prices. For carriers in Central Asia and the South Caucasus, these figures are increasing the importance of data-driven operations to find additional fuel savings.

According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), global airline profitability is expected to fall to around 2% this year, down from 4.2% in 2025. IATA also reported that 90% of airlines surveyed in March identified fuel efficiency as a priority, rising to 96% among finance and procurement executives.

The pressure is particularly relevant for airlines in Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan, where passenger and cargo markets are expanding while fuel remains a major operating cost.

Fleet renewal is only part of the solution

Airlines have traditionally improved fuel efficiency by replacing older aircraft with newer models.

Air Astana received eight Airbus A320-family aircraft in 2025 and retired three Embraer E2 aircraft, while Azerbaijan Airlines has continued adding Airbus A320neo aircraft. Uzbekistan Airways is also introducing Boeing 787-9 and Airbus A321neo aircraft.

New-generation aircraft can significantly reduce fuel consumption, but airlines are increasingly looking for additional operational savings.

Stuart Fox, IATA’s Director of Flight and Operations, said the next fuel savings are increasingly likely to come from “better operational decisions supported by data.” He pointed to benchmarking as a way for airlines to compare their performance with operators using similar aircraft on comparable routes.

Turning data into fuel savings

IATA uses operational information from more than 240 airlines to identify efficiency opportunities. Its Fuel Efficiency Gap Analysis (FEGA) service and FuelIS platform allow carriers to compare fuel performance by aircraft type, route, flight stage and geographic region.

The approach can reveal, for example, when an airline consistently lands with higher fuel reserves than comparable operators, identifying potential efficiency gains without compromising safety.

Air Astana has already applied artificial intelligence to fuel management and estimates that the technology can reduce fuel consumption by up to 2%.

Beyond the aircraft

Fuel efficiency also depends on the wider aviation system. Flight paths, airspace design and air traffic management can create additional fuel consumption even when an aircraft itself is operating efficiently.

IATA has implemented Performance-based Navigation (PBN) projects in Azerbaijan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan over the past six years. The projects have supported more efficient airspace design and improved operational performance.

For Central Asian and South Caucasus airlines, the data suggests that the next stage of fuel efficiency will not depend only on buying newer aircraft. Better use of operational data, benchmarking and more efficient airspace could provide another source of savings as regional aviation markets continue to grow.

This also raises the broader question of how Kazakhstan can turn its growing role in international aviation into greater economic value. As financial analyst Rassul Rysmambetov told The Astana Times, “the aviation hub is not simply the transportation of someone else’s cargo through Kazakhstan with refueling,” highlighting the need to create value beyond transit itself.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s First Kurultai Takes on Legislative Modernization and Institutional Reform
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has outlined a broad legislative and institutional agenda for Kazakhstan’s first Kurultai, calling on deputies to modernize national legislation, strengthen the quality of lawmaking and help build a stronger system of checks and balances.

Speaking at the opening session of the first Kurultai on Aug. 28, Tokayev said the new legislative body has received significantly broader powers under the New Constitution and will play an important role in shaping the country’s system of government.

“The beginning of the Kurultai’s activities gives a start to fundamental institutional changes in the system of public administration, since this body plays an important role in shaping the system of government,” he said.

The Kurultai will participate in appointing Constitutional Court judges, members of the Central Election Commission, and the Supreme Audit Chamber. Deputies will also have the authority to appoint and dismiss Supreme Court judges upon the President’s proposal, as well as address topics concerning the legal immunity of judges and deputies.

According to Tokayev, these powers significantly expand the legislature’s influence.

“Thus, we have significantly strengthened the influence of the legislative body. This means strengthening the system of checks and balances between the branches of government,” he said.

First Deputy Head of the Presidential Administration Erlan Karin said the launch of the Kurultai marks a new stage in the country’s institutional transformation.

“Thus, President Tokayev’s reforms provide a real opportunity for many bright citizens and professionals in their fields to realize their potential,” Karin said in a Telegram post.

“With the beginning of Kurultai’s work, a complete institutional reboot of the political system is beginning. This will ensure the final transition to a new, more dynamic and open state-political model,” he added.

Legislative modernization

Kurultai’s first major task is to update Kazakhstan’s legislation in line with the New Constitution.

Tokayev instructed deputies to comprehensively review the existing regulatory framework and bring it into compliance with constitutional principles. He also called for stronger scrutiny of draft laws to address legal gaps and ensure consistency between legislative provisions.

“Lawmaking is a very responsible job. Laws must be fair, understandable to people and progressive, that is, meet modern requirements,” he said.

President Tokayev called for broader use of artificial intelligence to improve legislative analysis and minimize corruption risks, while stressing that digital technologies cannot replace professional legal expertise.

An e-Parliament information system is being developed to identify legal risks and integrate digital services. Tokayev instructed state bodies and deputies to introduce it into Kurultai’s work as soon as possible.

Priority legislation

During its first session, the Kurultai is expected to consider a package of key bills, including legislation on artificial intelligence in secondary education, digital assets and the Digital Qazaqstan strategy.

The government is also expected to submit a bill on migration policy. The measures are intended to support efforts to attract highly qualified specialists, advanced technologies and foreign investment, including through the introduction of the Altyn (Golden) Visa.

Another priority is a new law on library and publishing activities, which Tokayev said is important for strengthening the nation’s intellectual potential.

The Kurultai will also consider legislation on comprehensive support for children with special needs, including measures to improve access to education and the quality of medical and social services.

The President also supported the government’s proposal to prohibit registering children under 16 on social networks.

“I support this initiative. I believe this issue should be considered as a matter of priority,” Tokayev said, while stressing that the mechanisms for implementing the measure must be carefully developed.

New generation in government

Tokayev also highlighted Kurultai’s role in the broader renewal of Kazakhstan’s political and public institutions.

He noted that the proportion of women and young people has increased significantly compared with the previous Parliament, describing the emergence of a new generation in government, public organizations and business as an important result of the reforms.

“The ultimate goal of institutional transformations is precisely the renewal of personnel in all branches of government, that is, the involvement in politics of innovative-minded, constructive citizens,” he said.

The President called on deputies to demonstrate professionalism, initiative and responsibility and to put national interests above personal interests.

“If we do not bring the reforms to completion and miss the historic opportunity on the path of building a just and fair Kazakhstan, future generations will never forgive us,” Tokayev said.

The President also announced that the Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi (People’s Council) is expected to be formed in the second half of September. The new constitutional consultative body will represent the country’s ethnic, regional, social and socio-political diversity and will have the right of legislative initiative.

“The first convocation of the Kurultai opens a new chapter in the development of the country. The people place great hopes in you,” Tokayev said.

Following the President’s address, deputies supported Tokayev’s nomination of Aibek Dadebai as Chairman of the Kurultai. Dadebai is the former Head of the Presidential Administration and current Chairman of the ruling Adilet party.

World.title: Semipalatinsk Legacy 35 Years On: Can Research Translate Into Care?
World.content:
ASTANA — Thirty-five years after Kazakhstan closed the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site, researchers and community advocates say its legacy still shapes health, science and policy. As evidence becomes more precise, experts say the focus is shifting toward how that knowledge can better support affected communities.

The Aug. 29, 1991, closure ended more than four decades of Soviet nuclear testing at the site in eastern Kazakhstan. Between 1949 and 1989, 456 nuclear tests were conducted there, including 116 atmospheric explosions, some of which sent radioactive fallout over surrounding populated areas.

The date later gained international significance when the United Nations General Assembly, at Kazakhstan’s initiative, designated Aug. 29 as the International Day against Nuclear Tests. The anniversary now marks both the historic closure and continuing questions surrounding the long-term effects of exposure.

Reconstructing invisible exposure

Radiation exposure was far from uniform. Doses could differ significantly depending on the test, the path of radioactive fallout, where a person lived, their age, activities and diet. Reconstructing individual exposure decades later is particularly difficult because personal radiation measurements were generally unavailable at the time.

In a comment for this story, Vladimir Drozdovitch, a staff scientist in the Radiation Epidemiology Branch of the United States National Cancer Institute’s Division of Cancer Epidemiology and Genetics, said researchers therefore combine historical environmental data with information about individual circumstances.

“Even when exposure occurred 60-75 years ago and individual radiation measurements were not made at the time, scientists can reconstruct doses by combining many different types of historical evidence,” Drozdovitch told The Astana Times.

“For the Semipalatinsk population, this includes archival measurements of radiation exposure rates in air made after the nuclear tests, information about the nuclear tests and radioactive fallout, measurements of residual radionuclides in soil and, where available, retrospective physical dosimetry using materials such as bricks and tooth enamel,” he said.

Researchers must then establish where people lived during individual tests, whether they were temporarily away, their age and occupation, housing conditions and, for internal exposure, their consumption of locally produced food. Milk and dairy products were particularly relevant because radioactive iodine deposited on pasture could enter the food chain.

A 2026 study by Drozdovitch and an international team estimated external whole-body doses for 14,789 people from 15 settlements affected by fallout between 1949 and 1962. Such estimates allow epidemiologists to examine whether disease risk changes with radiation dose rather than treating everyone living near the test site as a uniformly exposed population.

“Dose reconstruction tells us who was exposed, how much they were exposed, and why some people received much larger doses than others,” said Drozdovitch.

That evidence can help distinguish possible radiation effects from other influences on health and inform how decades of research might translate into healthcare today.

From research to healthcare

Aigerim Seitenova, a human rights professional, nuclear disarmament advocate and co-founder of the Qazaq Nuclear Frontline Coalition (QNFC), said access to specialists, diagnostics, medicines, rehabilitation and long-term treatment remains a concern in affected communities.

“For remote villages and rural areas, it is still difficult for people to get access to proper medical healthcare. The lack of proper medical equipment and technology is still one of the concerns,” Seitenova told The Astana Times.

Seitenova and Yerdaulet Rakhmatulla, co-founder and director of operations and communications at QNFC, co-authored the coalition’s June 2026 policy paper, “From Harm to Justice.” Based on a nationwide survey of 516 respondents, two focus group workshops and interviews, the paper examined healthcare, recognition, social protection and other needs among nuclear-affected communities.

Among respondents who reported health conditions they associated with nuclear testing, 63.4% said they were not receiving medical assistance, while 68.6% said they needed financial assistance.

The paper’s recommendations include expanding diagnostic capacity and specialized medical infrastructure, providing long-term treatment and rehabilitation, incorporating mental health and psychosocial support, and strengthening long-term health monitoring and research.

“We also highlight the issue of mental and psychosocial health, because nuclear harm is often discussed primarily through cancer or radiation-related physical illnesses. However, affected communities also live with anxiety and uncertainty about their own health and the health of their children, about social vulnerabilities and the psychological burden of living with the nuclear legacy,” said Seitenova.

She said new scientific findings should increasingly inform screening, diagnostic protocols and information available to doctors and patients, bringing research closer to practical care.

Closing gap between recognition and access

Similar concerns emerged from a 2025 Community Needs Assessment by the Steppe Organization for Peace (STOP), conducted with support from the Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung in Kazakhstan. The research involved 200 participants in community discussions and 27 in-depth interviews across eight affected locations.

“One of our strongest findings in healthcare is that the problem is often not simply the absence of services, but the gap between formally recognised rights and people’s actual ability to access assistance,” STOP founding member Alisher Khassengaliyev told The Astana Times.

Participants described traveling long distances for specialists and diagnostics, paying out of pocket when services were unavailable locally, difficulties obtaining medicines and rehabilitation, and limited regular screening and long-term follow-up.

Khassengaliyev said formal recognition as a person affected by the Semipalatinsk tests, including through a Polygon certificate, does not always correspond to a clearly defined healthcare pathway. Clearer links between recognized status, healthcare and social assistance, he said, could make existing support easier to navigate.

“Kazakhstan has achieved something historically extraordinary: it closed the Semipalatinsk test site, renounced its inherited nuclear arsenal and became a global leader on nuclear disarmament. Thirty-five years later, the next step should be to make that leadership equally visible in the everyday lives of nuclear-affected communities,” said Khassengaliyev.

Legacy across generations

For younger people from affected families, the test site belongs to history but remains part of family memory.

Diana Murzagaliyeva, founder of Inclusive Academy and an advocate on the intergenerational impacts of nuclear testing, was born years after the test site closed. She told The Astana Times that the anniversary carries a distinct meaning for a generation that did not witness the testing but grew up with its consequences and family stories.

“For me, the 35th anniversary of the test site’s closure is both a reminder of an important historical decision by Kazakhstan and a responsibility for our generation to ensure that this history is not forgotten,” she said.

Murzagaliyeva also said affected communities should participate directly in decisions concerning their health, land and future.

“It is important that communities affected by nuclear testing are not seen only as victims of a tragedy. We have our own voice, experience and the right to participate in decisions that concern our health, our land and our future. It is also important that decisions are not made without affected people themselves,” she said.

Khassengaliyev said STOP follows the same principle: “nothing about nuclear-affected communities without nuclear-affected communities.” QNFC’s policy paper similarly calls for their meaningful participation in healthcare, environmental remediation and other forms of assistance.

“I think one issue discussed too little is trust and access to information as part of nuclear justice. Residents told us that they often do not have access to understandable and regularly updated information about radiation conditions. The problem, therefore, is not simply whether monitoring exists institutionally. It is whether communities can access its results, understand them and trust them,” said Khassengaliyev.

Scientific questions also remain unresolved decades after the last test.

“The nuclear tests occurred decades ago, but the scientific questions remain highly relevant today. We know a great deal about the health effects of relatively high radiation doses. There is considerably greater uncertainty about risks from low and moderate doses, particularly for environmental exposures involving both external and internal irradiation,” said Drozdovitch.

According to Drozdovitch, the research on the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site can help narrow that uncertainty because affected populations experienced environmental exposure across a broad range of doses. The findings complement research on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Chernobyl, occupational radiation and medical exposure, while dose-reconstruction methods can also be applied after nuclear accidents or radioactive releases when individual measurements are incomplete.

The connection between past exposure and present-day response also extends to international policy. Articles 6 and 7 of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons address victim assistance, environmental remediation and international cooperation. QNFC recommends using that framework to advance long-term health monitoring, research, psychosocial support and community participation.

For Murzagaliyeva, the future is also about changing how the region itself is seen. With appropriate safety standards, she said, parts of the former test site could eventually support educational and memorial tourism centered on the experiences of affected communities.

“We do not want Semipalatinsk to be associated only with pain and radiation. I want this land to have a future. I want there to come a day when people can go there not with fear, but with a thermos of tea and a blanket for a picnic,” she said.

World.title: Singapore’s Lee: Nations Must Keep Reinventing to Stay Competitive
World.content:
ASTANA – Singapore’s experience shows that countries seeking long-term economic competitiveness must be prepared to adapt their policies and institutions to changing circumstances continuously, Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong said during a lecture at Nazarbayev University on Aug. 27.

Speaking to students and the academic community, Lee outlined Singapore’s development journey from the 1950s, highlighting the policies that helped the small, resource-scarce country build a globally competitive economy.

A different path to competitiveness

He stressed that Singapore and Kazakhstan have very different geographical and economic circumstances. Singapore is a small island nation with limited natural resources, while Kazakhstan is a vast landlocked country rich in energy and mineral resources. Nevertheless, he said, the two countries share similarities, including their experience of gaining independence from larger federations and their efforts to build strong international partnerships.

Lee said Singapore’s economic development was driven by a willingness to look outward and compete globally. After becoming independent in 1965, the country focused on export-oriented manufacturing, attracted multinational corporations, developed its financial sector and invested heavily in infrastructure and human capital.

Over time, Singapore repeatedly adjusted its economic strategy, moving toward higher-value and technology-intensive industries, research and development, advanced manufacturing and services.

“Singapore has not progressed in a straight line. We have repeatedly had to reinvent ourselves in order to overcome setbacks and change circumstances and resume our journey forward,” Lee said.

Adapting to a changing world

He noted that Singapore is now facing another major turning point amid growing geopolitical rivalry, weaker multilateralism and increasing concerns over economic and supply-chain resilience.

In response, Singapore intends to remain open and outward-looking while strengthening ties with non-traditional partners, including Kazakhstan and other Central Asian economies, Lee said.

He also stressed the importance of maintaining multilateral cooperation and supporting rules that apply to both large and small countries. He cited cooperation within the World Trade Organization, including Singapore’s work with Japan and Australia on e-commerce.

Lee identified state capacity, market discipline and an active government role as important elements of Singapore’s approach. While market forces remain central to creating wealth and encouraging enterprise, he said the government must invest in infrastructure and skills, develop new economic activities and address market failures.

Artificial intelligence is another area where government action will be important, notably in helping businesses adopt new technologies and preparing workers for changes brought by AI.

“Singapore must remake our economy again and again,” Lee said, stressing the importance of continuing education, worker retraining and support for people transitioning into new jobs.

He also highlighted social cohesion as a fundamental condition for economic success. Inclusive growth, public housing, healthcare and education, he said, help ensure that the benefits of economic development are broadly shared and that society remains united.

Lessons for Kazakhstan

The lecture comes amid intensifying Kazakhstan-Singapore relations. During a meeting with President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Aug. 26, Lee noted that bilateral ties had reached a new level, while Tokayev highlighted opportunities for cooperation in areas including AI, digitalization, transport, logistics, smart cities, agriculture, critical minerals and tourism.

Talgat Chinikeyev, Honorary Consul of Singapore in Kazakhstan, said Lee’s engagement with students was an important part of strengthening bilateral ties.

“Relations between countries are built not only through governments and businesses, but also through education, knowledge exchange and direct interaction between people,” he told The Astana Times.

According to Chinikeyev, Singapore’s development experience offers valuable lessons, while Kazakhstan has its own development path and ambitions. He said exchanges with the younger generation could help deepen mutual understanding and encourage new educational, academic and professional links between the two countries.

Lee concluded that while Kazakhstan may need to make different policy choices because of its distinct circumstances, the broader lesson from Singapore is the importance of building systems that can continuously adapt.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s First Kurultai Session Begins in Astana
World.content:
ASTANA – The first session of Kazakhstan’s Kurultai of the first convocation began on Aug. 28, marking the start of work of the country’s new unicameral legislature. President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said the launch of the Kurultai marks the beginning of a new stage in Kazakhstan’s political development.

“The unicameral legislative body of the country, the Kurultai, officially begins its work. This means that from this day the process of renewing the state’s political system begins,” Tokayev said.

He said the new institution should play a special role at this stage of Kazakhstan’s development and “give a powerful impetus to the work of the entire state apparatus.”

Business, science and media represented

The new Kurultai brings together representatives of business, public administration, education and science, media, medicine, law, agriculture and the public sector, including entrepreneurs, lawyers, academics, journalists, doctors and civil society representatives. Several deputies also have previous parliamentary experience, having served in the Mazhilis or Senate.

“Being a deputy of the Kurultai of the first convocation is, above all, a special and, without exaggeration, a happy moment. I am confident that you will serve the country with dignity, fully living up to the high authority entrusted to you,” Tokayev said.

The legislature consists of 145 deputies elected for five years through party lists. The Central Election Commission registered all elected deputies on Aug. 27.

The first session follows the Aug. 23 elections, held under Kazakhstan’s new constitutional framework and resulting in the formation of the country’s new unicameral legislature.

World.title: Abkhaz blogger who spoke of ‘shared future’: Who was late Daur Buava?
World.content:
Abkhaz blogger found dead in Georgia

Young Abkhaz blogger Daur Buava has been found dead in the Georgian capital, Tbilisi. According to neighbours, they raised the alarm after Buava had not been seen for several days. Emergency services called to his rented flat found his body inside.

The cause of his death has not yet been established, and an initial examination of the body found no signs of violence. Georgia’s Interior Ministry has opened an investigation under the article covering “incitement to suicide”.

Who was Daur Buava?

Daur Buava, 32, was an Abkhaz blogger who attracted public attention for his open and unconventional views on Georgian-Abkhaz relations. On social media, particularly TikTok, he regularly posted videos advocating peaceful coexistence, dialogue and the rebuilding of trust between Georgians and Abkhaz.

Buava was born in Abkhazia in 1994. The Georgian-Abkhaz war had ended a year before he was born, meaning his understanding of the conflict was largely shaped by what he had been told by those around him. In 2021, Buava travelled to Tbilisi in an attempt to examine that version of events for himself.

“Later, I realised that it was the truth as seen by only one side. I learned the other side’s truth here,” he told Georgian media outlet Netgazeti that same year.

Within months, Buava had become one of the most recognisable Abkhaz bloggers on TikTok. His videos focused primarily on relations between Georgians and Abkhaz, the war, peace and Abkhazia’s future. He had tens of thousands of followers, including young people in Abkhazia.

Buava’s public activities were not confined to social media. He gradually became one of the few Abkhaz voices openly advocating dialogue with Georgians. It was this position that made him a target of persecution in Abkhazia.

Meeting the “enemy”

Buava said that before travelling to Tbilisi, his views of Georgia had been based largely on the information he received in Abkhazia.

One of the reasons he decided to visit Georgia was a TikTok livestream in which Georgians and Abkhaz called each other enemies and exchanged insults. For Buava, this became another reason to see for himself the place he had been taught since childhood to regard as hostile.

He said that in both societies there was a small group of people fuelling hatred, while most people wanted to communicate with one another.

Daur Buava

Persecution in Abkhazia

Buava’s activities did not receive unequivocal support in Abkhazia from the outset. In late 2021, he said that many people criticised his presence and activities in Tbilisi, although he also received messages of support from Abkhazia. Over time, however, criticism was followed by threats.

According to Buava, his supporters also faced pressure. He said that people who posted positive comments during his livestreams were identified and, in some cases, people even went to their homes. Buava also said that several of his supporters had been beaten.

In June 2022, Abkhazia’s de facto security service opened a criminal case against Buava on charges of “high treason”.

The agency said that videos posted by Buava on TikTok contained appeals that undermined Abkhazia’s “sovereignty, territorial integrity, state security and defence capabilities”. It also accused him of promoting the idea of Abkhazia existing as an autonomous republic within Georgia.

The case against Buava was opened in absentia. He remained in Tbilisi and no longer planned to return to Abkhazia.

‘Amra’ and idea of shared future

In Tbilisi, Buava and his Georgian friend Mikheil Kvatashidze founded the Amra youth movement. The name means “Sun” in Abkhaz. The organisation aimed to create opportunities for young Georgians and Abkhaz to communicate with one another.

In December 2022, Buava obtained Georgian citizenship, which he said was granted under a simplified procedure. This became another source of criticism against him within Abkhaz society.

In 2023, Buava was invited to the European Parliament, where he spoke about relations between young Georgians and Abkhaz, the free exchange of information and overcoming the conflict.

“We must move forward and build a shared future,” he said.

At the European Parliament, Buava also addressed Russia’s role. In his view, Moscow had contributed to the escalation of the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict and was continuing to obstruct dialogue between Georgians and Abkhaz.

That same year, Buava opposed the adoption of the so-called “apartments law” in Abkhazia, saying he did not want Russians to buy property and settle in Abkhazia in large numbers. He regarded the main threat to Abkhazia as not the restoration of relations with Georgians, but the loss of its own demographic and cultural identity.
