World.title: Downsizer beats Sydney bidder to buy Fitzroy North terrace for $1,572,000
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Downsizer beats Sydney bidder to buy Fitzroy North terrace for $1,572,000 Wes Mountain August 29, 2026 — 2:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A three-bedroom art deco house in a quiet pocket of Fitzroy North sold for $1,572,000 at auction on Saturday, with a downsizer paying $72,000 above reserve. Behind 15 King Street’s original facade, the home had been renovated to feature polished floorboards, light-filled rooms and large windows looking onto a small paved courtyard. It had a price guide of $1.4 million to $1.5 million, and a reserve of $1.5 million. Jellis Craig agent and auctioneer David Sanguinedo said he opened the auction with a vendor bid of $1.4 million, which was quickly countered with a bid from the downsizer of $1.41 million. From there it jumped up in $20,000 and $10,000 increments – the downsizer competing with one other bidder, who was from Sydney – before trickling down to smaller bids to bring it to a close.



The light-filled entertaining area was one of the modern additions that made the most of the home’s art deco bones. Jellis Craig Fitzroy Sanguinedo said the vendors were upsizing and staying local. “They had their kids there, they outgrew it, and they wanted to stay in the neighbourhood because they love it so much,” he said. Sanguinedo thought the end of winter would see more competition for properties, with less supply coming online than in a typical spring, and many buyers still looking in an increasingly tight market. “We have more buyers than we have stock, so I think it’s evening out,” he said.



The property was one of 647 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne this week. In West Footscray, a four-bedroom modern townhouse sold for $900,000 in post-auction negotiations, after passing in at $820,000. The double-storey home at 32B Wellington Street features floating floorboards, fresh white walls and front and rear gardens, with a rainwater tank, all within minutes of nearby Shepherd Gardens, Tottenham station and Barkly Street shopping precinct. The property had a price guide of $800,000 to $880,000, and a reserve of $900,000. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide.



Buxton Inner West agent and auctioneer Matthew John said bidding opened with a vendor bid of $800,000, followed by the only genuine bid of $820,000 from a first home buyer couple, after which the property passed in. The rear garden features a rainwater tank and small al fresco area. Buxton Inner West John said there had been three interested parties, but only the first home buyers were ready to buy, and once the property passed in, both the vendors and buyers were keen to negotiate to meet the reserve and avoid a protracted sales process. The vendors had held the property as an investment. John said post-auction negotiations were becoming “more commonplace”, and thought there was less confidence from buyers to “put their hands up”. “And it doesn’t feel like [spring] this year will be as busy as a usual spring,” he said.

World.title: Game, set, match: 68,000 players face eviction in north shore tennis stoush
World.content:
One of Sydney’s longest-running community tennis centres has been ordered to vacate its north shore home after an Aboriginal land council secured ownership of the site, setting up a high-stakes dispute that has drawn involvement from sporting champions, politicians and prominent media figures. The Northern Suburbs Tennis Association (NSTA) will be required to hand over the keys to the eight-court Talus Street Tennis Centre at Naremburn by September 30 after receiving a formal eviction notice from the Metropolitan Local Aboriginal Land Council (MLALC), which took ownership of the Crown land reserve as part of a successful land claim in 2022. Jo Chapple and her son George Tams are among residents rallying to save the tennis operations. Sitthixay Ditthavong The move threatens to end almost 50 years of tennis at the site, where generations of players have graced its courts alongside Australian champions Evonne Goolagong Cawley and Pat Cash. The eviction notice has stunned members of the centre, which records more than 62,000 player visits annually and is regarded as one of the busiest community tennis facilities of its size in Sydney.



It has also thrust the reserve into an increasingly contentious debate over NSW Aboriginal land rights laws, particularly when land returned under the legislation is home to long-established community facilities. At the centre of the dispute is the financial arrangement governing the site. The eviction notice requires current operators to vacate the site by the end of September. Sitthixay Ditthavong When the MLALC acquired the reserve, it inherited existing lease arrangements involving the NSTA, which has occupied the site since 1978, and Love’n Deuce, the private operator that has managed the tennis centre for about four decades. Under those arrangements, the NSTA pays annual rent of $46,000 – a figure the MLALC has long argued falls well below the market value of a commercial operation occupying more than a hectare of valuable north shore land.



MLALC chief executive Nathan Moran said the land council had spent the past year reviewing the arrangements and considering whether to increase the association’s rent or seek an alternative operator willing to pay what it considers a fair return. “As the owner, we have to cover insurance, rates and maintenance of the site, and the challenge is for us to ensure the site does not become a financial liability when it was meant to be provided as recompense under land rights,” Moran said. Nathan Moran, chief executive of the Metropolitan Local Aboriginal Land Council. Dominic Lorrimer “Paying $46,000 for operating eight commercial courts does not pass the pub test.” The land council has also been examining redevelopment options. Earlier this year, it submitted plans to the NSW government’s Housing Delivery Authority for an 18-storey, 303-apartment tower on the reserve. The proposal was rejected by the panel, although it noted alternative planning pathways remained open should the land council pursue redevelopment in the future.



NSTA president Wayne Pascoe said the association was prepared to consider paying substantially more to remain at the site but had been unable to secure a meeting with the land council to negotiate. “Of course we were willing to look at the arrangements and increasing the amount we pay, and it’s been disappointing we haven’t had that opportunity,” he said. The facility has been hosting tennis since 1979. Sitthixay Ditthavong Pascoe said the association had spent more than $10 million building and maintaining the facility since 1979, including more than $500,000 on upgrades during the past three years. Financial records show the association generated $614,223 in revenue in 2025 and recorded an operating surplus of $98,465.



The prospect of losing the courts has alarmed club members, staff and residents, many of whom fear the community facility could be permanently lost. Love’n Deuce executive director Paul Francis has established an advisory group including veteran broadcaster Ray Martin and former television presenter Steve Liebmann in an effort to negotiate a solution with the land council. “People play here from age two to 82. I’ve got over 30 staff and their families, and some have been here 25 years. They’re already looking for other jobs, which breaks my heart,” Francis said. “It’s not just about tennis. It’s about the social interaction. People have made lifetime friends here.” Cammeray resident Jo Chapple, who regularly uses the centre while caring for her son with a disability, said the site’s value extended well beyond the courts.



Related Article City life The slice of Sydney harbourfront land that carries an unexpected burden “The less recreational sites we have in our city, the less liveable it will become,” she said. “Everyone is completely shocked.” The dispute is unfolding against the backdrop of a broader political battle over Aboriginal land claims in NSW. Earlier this year, the NSW government proposed limiting the transfer of Crown land occupied by community and sporting assets to Aboriginal land councils following a string of successful claims involving prominent sites including Paddington Bowling Club.



The proposed legislation has faced strong opposition from Aboriginal organisations, including the NSW Aboriginal Land Council, which has argued the changes threaten to undermine established land rights. Willoughby MP Tim James, a patron of the tennis centre, has called for government intervention, arguing the community facility should not be lost. “It doesn’t sit right with me that a community asset that has served generations of local families is being forced out of a site it’s occupied for more than 40 years,” he said. World.title: Tenzin can never return to his birthplace. Now Brisbane is his home, and music legends are his friends
World.content:
NationalQueenslandEntertainment Tenzin can never return to his birthplace. Now Brisbane is his home, and music legends are his friends Liam Heitmann-Ryce-LeMercier August 29, 2026 — 1:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brisbane-based musician Tenzin Choegyal first met legendary composer Philip Glass in 2011. Choegyal had no idea who Glass was – arguably the world’s most famous modern classical composer, widely recognised for film scores such as The Truman Show and Koyaanisqatsi. But Glass had certainly heard of Choegyal, and invited him to New York to perform at Carnegie Hall in the Tibet House Annual Benefit Concert. This longstanding event, which Glass curates, brings traditional Tibetan musicians together with major pop acts to raise funds with the aim of preserving Tibetan culture. Philip Glass and Tenzin Choegyal. Andreas H Bitesnich Choegyal has been invited back 11 times, and has worked with Glass between New York and Brisbane on projects such as the soundtrack to a feature-length documentary, The Last Dalai Lama? In March, he again joined Glass on stage at Carnegie Hall, with the likes of Elvis Costello, Elysian Fields, Kate Pierson and Robert De Niro.



This September, he will perform Be the Sky, an album he co-composed with Glass, at Brisbane Festival. Featuring texts from the Tibetan yogi Milarepa and prayers by His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama, Be the Sky is a reflective song cycle built around themes of exile, which are close to Choegyal’s heart. “The music carries me to places I can no longer physically go, especially Tibet,” he says. “Although I live far from my homeland, Tibet resides within me, and this album became a way of returning through music,” he says. The child of nomads, Choegyal fled the Chinese occupation of Tibet with his family in the early 1970s. They went to Nepal, where his father died, and his mother sent him on to the Tibetan Children’s Village in Dharamsala, northern India, where the Dalai Lama has found refuge since 1960. Choegyal was born in Tibet, raised in India in an orphanage, and has lived in Brisbane since 1997. David Kelly It was here that Choegyal took up his parents’ mantle and became a musician – his father played the lingbu (transverse bamboo flute), and his mother’s traditional chanting is one of his earliest memories. He also learnt to play the dranyen, a Tibetan lute.



In 1997, he resettled in Brisbane. “One of my very first experiences was performing at the Woodford Folk Festival,” he recalls, “where I was embraced by audiences and fellow musicians in a way that made me feel I had found another home.” Written for strings, saxophones, guitars, piano, children’s choir, the lingbu and dranyen, Be the Sky evokes many of Glass’s previous compositions rooted in Tibetan culture, such as his score for the Martin Scorsese-directed Dalai Lama biopic Kundun and his solo piano piece Mad Rush. The 70-minute Be the Sky captures a unique fusion of Western and Eastern musical philosophies, balancing the propulsive, repetitive arpeggios of Glass’ minimalist style with the graceful, high arcs of Choegyal’s Tibetan singing. This premiere in Brisbane is especially meaningful for Choegyal, as the city has fostered much of his artistic and personal growth.



“I found an incredibly generous artistic community here, where I could share my stories through my songs and music with much freedom,” he says. “I am super-looking forward to presenting it in my home.” Be The Sky was released as an album in November 2025, featuring refugee children from the Tibetan Children’s Village as well as Glass associate, Nashville-born musician Alex Ring Gray, who will also be performing in Brisbane. “We chose to release the album as a way of honouring two extraordinary people who have profoundly shaped my life: His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama, and Philip Glass,” Choegyal says. “Both entering their 90th year, their wisdom, compassion and generosity – expressed through their lives and their art – continue to inspire me every day.”



Choegyal says his relationship with Glass has become much more collaborative and fluid in recent years, with some creative material for Be the Sky deriving from his own earlier compositions, while other parts were developed exclusively with Glass. “In many cases,” he adds, “this material evolved further through performers we trusted deeply.” One such performer is Vanessa Tomlinson, a percussionist and director of the Queensland Conservatorium, where Be the Sky will receive its one-night-only performance on September 7. “The music in Be the Sky will be both familiar and new,” Tomlinson says, “with some of it being improvised in real time in front of you, and parts of it refined with some of the best emerging musicians in Australia: students at the Queensland Conservatorium.”



Related Article Entertainment Brisbane River to get spectacular fountain and light display at South Bank Tomlinson is eager to emphasise the beguiling qualities of Choegyal’s unique voice when paired with Glass’ stately, highly structured musical forms. “This is music to listen to, to dream to, to allow yourself to be mesmerised by,” she promises. “Choegyal is a master of the mountaintop, with his voice soaring and cascading from the stage, filling every corner of the concert hall.” Tomlinson says Choegyal is a rare musician who is at once at home on the world’s biggest stages and also happy to perform in Brisbane at humble venues such as The Cave Inn with local improvisers. “Tenzin has orbited my life in Brisbane for the past 20 years,” she says.



“Having a bridge between Philip Glass and the Queensland Conservatorium through Tenzin is such a great opportunity for students, staff and Brisbane audiences.” As a Tibetan artist rooted in the wisdom traditions of Tibetan nomads, Choegyal says a sense of lineage is always present in his music. “It lives in the way I sing, in the stories I carry, and in the emotions that naturally surface. “As Philip Glass would say, ‘if you hold on to your lineage, you are never really alone’.” Be the Sky will be performed at the Conservatorium Theatre, Queensland Conservatorium, Griffith University, Monday, September 7, 7.30pm. World.title: Alcohol abuse combined with social isolation can be lethal. It’s what killed my brother
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessDepression Opinion Alcohol abuse combined with social isolation can be lethal. It’s what killed my brother Dominic Cadden Physiologist August 29, 2026 — 1:30pm

August 29, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two of the most popularly underrated threats to the health of Australians are alcohol abuse and social isolation (with or without loneliness). Combine them and the synergy is devastating and lethal. It’s what killed my brother, Jason, the day after his 61st birthday. The combination of alcohol abuse and social isolation can kill. Much is said and written about the effects of alcohol abuse on others – namely violence from or among abusers, dangerous driving, work accidents, alienating family. This is all valid, but the longer-term effects on health need greater consideration. These include gradual liver damage and the effects on the brain that may start with mild memory lapses but become much more significant later in life. Alcohol abuse also exacerbates or triggers long-term anxiety and depression by disrupting mood regulation and the balance of brain chemicals. There are also the metabolic effects that promote fat accumulation, whole-body inflammation, insulin resistance and a higher risk of type 2 diabetes. The digestive system can become chronically inflamed, resulting in ulcers, pancreatitis and liver disease. My brother had debilitating diarrhoea in the last two to three years of his life, and he died with (but not because of) small bowel cancer. Alcohol is also classed as a Group 1 carcinogen by the International Agency for Research (part of the World Health Organisation). Heavy alcohol use can increase the risk of contracting mouth, throat, oesophageal and laryngeal cancers by five times. Liver, colorectal and breast cancer risk also increases, as does pancreatic cancer when chronic pancreatitis has set in (as occurred with another dead brother, also a heavy drinker).



Jason Cadden, who worked as a desk editor with the Sydney Morning Herald, died on July 21, one day after his 61st birthday. Often people split hairs on the defining points between a “heavy drinker” and an alcoholic. The term “functional alcoholic” is frequently bandied about, often jokingly. In my brother’s case, he was probably considered “functional” by doctors and colleagues only because he could hold on to a job (albeit often getting up 20 minutes before working from home). This was misleading, as absolutely nothing else was functional about his life – household management, health management, social connections or family and community interaction. After living in the same area for 26 years, the names most often seen around his home were Dan Murphy, Jack Daniels and Charles Lindeman. For the heavy drinker, the danger of social isolation is that there is no accountability. Heavy drinkers with plenty of social contacts either in or out of the home may tend to have at least some accountability to the times they drink, the amounts they drink, their behaviour, health, hygiene and day-to-day responsibilities – which may be for others, or even just themselves. These can all get lost for the heavy drinker in social isolation. Perspective is lost – with time (“I’ll give up … soon”); with wellbeing (“I’m sick/not feeling well/I stumbled” as opposed to “I fell because I was drunk”); with limits to drinking, social behaviour and self-control. It is too easy to lie to other people about the scale and volume of the drinking, which in turn makes it easier for the drinker to lie to themselves. There is no distraction from the psychological pull of alcohol – and it is a behavioural habit and psychological addiction as much as it is physical.



This is a detail that can slip past family and medical staff alike. My brother spent four months in hospital in 2025, so it was possibly assumed that sobriety would stick once he returned home, since the physical symptoms of alcohol withdrawal tend to peak 24 to 72 hours after the last drink (although they may linger for a few weeks). The psychological symptoms, however, may kick on for several months. Related Article Science The five everyday products linked to nearly one-third of all deaths globally The situation becomes more dire in social isolation. With no distraction, everything in life can be centred around or an excuse for the habit of drinking. Without other people, the drinking becomes the reward, the consoler, the comfort, the companion, even – in extreme cases such as my brother – when the alcohol is the cause of the problems the drinker is attempting to escape from or address. In his case, it was the alienation of morbid obesity, then diabetes, then cancer. In all these cases, heavy alcohol use interfered with or worked against drug therapy. The worst was when my brother turned up for a new, extremely expensive and time-sensitive nuclear medicine treatment for his cancer, only for medical staff to find that his potassium levels and liver function were too low for treatment due to his wholehearted return to drinking after being discharged from hospital. In social isolation, the heavy drinker has no sense of responsibility to anything other than fuelling the next drinking session. The vicious cycle might include functioning at a job and other tasks required to finance and maintain a nice, safe, comfortable environment for drinking where the drinker won’t be judged or interrupted. Alcohol is the fuel to maintain a routine, but social isolation is the dangerous spark for fiery self-destruction. Dominic Cadden is a health writer and accredited clinical exercise physiologist. His late brother, Jason Cadden, was a Herald desk editor. This piece is published with the permission of Jason’s other two siblings.

World.title: Answers, not condolences: Inside the fight for AFL action on head trauma
World.content:
SportAFLConcussion crisis Answers, not condolences: Inside the fight for AFL action on head trauma Bridget McArthur August 29, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As the AFL drags its heels on head trauma research, and launches yet another review of its safety protocols – the timeline for which is unclear – a startling new study of late NFL players’ brains has sent a shiver down the spines of Australian neuroscientists. Published this week in medical journal The BMJ, the research shows that, at an absolute minimum, one in four of NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 had chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). A new study out of the US has revealed a worrying rate of CTE among former NFL players. AP About a quarter of players who died in that six years donated their brains to science. More than 90 per cent of those 235 brains were posthumously diagnosed with CTE, meaning that, at a minimum, 24.5 per cent of all players who died during that period had CTE. The number could be as high as 97.7 per cent. The data presents a stark comparison to the roughly 1 per cent of the general population posthumously diagnosed with CTE in community brain bank studies.



The study also found a high rate of dementia among NFL players posthumously diagnosed with CTE, particularly those with more severe diagnoses. The NFL did not respond to The Age’s request for comment, but a spokesperson told Reuters it was continuously striving to make the game of football safer, and had implemented several strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts. It also released a joint statement with the NFL Players Association outlining new sanctions for players found guilty of repeated on-field health and safety violations, like dangerous tackles. Thousands of kilometres away, Australian neuroscientists have been taking note. While the Boston Brain Bank started around two decades ago, the Australian Sports Brain Bank (ASBB) opened only in 2018. The bank’s Victorian manager Dr Alan Pearce said the US study provided the clearest picture yet of the prevalence of CTE among athletes exposed to repeated head knocks. His team has analysed around 150 sportspeople’s brains, about half of which were found to have CTE, though Pearce said this was skewed by the fact that people suffering CTE-like symptoms were more likely to donate their brains.



Pearce said this dataset likely could have been much more complete by now if the AFL had been more cooperative. Instead, he said, the AFL has consistently hidden behind research gaps as an excuse for inaction, focusing brain health discussions on concussions, which are easier to prevent, and largely ignoring CTE, which is associated with repeated head knocks over an extended period. “It’s a dirty word,” Pearce said. “If you look at Spud’s Game from a couple of weeks ago, they talk about mental health, but they never mention CTE at all, even though Danny Frawley died with stage two CTE.” Danny Frawley died in 2019. Getty Images Looking through the archives of media releases and articles on the AFL website, CTE has been mentioned in connection to Spud’s Game only twice – once in 2013, and once in 2021. During his tenure as a lead brain health adviser to the AFL, Dr Paul McCrory was accused of downplaying the link between head trauma in sports and CTE, giving a speech in 2016 in which he argued that the dangers of concussion in the NFL were not nearly as serious as some reports suggested.



Study timeline remains unclear In early 2023, the AFL announced a $25 million longitudinal study into the brain health of current and former players. Its stated aim was to answer questions about the prevention, diagnosis and management of sport-related concussion and repetitive head impacts, and potentially help identify at-risk players sooner. Related Article Concussion research ‘worthless’ due to AFL attitude: doctor The league submitted the study for ethics approval in November 2024. The first participant was enrolled eight months later and, to date, the study has recruited just 102 of its sample size target of 3000 players, according to the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry. The study methodology spans at least 40 years. The Age has repeatedly asked the AFL in recent weeks for an update on the study, including when results would be published. The league did not answer specific questions, other than to say that two teams were involved with more to come.



The AFL Players Association said it had a representative on the study’s steering committee, but that its role was purely advisory. It was not sure which players were participating, or even how many. Pearce has called on the AFL to commit to a timeline for publishing interim results. The Australian Sports Brain Bank’s Victorian manager Alan Pearce. Jason South “They say they’re doing ongoing research, particularly in the long-term retired athlete space, and they’ve been doing that apparently since 2009 or 2010, but we’ve never actually seen any data at all,” Pearce said. Ideally, though, he said he would like to see the AFL fund fully independent studies to eliminate any possible perception of bias or obfuscation.



Pearce has long been at loggerheads with the AFL. He first fell out with them in 2017 after an unfruitful two-year research project, which the league had contracted him to lead. Pearce said he felt the AFL purposely frustrated his efforts by failing to provide him with enough former players to test. He said subsequent AFL-funded research appeared to have been similarly stalled, including into the use of instrumented mouthguards such as those made by Australian technology company HITIQ, which contain sensors designed to detect both concussive and sub-concussive impacts. This information can be fed live to medical staff on the sidelines during a game. The company’s technology is widely used in rugby union after being accredited by World Rugby. HITIQ was also recently selected by a US military research centre to help measure head impact in military and tactical training environments. Despite significant research pointing to the efficacy of the technology – which the AFL is using as a tool to gather metrics in its own brain health study – the league has not yet sought to roll it out more widely. Several years ago it commissioned Monash University to conduct research into the efficacy and viability of HITIQ’s mouthguards, which have since been tested on hundreds of players. The results are yet to be fully published.



Monash University associate professor Stuart McDonald, who is leading the research, said they had already published one paper in collaboration with the AFL that showed HITIQ mouthguards provide accurate, biologically meaningful head impact data. McDonald said the further study that was yet to be published was looking at how they could be used to flag impacts of clinical or neurobiological concern during games. He said the league had signed off on it and a final version had been submitted to a journal for peer review. While there is still a long way to go, McDonald said it was important to acknowledge that a lot of other good research was underway, including exploring the use of blood biomarkers to assess head impacts. Research will also be a key factor in upcoming class actions, according to legal experts. Dr David Thorpe, who teaches sports law at the University of Sydney, said potential liability existed in the gap between when the league should have feasibly known about the links between repeated head trauma and CTE based on available research, and when that information became common knowledge among players.



Players’ loved ones demand answers, not condolences Related Article Opinion

Concussion crisis The system failure at the heart of the Jake Kolodjashnij case - and the moral questions it raises Peter Ryan Sports reporter Despite a 2023 federal parliamentary inquiry into concussions and repeated head trauma in contact sports, the national discourse has remained scattered, largely reactive, and often narrowly focused on concussion. But after the persistence of a few headstrong individuals undaunted by the prospect of AFL exile, momentum has shifted this year. The number of impassioned dissidents is growing – among them, the friends and family of loved ones posthumously diagnosed with CTE. A deep-dive by the ABC’s Four Corners and revelations in the Herald Sun about Geelong’s Jake Kolodjashnij signing a waiver assuming responsibility for future on-field head injuries have fuelled the snowball effect.



The AFL appears to have taken note of this temperature change. The Age has spoken to three people, whose loved ones have been posthumously diagnosed with CTE, who have been contacted by the league for the first time in recent months. Adam Hunter with the 2006 premiership cup. Getty Images Premiership Eagle Adam Hunter’s close friend Dave Andrews – a strident advocate for current and former players – has received calls from both the league’s football operations executive general manager Laura Kane and chief executive Andrew Dillon. Dillon also wrote back to a letter sent by Andrews to the AFL. In this response, seen by The Age, the AFL boss said the league was “ramping up” its Brain Health Initiative, which would run over at least the next decade and involve all clubs, and committed to putting in place contact training limits. “The AFL has been subject to much scrutiny with respect to the way in which it deals with concussion and head trauma ... The AFL welcomes that scrutiny and fully cooperates with such inquiries and has actioned all such recommendations directed to it,” he said.



Dillon conveyed the league’s sympathies for Andrews’ loss and said it had done the same for Hunter’s parents, responding to “concerns as were raised by them in the recent ABC Four Corners program”. Hunter died in February 2025. His parents first spoke publicly about his CTE diagnosis the following August. Adam Hunter’s mum Jo Brown, who received a call from Kane about a month ago, said it was too little, too late. “I said, ‘it happened nearly 18 months ago. Where were you then? … They played for you. Where were you?’” Brown recalled. She said the call lasted about five minutes. She said she did not want condolences, she wanted answers, and to receive her son’s medical records from his time playing in the league, which she was unsure how to secure.



On Thursday, the AFL and AFLPA issued a joint statement committing to strengthening the game’s concussion framework through a review of existing safety nets. Dillon said the Geelong matter had highlighted the challenges faced by clubs, boards, doctors, and players navigating the complex legal and risk management issues around head trauma and concussion. The review will consider the challenges of insurance protections for players and officials, increasing the scope of the player association’s injury and support fund, and reviewing data collection practices. Next month, representatives of sports codes and research institutions from around the world will meet in Melbourne for the inaugural International Sports Concussion Conference, co-hosted by the AFL and NFL. Neither Pearce nor his Australian Sports Brain Bank colleague Michael Buckland have been invited to speak. Get the best of Good Weekend delivered to your inbox every Saturday morning.

World.title: Six months in, Iran’s regime stands, US goals remain unmet
World.content:
Men on motorbikes ride past buildings in Tehran damaged in US and Israeli strikes during the opening days of the war.

Trump’s replacement of a military war with a heightened economic one is not expected to alter Iran’s strategy, while further impoverishing its people.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It was supposed to be quick. Still, six months after the US and Israel launched massive airstrikes on Iran, the conflict drags on. The Trump administration has replaced its military war with an economic one, but the result is likely to be no different, analysts say, with a lack of American clarity about goals, a decline in US credibility and a strategic defeat. One thing remains constant, however. The ordinary people of Iran are bearing the brunt of the war, victims of both the United States and their own leaders. On the first day of the war, February 28, US President Donald Trump promised Iranians that “the hour of your freedom is at hand”. Six months later, his administration is trying to impoverish them further, hoping against hope that they will revolt and overthrow a repressive, militarised regime. A Tehran billboard with a message that reads in Farsi, “We must rise up”, and an image of the late Iranian supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. AP The Iranian leadership, increasingly dominated by military men, sees its own survival as the nation’s, and considers the sacrifices of ordinary Iranians as a necessary act of patriotism and even martyrdom. It has become ever more ruthless in stamping out the slightest signs of dissent. It is difficult to dress up what has clearly been a US failure to bend Iran to its will, despite the might of the combined US and Israeli militaries. Not only has the Islamic Republic survived, but it effectively controls the Strait of Hormuz. It has strengthened its influence in the region, with even the countries it was bombing a few months ago trying to reinvigorate ties with Iran.



Trump, who once described the war as a “little diversion”, appears unable to bring it to a satisfactory conclusion. AP Photo/Manuel Balce Ceneta “The war has failed to deliver US objectives,” says Sanam Vakil, director of the Middle East and North Africa program at Chatham House. Suzanne Maloney, an Iran expert and head of foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, judges the war a failure. “We did a lot of damage to Iran, but they have come out stronger than before,” she says. Iran’s neighbours have decided they must find a modus vivendi with an Islamic Republic that is not going away. ‘The capacity to hurt Iran is clear. The path from pain to capitulation or collapse is not.’ Sina Toosi, Centre for International Policy American credibility among allies has suffered along with Trump’s own reputation for avoiding costly, interminable wars in the Middle East and promoting “affordability” at home. And it has made his promise to liberate ordinary Iranians look hollow. “This war has really overtaken the Trump presidency,” Maloney says.



The regime survives Operation Epic Fury began with a joint US-Israeli surprise attack on Iran, which killed the supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and many of his officials, while badly wounding his son and now successor, Mojtaba Khamenei. Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war Trump is clutching at straws and the world knows it Weeks of intense bombing destroyed much of Iran’s air force and navy and badly damaged its missile program. But the population did not rise up, and the leadership did not fracture. Iran’s military restored many of its missile launchers and attacked key US allies in the region as well as US bases, which were inadequately defended. It effectively shut down the Strait of Hormuz and caused global economic disruption. Several thousand Iranians, including children, have died – the numbers are hard to verify – as have 18 American service members. The original Operation Epic Fury has been replaced with what Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last Monday announced as Operation Economic Outcast, designed to isolate Iran further and crash its badly damaged economy.



US allies in the Gulf, including the UAE, have borne the brunt of Iran’s retaliation. AP Photo/Altaf Qadri “This is a sustained campaign to collapse every last option for Iran,” Bessent said. “The campaign we begin today will gather force with every day that follows, and it will not end until this regime stands alone.” Despite rhetorical flourishes about D-Day and the fall of the Berlin Wall, Bessent did not indicate how long this economic war would last, what instruments it would use, or what it aimed to achieve. Is the US goal once again the collapse of the regime? Or to force the opening of the Strait of Hormuz? Or to bring a more desperate Iran back to the negotiating table to reach a sustainable settlement of both the strait and Iran’s nuclear program? “There is no clear articulation of America’s goals,” says Esfandyar Batmanghelidj of the Bourse & Bazaar Foundation, a research organisation based in London. “But if you don’t define behaviour change, sanctions as coercion fail.” Iran’s hardliners have consolidated their grip on power. AP Photo/Anmar Khalil Iran, already the target of thousands of sanctions, is considered unlikely to surrender because of a few more. More likely, analysts say, is that the country will respond in time by escalating its attacks on ships in the Persian Gulf and on American allies, which could produce another round of US bombing.



Washington is betting it can achieve through tighter economic strangulation what six months of war could not, says Sina Toossi of the Centre for International Policy, a Washington think tank. The Trump administration is trying to do that by demanding international compliance even as its relations with much of the world grow more coercive and transactional, with more countries choosing to ignore the president’s dictates. “The capacity to hurt Iran is clear,” Toossi says. “The path from pain to capitulation or collapse is not.” A risky stalemate With US objectives unclear, the confusion is real in Iran, too, says Ali Vaez, Iran project director for the International Crisis Group. They will wonder, he says: “Does the US want to achieve collapse, capitulation or compromise?” Related Article Middle East at war ‘Band of brothers’: These hardliners are now running Iran, and they are not scared of Trump Given that Iran’s leaders see the effort to strangle them as another form of warfare, Vaez says, the new US strategy has two risks. If it fails, the only option left is to return to military escalation. And if it works, it may lead Iran to escalate and break the US naval blockade.

World.title: ‘Tightly held’ pocket: Inner west home sells for $260,000 over reserve
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions ‘Tightly held’ pocket: Inner west home sells for $260,000 over reserve Robyn Willis August 29, 2026 — 1:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A three-bedroom single fronted home sold for $2,461,000 in Petersham, more than $260,000 over the reserve on Saturday. Bidding for the home on 244 square metres at 66 Brighton Street opened at $2.1 million. A further bid of $50,000 followed, with bids going up in increments of $25,000, $20,000 and $10,000 before final bids of $5000 and $1000 drew the auctioneer’s hammer. The home, which has large bi-fold doors and windows leading onto a north-facing courtyard, had an advertised guide of $2 million and a reserve of $2.2 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide.



A buyer’s agent was acting on behalf of the successful bidders, a family from Balmain, while the underbidders were a family from Birchgrove. Seven parties registered to bid for the property, with three active. Sales agent for BresicWhitney Inner West, Frederico Fraga-Matos said buyers were attracted by the size of the property and its proximity to local amenities such as Petersham Park and Petersham Bowling Club, a popular venue for families. Related Article Housing slump ‘Situational selling’: The home owners who are selling in a downturn “This particular pocket is pretty tightly held,” he said. Buyers had become accustomed to the “new environment”, he said.



“What we are finding now, a lot of the outcomes that happened earlier in the year [such as interest rate increases], they have come out,” he said. “This is the new environment we are operating in and people are feeling more confident buying.” The renovated property at 66 Brighton Street has large bifolds opening onto a north-facing courtyard. Domain The property was one of 532 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this week. It was a similar result in Paddington, where a one-bedroom apartment with an enclosed balcony sold for $1.48 million, $180,000 above the reserve. Five parties registered to bid for 17/24 Gordon Street, with four active. Bidding opened at $1.2 million, followed by increments of $10,000 and $20,000. The property had a reserve of $1.3 million and a guide of $1,225,000.



The successful bidder was a Queenslander who wanted to use the apartment as a Sydney bolthole. The underbidder was a downsizer seeking a property to be closer to family. Buyers were attracted to the contemporary building in the heritage suburb of Paddington. It’s also a flat walk to the shops. Domain Sales agent for LJ Hooker Double Bay Darran Wyatt said buyers were attracted by the contemporary nature of the building and the fact that it was a flat walk to the shops. Market conditions, he said, felt “normal”. “People are looking to buy and properties are selling.”

World.title: Warriors v Knights: Jett Cleary to debut, when they play, kick-off time, team list, injuries, NRL ladder - what to know
World.content:
NRL: NZ Warriors v Newcastle Knights

Kickoff 4pm Sunday, 30 August

Go Media Stadium, Auckland

Live blog updates on RNZ

Jett Cleary will make his long-awaited Warriors debut against the Knights on Sunday.

Cleary will make his debut paired with Luke Hanson. On Saturday afternoon, the team said it was the least experienced halves combination in Warriors history.

They take the place of the halves pairing of Te Maire Martin and Chanel Harris-Tavita.

"It has been decided not to risk the established halves this week," the Warriors said.

"Martin was named on Tuesday to return from a hamstring complaint which kept him out of the last three matches against Penrith, Brisbane and South Sydney.

"However, he has been omitted tomorrow as has Harris-Tavita who has a minor hamstring issue. Both will train fully next week to line up in the final regular season match against Manly Warringah on Saturday (September 5).

It had been looking highly unlikely Jett - the son of former Warrior Ivan Cleary, and younger brother of of four-time premiership winner Nathan - would ever make his first grade debut with the Warriors after being granted an early release from his contract on compassionate grounds.

It allows him to return to Australia at the end of the 2026 season.

Quiet force behind Warriors' rise

While Leka Halasima will happily charge headfirst into an NRL defence line, when it comes to fronting the cameras, he is quick to turn the other way.

The NZ Warriors superstar has been notorious for avoiding media since exploding onto the rugby league scene, admitting as much during his one and only appearance in front of journalists this season.

"I've been hiding," he said with a smile.

Though uncomfortable with the spotlight, Halasima plays a big role behind the scenes at the club.

Teammate Demitric Vaimauga said 'Leka the Wrecker' was equally impressive off the pitch.

"There's way more to Leka than his special plays and his quietness, his shyness," the Warriors second-rower said. "He's a real intelligent guy."

After a mid-season slump, Vaimauga said Halasima took it upon himself to inspire his fellow rookies and get things back on track.

"We have a little group chat, Leka started it. We weren't going so well in the middle of the season, we had a little rough patch, so Leka brought us all together, fired us up and just reminded us how how special it is to be on the the big stage all together.

"It was, like, just remember why we're here, what got us here, go back to our superpowers, our strengths and just play footy."

Vaimauga said the pep talk was the catalyst for the younger members in the squad rediscovering their form.

"There was a stretch there where Jakey [Jacob Laban] was playing probably the best footy for us. Ali [Leiataua] found his groove again, and I just felt most of us young boys stepped up and were playing some good footy, which has taken us to where we are now."

Warriors superstar Leka Halasima is making his voice heard behind the scenes. Andrew Cornaga/Photosport

Sitting pretty

Dare to dream, Warriors fans.

The club is sitting high up on the NRL ladder and have a maiden championship in their sights, but with two rounds remaining in the regular season, the race for the minor premiership looms as a dramatic one.

The penultimate assignment for the Warriors before playoffs sees them host the Knights in Auckland on Sunday afternoon.

History

The Warriors have played the Knights 52 times since 1998 and hold a 28-23 head-to-head advantage, with one draw.

The Warriors have won their past three against the Newcastle side - their last loss came in 2024, when they went down 14-8.

The biggest win for the Warriors came back in 2007, when Wade McKinnon, Jerome Ropati and Grant Roveli all bagged try doubles in a 52-10 rout.

The sole draw occurred in 2000, when the sides could not be separated and shared the spoils in an 18-18 deadlock.

Form

The Warriors are coming off a strong 45-26 victory over South Sydney, ending an eight-match winning streak at Allianz for the Bunnies and marking a fourth successive win for the New Zealand club.

This sent them to No.1 in the competition on points differential, one clear of Penrith Panthers.

Meanwhile, the Knights lost 44-24 at home to the Sea Eagles, but kept their sixth spot on the points table.

The Warriors will be without prolific tryscorer Dallin Watene-Zelezniak for the rest of the regular season, after the star winger broke his collarbone in the weekend's win over the Rabbitohs. Photosport

Teams

The Warriors have made three changes for Sunday's match, including the addition of right winger Luke Laulilii, who comes in for [https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/sport/1084351/injury-blow-to-warriors-as-star-winger-dallin-watene-zelezniak-sidelined-with-broken-collarbone Dallin Watene-Zelezniak, who broke his collarbone in last weekend's win over the Rabbitohs.

Laulilii will become the Warriors' 300th NRL player, after signing from Wests Tigers in June. The 20-year-old scored 10 tries in 17 NRL appearances for his former club.

Halfback Te Maire Martin comes back from injury to partner Chanel Harris-Tavita, after missing the last three matches with a hamstring injury.

For the Knights, both Dane Gagai and Francis Manuleleua have been named to return, after missing last week's clash with Manly, but both Dominic Young and Tyson Frizell are sidelined due to suspension. Kiwi Phoenix Crossland has also been ruled out, after undergoing knee surgery.

Team lists

Warriors: 1.Taine Tuaupiki, 2. Luke Laulilii, 3. Ali Leiataua, 4. Leka Halasima, 5. Alofiana Khan-Pereira, 6. Luke Hanson, 7.Jett Cleary, 8. James Fisher-Harris, 9. Wayde Egan, 10. Mitchell Barnett, 11. Kurt Capewell, 12. Jacob Laban, 13. Erin Clark

Interchange: 14. Sam Healey, 15. Tanner Stowers-Smith, 16. Demitric Vaimauga, 17. Eddie Ieremia-Toeava, 18. Adam Pompey, 19.Morgan Gannon.

Knights: 1. Kalyn Ponga, 2. Fletcher Hunt, 3. Dane Gagai, 4. Bradman Best, 5. Greg Marzhew, 6. Fletcher Sharpe, 7. Sandon Smith, 8. Jacob Saifiti, 9. Harrison Graham, 10. Trey Mooney, 11. Jermaine McEwen, 12. Francis Manuleleua, 13. Mat Croker

Interchange: 14. Thomas Cant, 15. Cody Hopwood, 16. Lachlan Crouch, 17. Pasami Saulo, 18. Toby Winter, 19. Diesel Hagan.

What will happen

There is far too much on the line for the Warriors and coach Andrew Webster has them playing far too cohesively for them to drop this one. With the added motivation of a minor premiership in sight, the home side should put on another dominant display in front of the faithful.

A frenetic final fortnight

With the Roosters, Panthers and Warriors all on 38 points, the fight for first will be fierce. The Warriors edge Penrith by just one in the points differential, although they enjoy a decent run home with games in Auckland against the Knights and Sea Eagles.

World.title: Government imposes 10 years of performance requirements on Tiaki Wai
World.content:
The government is imposing performance requirements on Tiaki Wai, amid outrage in Wellington over high bills from the water services provider.

It is the first time such a tool has been used on a water services provider.

Under the rules, the Commerce Commission is able to set binding requirements on Tiaki Wai's performance. That means it can specify what it must deliver, and by when.

The performance requirements will be in place for the next 10 years.

Local Government Minister Simon Watts said Wellingtonians were being asked to pay a lot for water, and they were entitled to know what they were getting for their money.

"Decades of local underinvestment have left this region with water networks that are not up to standard, and the cost of fixing them is now landing directly on households. Given the scale of investment required, strong accountability is essential.

Simon Watts RNZ/Baz Macdonald

"The government will be watching Tiaki Wai very closely.

"I have a low threshold for considering further intervention if we do not see clear and sustained performance improvements," Watts said.

"This is about restoring confidence that the money being collected is delivering the infrastructure and services people have been promised."

Consumer Affairs Minister Cameron Brewer said transparency on its own was not enough. That was why the government was giving the Commerce Commission "real teeth" to deal with the provider.

"For years the cost of water services was buried inside rates while networks were left to deteriorate - which is partly why Wellington ended up here," he said.

"Tiaki Wai faces an estimated $25 billion of investment over the next 30 years. That is an enormous amount of other people's money, and Wellingtonians are entitled to expect it goes into pipes and treatment plants."

Tiaki Wai chair Will Peet discusses Wellington water bills Morning Report Download MP3 4m

The Commission had signalled that its initial focus would be on the critical, high-risk projects Tiaki Wai has already committed to, he said.

Stop Tiaki Wai organiser Guy Nunns said the water provider needed a major change in how it operates to focus on affordability - not just more oversight.

"Talk is cheap," he told RNZ.

"We want to be optimistic about anything that's coming from our politicians and our government but history has shown that often what they say and what they do are two different things."

World.title: An oasis of calm to consider RMA as politics gets frantic
World.content:
As the election nears, politics gets increasingly frantic and aggressive. Question Time has frequently dissembled into a sideshow of attack, obfuscation, rhetoric and hyperbole with information seldom emerging.

But the majority of this week was a very different version of Parliament. A clutch of MPs from across the House, who specialise in planning and environment law, spent achingly long days considering the minutiae of two bills designed to replace the Resource Management Act. Its consideration - from both sides of the House - was dedicated and careful, professional and informed, unemotional and earnest.

It was a blessed respite and refreshingly encouraging.

RMA week: a sane, slow respite from frantic politics The House Download MP3 5m

Parliament's week was spent under urgency, from dinner time on Tuesday. The House sat from Breakfast until midnight, concluding two minutes short of the witching hour on Friday - a gruelling schedule, but one that was a model of sanity.

The plan was to progress five bills through eleven stages of debate. The focus was on completing the time-unlimited committee stages of the twin bills that together will replace the Resource Management Act (RMA).

It took until Friday morning to wade through the two Committee of the Whole stages. These are typically about detail and MPs with a focus on the specialist area or from relevant committees do the overwhelming amount of discussion.

Afterwards, time suddenly sped up again and MPs practically galloped through eight of the remaining nine planned stages of debate in the remainder of Friday. MPs were then free to return home to recall the names of their partners, pets and progeny.

This is the second attempt at replacing the RMA in just three years. The first was also a twin-set shepherded to completion exactly three years ago by Labour's David Parker. That law was repealed a few months later by National in their first weeks of Government, with a promise to start from scratch rather than tweak the status quo.

This second attempt has taken almost as long to build, though at times it seems to have stood on the shoulders of its predecessor. The architect this time is Chris Bishop (National), with assistance from parliamentary under-secretary Simon Court (ACT).

The Planning Bill and the Natural Environment Bill are vast and complex, and crucially important to pretty much every aspect of New Zealand, and a small number of MPs have really been giving it their all. Because of urgency there were scant Select Committees, so most other MPs are likely to have had a very dull week.

Considering the time taken on these bills you would presume there was relentless filibustering - where the Opposition slow down the process, just to slow down the process - but it seldom felt like that; the to-and-fro was that of a small group of informed, involved, clever people having a brutally detailed discussion of how best to steer a complex legislative vehicle with decent amounts of case law hanging off the sides of it.

It was a well-reasoned and unemotional argument about the best way to achieve things. Three 13-hour long days of talking surely took a toll on everyone's vocal chords.

Half the credit for this must go to Opposition backbenchers - key players were Rachel Brooking and Arena Williams for Labour, and Lan Pham and Steve Abel for the Greens.

Sadly, no credit goes to the governing-party backbench MPs. They attend Committee Stages in double digits despite staying entirely silent - even those from the select committee that previously considered the bill. Like automatons, every few hours they come to life to call out during the voice votes.

The second half of the credit goes to the two Executive MPs who took turns at The Table. A constructive committee stage also requires the minister in charge of a bill to take it seriously. When a minister's answers to questions are dismissive or aggressive it can go downhill fast and get a bit feral.

At the Table answering questions and responding to proposed amendments were National's Minister for RMA Reform Chris Bishop, and his associate the ACT MP and Parliamentary Undersecretary Simon Court. Both kept things constructive and even at times cheerful, which is quite a feat during such long days.

One last thing to note: even at this penultimate stage of consideration, complex bills often get tweaks, as this one did. That is not a flaw; it is meant to happen. Those tweaks weren't the hundreds of opposition suggestions, but they may well have approved of, and maybe influenced some. Debate and discussion should and can influence the outcome right up until the Third Reading debate begins. This is the last chance to influence the outcome, so it is worth getting in while you can.

World.title: Kiwi scientists trying to fathom why Nepal flash floods generated so much water
World.content:
Connecting the Dots: Climate, Oceans and Extreme Events Saturday Morning Download MP3 22m

This week devastating flash flooding hit the Nepal-China border, leaving at least 600 people dead and around 2500 more missing, including five New Zealanders.

This year alone we've already recorded a number of tragic disasters across the planet caused by heatwaves, cyclones, floods and droughts. Some of them could be linked to increasingly turbulent weather patterns as the climate changes.

But how do we make sense of the link between seismic activity, ocean currents and rising temperatures?

Earth Sciences New Zealand principal scientist Graham Leonard said while details were still emerging about the disaster in Nepal, a large volume of rock and ice broke away from an area more than 600 metres wide high up in the mountains in the headwaters near the Nepal border with China in the Tibet Autonomous Region.

It collapsed suddenly and the material fell rapidly about 2km.

"So it was moving fast. It transformed into a large valley debris flow... It generated a lot of water and was picking up sediments and boulders as it went.

"It travelled about 60km through river valleys until it was finally able to spread out onto a wide alluvial fan."

Earth Sciences New Zealand principal scientist Graham Leonard Jeff McEwan, Capture Studios

Scientists like Leonard were still trying to work out why such "a remarkable amount of water" was generated.

Initially, the ground tremor was thought to be a 5.2 magnitude earthquake.

While the disaster could not be directly linked to climate change and global warming, a warmer planet was generating conditions that destablised high mountains and rock and ice and making them "a lot more frequent". Glaciers, ground water and permafrost were also being adversely affected, Leonard said.

"Nepal and high mountainous areas are definitely a hot spot."

Warming meant more landslides, bigger debris events and more flooding on the plains.

The same thing was also happening in New Zealand's Southern Alps with Aoraki Mt Cook being pushed up and glaciers eroding rapidly.

Screen recordings of surveillance camera footage posted on Chinese social media platforms, reportedly show flash flooding hitting the Gyirong Port in the Tibet Autonomous Region on August 26, 2026. -

Rough run for quakes

Regarding the recent run of earthquakes, including in New Zealand, he said it had been a rough few months globally.

Earthquakes were connected globally when they were measured, especially for those above 5 on the Richter scale.

"They go through the planet and around the planet."

For the run of quakes in New Zealand recently, in Fiordland, Taumarunui, around the East Coast and Edgecumbe they would have "stressed up the ground around them".

"But they won't have influenced the stress between those different places - it's too far apart. ...But they are connected through the fact we are on a plate boundary and we have faultlines and earthquakes all over the place."

It was a reminder that people needed to check their foundations and brick chimneys, have emergency supplies and a family escape plan, he said.

An undersea volcano eruption in Tonga on 15 January, 2022. Tonga Meteorological Services / EyePress via AFP

Tongan volcano 'erupted into space'

Referring to the global interconnectedness of an event having an impact in other parts of the world, Leonard recalled the Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai undersea volcano in Tonga in 2022.

"It sent a shock wave in the atmosphere and a tsunami around the entire global atmosphere and oceans because it was so huge.

"That eruption overshot the atmosphere and erupted into space because of the explosivity of a big cauldera collapse like generated Lake Taupō."

He said it was so enormous it was heard in Aotearoa as well as in the other direction, Alaska.

"It was incredibly loud," he said.

The atmospheric pressure in the ocean was so great it was able to generate a metres-high tsunami as far away as South America, Leonard said.

El Niño is tracking to be the strongest in the last 100 years and "we're in it, starting now", he said.

"It's a natural process but climate change is amplifying this."

The country was already seeing drier conditions in the east, westerly windflows and "spikier" conditions, meaning higher temperatures.

World.title: Mental health crisis looming and urgent investment needed, psychiatrists warn
World.content:
Psychiatrists are warning of a looming mental health staffing crisis and say urgent investment is needed to avoid a workforce cliff.

The Royal Australia and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists told RNZ that half of the current psychiatry workforce was retiring within a decade and one in five positions were vacant.

RANZCP board director Dr Mark Lawrence said urgent investment was needed to nearly double psychiatry training places.

"We don't have enough senior psychiatrists to then supervise our trainees and then we are not training enough trainees as well," he said. "It's a double-edged sword - if we don't do something soon, it's going to be a challenging space for all of us."

Lawrence said psychological distress was climbing, yet there had been a dramatic dropoff in New Zealanders accessing specialist mental health and addiction services over the past five years.

Dr Mark Lawrence Supplied

Services needed to meet the specific needs of Māori and Pasifika peoples, those living with long-term health conditions or disabilities, and people known to care, protection and justice services.

"There's been enduring concerns for Māori and Pasifika in terms of their access, particularly those aged between 15-25. That cohort is relatively underserved, and there's evidence that there's significant psychological distress in that particular group and it's that particular group that often have challenges in navigating the healthcare system."

The RANZCP also wanted increased inpatient beds and expanded school-based supports.

Services remain 'under pressure'

Health New Zealand executive national director of mental health and addiction Phil Grady said mental health and addiction services remained "under pressure", and recognised the need to grow the psychiatry workforce.

"We will continue to work with the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists on workforce recruitment and retention initiatives," he said.

Grady said Health NZ had exceeded its annual workforce target for the mental health and addiction sector.

"We exceeded the annual workforce target in 2025/26, with 514 new professionals entering training, including 74 clinical psychology interns and 48 stage one psychiatry registrars," he said. "In addition, the first cohort has commenced training for the new psychology assistant role, in partnership with the New Zealand Psychologists board, with a $28.45 million investment to support the implementation of the role."

Phil Grady of Health NZ recognises the need to grow the psychiatry workforce. Nathan Mckinnon / RNZ

Grady said the mental health and addiction workforce grew by more than 11 percent across key professions between September 2023 and September 2025, and the RANZCP's figures differed to Health NZ's workforce reporting.

"Health NZ's data shows our psychiatrist vacancy rate has fallen from 20.9 percent in March 2024 to 15.6 percent March 2026," he said. "Vacant psychiatrist FTE reduced from 123.7 in March 2024 to 89.9 in March 2026."

Grady said too many young people were experiencing acute mental health challenges.

"The latest mental health target data shows 77.3 percent of people under 25 referred to specialist mental health and addiction services were seen within three weeks, and improving access for young people remains a key focus for Health NZ," he said.

"We are continuing to invest in additional mental health infrastructure and service capacity, including new and redeveloped acute and forensic inpatient facilities as part of wider efforts to improve access to mental health care."

College stands by figures

In a statement to RNZ, the college said it stood by its figures on the shortages in the profession.

"In Health NZ's Mental Health and Addiction Workforce Plan, released in November 2025, Minister Doocey states that "growing the Health NZ funded psychiatry workforce remains our biggest challenge with an almost 20 percent vacancy rate".

This is consistent with Health NZ workforce data released under the OIA process in September 2025, which showed 111.2 vacant psychiatry FTE against 580.2 funded psychiatry FTE nationally, equating to a vacancy rate of approximately 19.2%. We note that vacancy data were unavailable for some districts, meaning the true vacancy rate may be higher.

Most recently, Te Pou's 2025 Health NZ Te Whatu Ora workforce estimates, published in January 2026, estimated the psychiatry vacancy rate within public adult mental health and addiction services at 19.7%, making it the highest vacancy rate of any major clinical workforce.

A vacancy rate of 19.7% is, by any reasonable interpretation, approximately one in five. The College therefore stands by its characterisation that around one in five psychiatry FTE are vacant within the public system.

If Health NZ or the Minister are referring to a different or more recent dataset, we would welcome clarification regarding which figures they are using and whether those data are publicly available.
