Tech.title: What Meta’s All-New Social Media Guidelines Promise to Change for Teen Users
Tech.content:
The fallout of an $18 billion lawsuit against Meta, announced on Wednesday, is already here. A new announcement from Meta is designed to meet the terms of the settled lawsuit while helping to prevent teen social media addiction.

In its post, Meta outlined a series of changes to both Instagram and Facebook that will apply only to those under 18. Most of the changes were required as part of the lawsuit settlement, notably the creation of daily limits and night mode controls for teens, as well as the adoption of age-assurance measures to help prevent cheating the system. As part of the agreement, Meta has denied any wrongdoing.

There’s been worldwide pushback against teens and children using social media, including the EU restricting access to social apps for kids under 13, and Australia banning apps like Instagram for anyone under 16. But some advocates worry Meta’s changes won’t be enough to fully protect teens.

In an interview with Democracy Now on Thursday, attorney and co-director of the AI Now research institute, Amba Kak, said the changes don’t address the platform’s architecture, which is designed to addict teenagers with features like infinite scroll. “It’s the business model of surveillance advertising, where it is the optimization of engagement and attention at any cost,” Kak said. “And I think if we don’t get at those root cause fixes, we’re going to be stuck playing whack-a-mole.”

A representative from Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Time limits for kids

Chief among the upcoming changes to Instagram and Facebook are time limitations for teens. A new default time limit will set the social media scrolling time to 2 hours a day for those under 18, and it can only be extended by parents.

An additional night mode will block most access to content such as feeds, stories, explore mode and reels between midnight and 6 a.m. and a school mode will mute notifications between 8 a.m. and 3 p.m.

Meta is also adding a feature to give 15-minute warnings to teens if they’ve been on the apps for an extended period of time, as well as 60-minute and 90-minute warnings they’re daily allotment is running down. To further reduce constant scrolling, autoplay for videos and clips will also be turned off by default, but like most features, it can be adjusted by parents.

Protection against toxic content

Meta is also implementing a number of changes intended to reduce toxicity and obsession with social media. By default, teens won’t see likes and reactions on posts, including their own. They’ll also be restricted from seeing certain content, such as cosmetic surgery and “extreme makeup” filters, although it’s not clear how far those limitations will extend (for example, a filter that adds dog ears).

Meta is adding age-appropriate content restrictions, but it remains vague on the details. While using movie ratings and parent feedback to build filters, the company fails to explain how this applies to social media posts or provide examples of blocked content.

In addition, teens will have the option to choose a non-algorithm version of their feeds that won’t be personalized by any Meta recommendations (which I also want for my own account).

Hazy tools for age verification

A new age-assurance strategy is also coming to Instagram and Facebook, but it’s unclear how it will work.

“We’re investing in even stronger technology to proactively catch accounts that may belong to under-13s,” Meta said on its blog. “We’re also strengthening the technology we use to identify accounts that may be between the ages of 13 and 17.”

Meta didn’t provide any details on how this tech would work, what it would look for or how it would flag accounts. I also asked about any appeals process for those incorrectly tagged, but Meta didn’t respond to my request.

It’s possible Meta will be using AI scan to profile context, account activity and visual cues to raise red flags, but there’s not much clarity otherwise.

Rolling out changes

The proposed changes were approved by a judge on Thursday, and Meta will roll out the first protections in the coming months, with the rest to follow afterward, although the exact timeline isn’t clear. As required by the agreement, Meta will also establish an independent social media research foundation to share “consented” user data in an effort to support teen well-being.

In its post, Meta said, “The fact is that teens move fluidly between dozens of apps a day. All platforms should empower parents and support teens by putting the same measures in place … we urge TikTok and YouTube to join us and state attorneys general in adopting this new standard.”

Other platforms have not responded to this call-out.

Tech.title: AT&T Sues Charter Over ‘Fiber’ Internet
Tech.content:
AT&T filed a lawsuit against Charter on Friday, alleging that its marketing of “fiber-powered” internet is misleading customers.

The argument centers around an ad campaign from Charter, which sells home internet under the Spectrum brand name.

Fiber is widely considered the gold standard for home internet. It’s the only connection type that delivers symmetrical upload and download speeds, which makes it especially valuable for activities like online gaming or videoconferencing. On Spectrum’s cable plans, typical upload speeds top out at 40Mbps, while download speeds exceed 1,000Mbps. I always advise readers to go with a fiber provider whenever it’s available.

Over the past couple of years, cable internet providers have increasingly tried to capitalize on that fiber cache. It’s technically true that Spectrum provides “fiber-powered” internet. Like all cable ISPs, Spectrum uses fiber-optic cables — thin glass strands that carry data through light signals — for the vast majority of its network. But it switches to copper coaxial cables in most cases to travel the proverbial last mile to your home. Fiber providers like AT&T, on the other hand, run the fiber connection all the way to the jack in your wall.

Many cable companies are in the process of upgrading that last mile to fiber. Spectrum currently reports to the FCC that 2.3% of US households have access to its fiber plans, while 29.9% can get its cable plans.

“We don’t think customers should have to be telecom experts or squint at the fine print to know what they’re buying,” an AT&T representative told me in an email. “When internet is marketed as fiber, customers deserve 100% fiber all the way to their home.”

I spot-checked a handful of addresses on Spectrum’s website in Dallas, where AT&T is filing its lawsuit, and some of them did return fiber plans. According to FCC data, which is self-reported by ISPs, Spectrum covers around 608,000 households in Dallas, while AT&T covers almost 495,000.

This isn’t the first time Charter has been chided for passing itself off as a fiber provider. In March, Spectrum agreed to modify its “fiber-powered” statements after AT&T brought a challenge through the Better Business Bureau’s National Advertising Division.

Spectrum’s advertising describes its service as “fiber-powered” but notes in the fine print that it’s connected via coaxial lines. Spectrum/Screenshot by CNET

As a part of that challenge, Spectrum agreed to “clearly and conspicuously” disclose that its “fiber-powered internet services are not delivered to customers’ homes over a fiber-to-the-home infrastructure.” The fine print on Spectrum’s internet page notes that the connection to the premises is delivered via coaxial lines.

A representative for Charter did not immediately respond to my request for comment.

Tech.title: Equifax Customers Have Until Tuesday to Claim Part of a $2.2M Class Action Settlement
Tech.content:
Users of Equifax’s consumer credit reports service may be eligible to claim part of an upcoming $2.2 million settlement payout. The case centered on allegations that Equifax violated the Fair Credit Reporting Act, a federal statute that dictates credit reporting companies must “follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of the information concerning the individual about whom the report relates.”

The class action lawsuit Bradberry v. Equifax Information Services LLC alleged that, in 2022, Equifax “wrongfully reported duplicates of negative accounts” on certain consumer reports and that these duplicated debt tradelines are a result of the company having inadequate datakeeping policies and procedures. The lawsuit alleges that Equifax “negligently and recklessly disseminated false and damaging information” regarding the credit of certain customers.

Essentially, the lawsuit alleges that Equifax’s negligent reporting made some customers’ debts appear larger than they actually were, potentially creating situations where affected individuals couldn’t secure loans, credit cards, mortgages and other lines of credit.

The plaintiff, Charmayne Bradberry, filed the suit in the US District Court for the Northern District of Georgia. Bradberry said that she received a report showing the same $305 collection account twice, and that each instance showed separate “opened” and “reported” dates for the debt. She alleges that her credit score dropped severely following this report, which may have prevented her from securing a vital mortgage application.

Bradberry is one of 37,651 customers Equifax identified as having received reports with duplicate debt tradelines.

Equifax has denied any wrongdoing and denied that settlement class members were harmed by its actions, and the court has not ruled in favor of either side. The settlement was agreed upon by both parties, and the court has preliminarily approved the $2.2 million payment, subject to a final approval hearing.

The settlement website is live now. The hearing is scheduled to take place on Oct. 6, during which the court will confirm the settlement sum, allocate funds for attorneys’ fees and create a plan to distribute money to the affected class members.

While some class action lawsuits automatically pay out from the agreed-upon sum, that isn’t the case with Bradberry v. Equifax. Affected individuals need to file a claim and provide valid payment information by Sept. 1 to receive a share of the funds.

If you wish to opt out of or object to the settlement, you must do so by the same Sept. 1 deadline. Failure to do so will mean you remain part of the settlement class and forfeit your right to separately sue Equifax for this incident.

Who can be part of the Equifax settlement?

Not every Equifax customer is automatically eligible to claim part of the settlement. The money is reserved for people who received reports with duplicated collection account information that reflected larger sums of debt than existed in reality.

In order to join, you must meet the following qualifications:

Be a living individual in the US or its territories. Received one of the identified Duplicate Reporting Letters from Equifax between August and September 2022.

The settlement class in this case is extremely well-defined. Equifax identified 37,651 people who received duplicated reports. These individuals are the qualifying settlement class members.

Affected class members need to file a paper claim or log in through the settlement website in order to receive a payout. In order to file a claim online, you need to use the unique settlement member ID number included within the initial communication sent to affected individuals. This communication was sent out via postcard and email.

How much will the Equifax settlement pay out?

The total payment for each claimant is capped at $600, but actual payouts will depend on how many settlement class members file claims and how much money the court sets aside for attorney and administrative fees.

Whether or not settlement class members file a claim, they will receive six months of Equifax Complete credit monitoring services, including credit reports, credit score monitoring and up to $500,000 insurance for identity theft-related expenses.

During the claims process, class members must select a valid payment method for their share of the settlement funds. According to the paper claim form, you can choose to have the money sent to a PayPal, Venmo or Zelle account, a virtual prepaid card or a check.

If you’re eligible to claim a piece of the settlement sum, you must file by Sept. 1. Payments will be distributed after the court’s final approval hearing, assuming there are no appeals.

Tech.title: The Crazy Taxi Remake Revives the Dreamcast Era’s Zany Energy
Tech.content:
The Dreamcast era of games was a fever dream of wild, original ideas — Space Channel 5, Seaman, Shenmue, Chu Chu Rocket, Power Stone, Jet Set Radio and more — and perhaps nothing exemplified it better than Crazy Taxi, a game with its pitch in the name. Now, Sega is bringing its zany taxi driving classic back for modern consoles with Crazy Taxi: World Tour — and I got my hands on it for a short preview.

At a hotel in downtown Los Angeles, Sega lined up a half-dozen games for its summer press showcase, but my retro gaming heart was fixed on Crazy Taxi. Our current string of remasters is bringing some iconic games to modern audiences, but some, like Silent Hill 2 Remastered and Metal Gear Solid Delta, are based on games so canonized that the revivals aren’t surprising. Crazy Taxi wasn’t a milestone in gaming, but it’s a standout representation of the kinetic energy found in the best of Dreamcast’s game catalog, and I’m delighted to see it brought back.

Mind you, I only got about an hour with the new Crazy Taxi, which is due out in 2027, but I appreciated seeing what Sega kept from the original game — mostly vibes and its vibrant visual style, along with its signature fare-pickup system. You still drive up to a colorful circle representing a person in dire need of a quick ride and slam the accelerator to get them to their destination, haplessly crashing through cars and around pedestrians as the timer counts down. And yes, that sweet late ’90s-to-early 2000s alt rock and pop punk soundtrack is back — just take a listen to Sega’s latest trailer.

Unlike the original, there’s more to the game than just picking up fares until your time runs out. There are several modes in Crazy Taxi: World Tour, and the one I played was more of a free-form sandbox that let players drive around. The preview only had the map for Germany, one of many international locations in the final game, which was a large loop broken up by smaller zones — an airport, a city downtown, a small village and a castle on a hill.

It was in these German-themed pockets that I found my favorite feature of World Tour — specialized fares with their own mini-quests to complete. There were about 10 scattered around the map, and they were all some variation of insane. One was an unsettlingly enthusiastic man in an Easter Bunny costume asking me to help “collect his eggs,” another a daredevil in a wingsuit who wanted to be launched off a cliff from my cab’s backseat. Their dialogue suggested that I’d likely run into these bizarre specimens in other maps and had similarly assisted their bizarre life goals.

What could you even begin to mean by this, bunny guy?

This, this, is the Sega Dreamcast energy — the juxtaposition of exaggerated life with funky characters who took it to the next level. After every exhaustingly serious samurai game about regaining honor, beyond each deep RPG with a desperate quest to save the planet, I yearn for a game where I can enter the most lighthearted, dumb-in-the-best-way world of escalating inanity.

Sure, I can find some of that wackiness in emergent gameplay with my friends during a Big Walk or Peak or other modern party games. But I want the delight of a scripted weirdo, someone the game developers unearthed from a twisted corner of their brain that makes me laugh. Unsurprisingly, I often find this in Sega studio RGG’s Yakuza games. But in what I’ve seen, Crazy Taxi: World Tour brings back a bit of that classic, no-explanation-necessary oddball style I remember from booting up the latest Dreamcast game at the turn of the millennium.

As I found in my World Tour preview, where else could I pick up a sleazeball Lothario trying to escape his latest failed amorous encounter, dodging the missiles fired from pursuing cop cars, so I can drop my fare off literally on the wheels of a plane taking off? Keep the fares coming — the crazier, the better.

Tech.title: Eyes Up, Stargazers! Here’s What You Can See in September Night Skies
Tech.content:
It’s been an eventful summer for skygazers, with a full solar eclipse, the Perseids meteor shower and a nearly full lunar eclipse taking center stage. The fall season is coming soon, but there are a few things for skygazers to see this coming month before we’re officially in apple cider and hoodie weather.

September starts on a bit of a whisper but gets going relatively quickly. Here’s what’s coming up for amateur astronomers, from moon meetups and meteor showers to constellations and asterisms.

Meteor showers: Sept. 1 and Sept. 20

Taurids and Aurigids are minor meteor showers, so they’ll likely show off one meteor at a time, even during their peak. National Park Service/Brad Sutton

September hosts two meteor showers, with one finishing at the beginning of the month, and the other starting at the end of the month.

The Aurigids meteor shower is a minor meteor shower that starts toward the end of August and is fueled by the C/1911 N1 Kiess comet. It lasts about four or five days and peaks on the evening of Sept. 1.

It’s visible by looking at the Auriga constellation, which is the radiant of the Aurigids meteor shower, or the point at which the meteors appear to originate in the sky. It rises from the northeastern horizon shortly after midnight on Sept. 1.

The other meteor shower in September is the Southern Taurids. This is one of the longest meteor showers of the year, lasting exactly two months from Sept. 20 to Nov. 20. It’s fueled by the 2P/Encke comet, which is the same entity that fuels the Northern Taurids. The Northern Taurids start in October.

The Southern Taurids won’t peak until early November, so you’ll have to wait until then to see most of the meteors. Even so, you may see a stray meteor in the late September skies now and then. Both Taurids meteor showers have what are called “swarm years” when they’re much stronger. The next such year is predicted to be 2032.

The meteors appear to originate from the Taurus constellation. It rises from the eastern horizon shortly after 1 a.m. in late September, and is right next to the Ariga constellation.

Moon and planet meetups: Sept. 7, 8, 12 and 14

The moon is planning several hangouts with the planets in the sky in September. NASA

The moon is going to be pretty close to almost every visible planet in the night sky in September over the span of eight days.

The fun starts early in the morning on Sept. 7, when the moon and Mars are set to streak across the sky together. It starts shortly after 3 a.m. local time when both objects come up over the northeastern horizon. The moon follows Mars across the sky the remainder of the night, so if you can see one, you can quickly find the other.

When the moon rises the next morning on Sept. 8, it’s going to be followed by Jupiter, making both quite easy to see right next to each other.

The most challenging one is Mercury and the moon. Those two meet up right at sunset on Sept. 12, and you’ll only have a few minutes to spot both in the sky before they sink below the horizon.

Finally, the moon meets up with Venus on Sept. 14-15, again right at sunset and shortly after.

These are fairly common occurrences as the moon lines up with planets all the time, but meeting up with all four in the span of about a week is pretty cool and worth checking out.

The clearest skies: Sept. 11

Daniel Reinhardt/Getty Images

Skygazers often enjoy the full moon because they get the best possible view for telescopes and general enjoyment. However, the new moon on Sept. 11 is also important for visibility.

A new moon is the first lunar phase when it sits directly between Earth and the Sun, making the lunar disk invisible from our planet. The moon is the single largest source of light pollution in the sky, so when it’s not there to drown out your subject, you might be able to view stuff in the sky that’s usually harder to see.

That said, other skygazing tips still apply. The moon may be gone, but if you’re in a suburb or a city, light pollution there will still hinder your ability to see fainter objects in the sky. The moon will remain barely noticeable for a few days before and after Sept. 11, so you have a weeklong window before the moon starts getting too bright again.

Venus at its brightest: Sept. 18

Venus sets in the western horizon just after sunset, so if you want to see it, you won’t have long! Stellarium

There are two days a year when Venus is at its brightest, and one of them is in September. The planet is visible in the western sky along the horizon just after sunset local time, and it’s pretty hard to miss unless your view is obstructed by trees or buildings. This is the brightest Venus gets while it’s in the evening sky, and makes for a simple skygazing activity.

The other date when Venus is at its brightest is Nov. 29, but this time in the morning sky. Either way, Venus is following the sun, so your best bet is to see it just after sunset in September and just before sunrise in November to see it at its brightest.

Fall equinox: Sept. 22

NASA and NOAA weather satellites captured this image of the autumnal equinox in 2019. NASA/NOAA

This year, fall officially begins on Sept. 22, and the equinox starts at 8:05 p.m. ET. At this time, when the sun passes through Earth’s celestial equator, astronomers and scientists mark the beginning of the next season. The day should be roughly 12 hours from sunrise to sunset for the entire Northern Hemisphere, which is why we call it the equinox.

Unlike meteor showers or full moons, you can’t see anything in the sky. However, it does mark the changing of the season, which is celebrated in a variety of different ways. It’s the start of apple cider, bonfire and hoodie season, and many people consider it the start of the Halloween season.

Neptune at opposition: Sept. 25

If you can find Saturn and the moon, Neptune is right between them. Stellarium

Opposition is a fancy astronomy term that means a planet has drifted as close as it can to Earth along its orbit. Amateur astronomers enjoy these events because it makes these planets easier to see in the night sky. Neptune is sketchy to find even on the best of days since it’s so far away, but during opposition, it’s getting a full face of sunlight, making it easier to see than normal.

Neptune is situated between Saturn and the moon in the night sky on Sept. 25. It rises out of the eastern sky just after sunset and streaks across the sky until setting along the western horizon at sunrise. Since it’s just one day before the full moon (see below), light pollution could make Neptune challenging to see. Take a telescope or some high-powered binoculars, and you should be able to find it more easily.

Harvest moon: Sept. 26

The harvest moon seen from Washington, DC, in 2013. Bill Ingalls/NASA

September’s full moon occurs on Sept. 26, with full illumination happening at 12:49 p.m. ET. That’s in the middle of the day, so the brightest you can see the moon is the prior morning before sunrise or the next evening after sunset. If you can’t see it on those days, it’ll be over 90% full for a few days before and after the full moon date.

September’s full moon is usually called the corn moon. However, the full moon closest to the autumn equinox is always called the harvest moon. Since this one is only a few days off, September’s full moon gets the honors this year. This year’s harvest moon is the second-to-last normal full moon of the year before the rotation of supermoons begins again in November.

Constellations and asterisms: All month

Even if you don’t make it to a specific event, there’s a lot of stuff in the sky to look for. Stellarium

September begins the transition from summer sky to autumn sky, and so the constellations are coming in and out.

You’ll have several constellations to look for, including Cygnus, Lyra, Aquila, Pegasus, Capricornus, Aquarius and Cassiopeia. The Big and Little Dippers (officially called Ursa Minor and Ursa Major) are also there, along with minor constellations like Cepheus and Delphinus.

Most of these are visible for the entire month, but the summer ones like Cygnus, Lyra and Aquila are going to get progressively lower in the sky until they sink below the horizon, which means September is your last chance to see them until next year. Some, like Bootes, are already well on their way out, so the end of September will look different from the beginning.

Some minor asterisms like the Summer Triangle, the Teapot, the Northern Cross and the Coathanger are also visible for portions of September. All of those should give you plenty to look for in the night sky.

Tech.title: Tech Companies Call for Improved Cyber Defenses After AI-Enabled Attacks
Tech.content:
Saying that the world has only a “limited window” to bolster its defense against widespread AI cyberattacks, OpenAI and more than 100 other companies issued a call Friday for businesses, governments and other institutions to act quickly to boost cybersecurity.

The open letter, titled “A call for collective action on cyber defense,” was signed by 128 companies, including some of the biggest players in the AI space, including Microsoft, Google, Anthropic and Oracle.

The letter warns that “AI-enabled cyberattacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable,” putting companies, governments and infrastructure at risk.

But there are “ways to fix weaknesses that have accumulated for years.” The letter says companies must invest much more in security teams to fix old bugs and other vulnerabilities, share their cyber-capable AI tools with other companies and mobilize globally and collectively to “raise security standards and find new solutions.”

The ‘nightmare’ is coming

AI agents have repeatedly made headlines this summer for wreaking havoc, whether intended or unintended. Models escaped an OpenAI test environment in which they weren’t supposed to access the open internet. They found a software vulnerability, exploited it and got online. Once there, hundreds of AI agents used stolen credentials, communicated with each other on makeshift message boards and eventually hacked into the AI platform Hugging Face.



There have been more than a dozen major incidents over the past year. Anthropic’s AI models breached three unnamed companies. Meta’s AI hacked a “third-party service” earlier this month. A Claude AI agent hacked a gym in Australia to get its user into a gym class. The problem is that AI agents, trained on heaps of code, are great at finding software flaws and vulnerabilities and will keep plugging away until they complete their tasks.

‘Urgency and coordination’

In its open letter, OpenAI describes four broad steps that must be taken. All organizations — both private and public — should fix “highest-risk weaknesses,” only deploy highly secure AI-generated code and strengthen permission and access controls. Cybersecurity companies should strengthen defenses against AI attacks and help deploy them for critical infrastructure operations, such as water and utility systems. Governments at all levels need to invest more funds in cyber defense — especially for greatly underfunded departments — and “give hospitals, water utilities, and local governments access to capable defensive AI.”

Finally, frontier AI companies should, among other things, “ensure agentic identities are traceable and accountable” and share “credible threat assessments with governments, security partners, and open-source maintainers.” Companies must monitor and invest more in monitoring, testing and fixing AI systems.

Teams in charge of essential services should be the initial focal point of getting cyber-capable AI, the letter says. “Fix the most dangerous weaknesses, verify the fixes, and share what works so others can build on it.”
